Among teachers, those employed in any educational institution of govt, local authority, aided or unaided private bodies, societies or trusts will be eligible to be hired as enumerators
NEW DELHI: The home ministry Friday expanded the pool of enumerators for the Census exercise, making teachers of not just govt schools but also that of aided or unaided private bodies, societies and trusts; and clerks or officials employed not just by central and state govts but also by public sector undertakings, banks etc, eligible for the assignment.Amending Census Rules 1990, the ministry, in a notification issued Friday, expanded the description of staff who can be hired as enumerators for Census 2027, the second phase of which is due to start in five poll-bound states in Nov, followed by the remaining states (barring the snow-bound UT of Ladakh and parts of Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh and J&K where it is already over) in Feb next year.The description of those who can be hired as enumerators — encapsulated in Rule 3 of the Census Rules — has been revised from “teachers, clerks or any official or any person” to three distinct categories.Among teachers, those employed in any educational institution of govt, local authority, aided or unaided private bodies, societies or trusts will be eligible to be hired as enumerators. Also, clerks or any official of central govt, state govt, local authority or establishment, including PSUs, statutory bodies, banks, companies, institutions, societies and trusts may be assigned the job of census enumerator.
This pool will now also include any person that the state govt or Union territory administration may consider suitable for performing the duties as an enumerator.The amended rules — to be called the Census (Amendment) Rules, 2026 — will offer more clarity to what classes of officials and staff may be hired to carry out the job of census enumerators, apart from expanding the talent pool. Given that the second phase of census — involving population enumeration — will, in a first since 1931, also record caste, the availability of a wide range of suitably qualified officials for engagement as enumerators is expected to help in correctly capturing the responses to the Phase 2 questionnaire.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

UK police assess Palestine Action post by national security adviser's wife
British police said on Friday they were assessing a social media post after the wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell appeared to express support for Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group banned as a terrorist organisation.
Journalist and author Sarah Helm, who is married to Powell, responded on X to a post about the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, who this week announced her books would no longer be sold in Britain over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action.

Asked for comment, a government spokeswoman said: "These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity."

Four members of the group were jailed in June over a 2024 raid on a factory operated by Israeli defence firm Elbit which caused more than £1 million of damage.
Amnesty International says more than 3,500 people have been arrested in Britain for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned last year, many of them for holding up placards.
Palestine Action challenged the government's decision to ban the group, but the Court of Appeal ruled in June that the proscription was lawful.

TOKYO, October 17. /TASS/. Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has sent an offering to the Yasukuni Shinto shrine, which is considered a symbol of militarism in China and several other Asian countries, according to Kyodo news agency.
Takaichi, as Kyodo notes, refrained from making a personal visit to the shrine not to create diplomatic problems with South Korea and China, which react sharply to such pilgrimages. Before becoming prime minister, Takaichi regularly visited this shrine twice a year, including as a minister. The last time the head of the Japanese government personally made a pilgrimage to Yasukuni was in December 2013, when Shinzo Abe held that position.
The current offering was made on the occasion of the traditional autumn festival celebrated at the shrine. Takaichi’s previous offering on the occasion of the 81st anniversary of the announcement of Tokyo’s surrender in World War II, which was marked on August 15 of this year, was made not as the head of the government, but as the leader of the ruling Liberal Democratic Party.
This Shinto shrine, located in the center of Tokyo, houses lists of names of the Japanese people who died on the battlefield since the second half of the 19th century. The list also includes war criminals who were executed after Tokyo’s surrender in World War II by order of the International Military Tribunal. Visits to Yasukuni by Japanese officials provoke protests and are perceived in China, South Korea, and other Asian countries as a justification of Japanese aggression.

Trump Fires White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia After Just Five Days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
23:44:02 UTC
08:44:02 KST

US President Donald Trump dismissed White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia on Friday, Oct. 16, just five days after she took office, following a series of public controversies involving her legal credentials, a widely criticized press briefing and remarks about China that drew a response from Beijing.
A White House official confirmed her departure to AFP after Fox News reported that the 41-year-old spokeswoman was “transitioning out” of the position, bringing an abrupt end to what is believed to be the shortest tenure of any White House press secretary in US history.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The dismissal came hours after Trump publicly suggested that Zacharia reconsider whether she wanted to remain in the high-profile job.
“I said, ‘Katie, is this for you?’” Trump told reporters Friday, recalling his conversation with the spokeswoman. “I said, ‘Katie, you don’t have to do this’... I said to her, ‘Honestly if I were you I’d reconsider.’”
Zacharia had replaced Karoline Leavitt, one of Trump’s most outspoken defenders, who frequently clashed with journalists and expanded access for conservative media outlets during her tenure.
Her dismissal comes as Trump faces mounting political challenges ahead of the Nov. 3 congressional midterm elections, including public dissatisfaction over inflation, the war against Iran and questions surrounding his administration’s conduct.
One briefing, three questions and a troubled debut
Zacharia’s first and only White House press briefing on Tuesday, Oct. 13, lasted less than 15 minutes and attracted criticism for its unusually slow opening statement and limited interaction with reporters.
Republican Fitzpatrick Warns of Funding Consequences Over Ukraine’s Starlink Restrictions
She began by reading a lengthy account of Trump’s accomplishments before taking just three questions from journalists.
The performance quickly drew scrutiny, raising questions about her readiness to serve as the administration’s chief spokesperson during a politically sensitive period.
Despite the criticism, the White House initially defended her performance. But the controversy soon shifted from her briefing-room appearance to her professional qualifications.
Failed bar exam raises questions about legal credentials
Zacharia had repeatedly described herself as a lawyer during television appearances and on social media. She had also been listed as general counsel for a California-based conservative nonprofit.
Trump himself introduced her as an attorney when announcing her appointment.
However, reports revealed that although she graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school, she had never passed the bar examination required to obtain a license to practice law in California.
In a Thursday interview with Fox News host Sean Hannity, Zacharia acknowledged that she had failed the examination.
When Hannity asked whether she had retaken it, she replied, “I did not.”
She maintained that she had never intended to practice law in the US.
“It was never my intent to go into the practice of law,” she said.
In another interview with the conservative outlet Real America’s Voice, Zacharia explained that she had registered for the examination but became distracted by plans to move to China with her husband.
She claimed that people in the legal profession had advised her that she could describe herself as a lawyer because she held a law degree.
The explanation failed to resolve questions about her previous descriptions of herself as an attorney.
According to a Washington Post examination of her credentials, there was no record of Zacharia being admitted to practice law in any US jurisdiction.
Comments about China’s toilets spark response from Beijing
The controversy widened Thursday after Zacharia made dismissive remarks about China during an interview with conservative commentator Jack Posobiec.
Recalling her time living in China and predictions that Beijing would eventually surpass Washington economically, Zacharia questioned how the country could become a global leader.
“I remember this very distinctly, having just come from China, thinking, ‘How is China the next country on the horizon? They don’t even have proper toilets,’” she said.
The comments drew attention because they came shortly after Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, where Trump had hosted him as part of efforts to manage relations between the two powers.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning responded Friday by suggesting Zacharia should “visit China more often.”
The exchange added an unexpected diplomatic controversy to the spokeswoman’s already troubled first week.
Trump ally questions whether she still has president’s confidence
Zacharia’s attempts to contain the fallout through interviews with conservative outlets appeared to create further difficulties.
During a Friday appearance on Fox & Friends, a program generally supportive of Trump, she was asked directly whether she still enjoyed the president’s confidence.
Rather than answer the question, Zacharia said, “I hope to be able to build the trust and confidence of everyone around me.”
The response came as speculation intensified about whether she would remain in the position.
Hours later, her departure was confirmed.
Trump has indicated that he is in no rush to appoint a replacement, leaving the White House without a permanent press secretary at a time when the administration faces a contentious election campaign and growing foreign policy challenges.

"I think there's no doubt that he wants to be back in the game for us, that's for sure," Kiss said.
"We'll continue our conversations and go from there. I'm not going to speak on his behalf at all. But we know where he wants to play."

Trump’s press secretary out after just five days
Katie Zacharia is stepping down as US President Donald Trump’s press secretary after just five days on the job, the White House confirmed on Friday.
A conservative political commentator, Zacharia has faced widespread criticism over her handling of her debut press briefing and allegations that she misrepresented her legal credentials.
Trump cast doubt on Zacharia’s future in the role while speaking to reporters outside the White House. “Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider,” he said, adding that he had spoken to her shortly beforehand. “Katie, do you need this? I don’t think you need this.”
Several hours later, White House communications director Steven Cheung said Zacharia would be “transitioning into a new role that will be announced at a later date.”
According to the New York Times, Zacharia largely read from a script during her first and only press briefing on Tuesday and ended the Q&A session after just five and a half minutes. Critics also accused her of misrepresenting herself as a lawyer after she failed to confirm whether she had passed a US bar exam. Zacharia later claimed to have passed a bar exam in China, where she worked for a Beijing-based law firm in the 2010s.
Zacharia’s five-day stint marks the shortest tenure of any White House press secretary in US history. During his first term, Trump fired White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci in July 2017, just ten days after his appointment, following a profanity-laden phone call with a reporter in which he attacked senior administration officials.

Several high-profile officials have left the Trump administration this year, including Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, Attorney General Pam Bondi, Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer, and Navy Secretary John Phelan.

UN Security Council holds 6th straw poll on secretary-general candidates
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:34:11 CST
08:34:11 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The UN Security Council on Friday held its sixth straw poll on candidates vying to become the next UN secretary-general.
"The sixth round of straw polls has taken place," said Aglaia Balta, Greece's permanent representative to the United Nations, whose country holds the rotating presidency of the Security Council for the month of October.
Each candidate will be informed of the results through the permanent representatives of nominating member states. The president of the UN General Assembly will also be informed that the poll has been conducted, Balta told reporters after the secret vote.
Security Council straw polls on secretary-general candidates are informal closed-door ballots used to determine the viability of the candidates. Their results are not officially released.
Through the polls, the Security Council selects a candidate to recommend to the General Assembly for appointment as the next UN secretary-general.
Security Council members were believed to receive one ballot per candidate, containing the candidate's name followed by three options: "encouraged," "discouraged" and "no opinion expressed."
To win the Security Council's recommendation, a candidate needs to gain at least nine "encouraged" votes and no "discouraged" votes from any of the five permanent members of the council.
Seven candidates remain in the race: Ivonne A-Baki, a former Ecuadorian minister and diplomat; Maria Fernanda Espinosa, a former president of the UN General Assembly and former foreign minister and defense minister of Ecuador; Rafael Grossi of Argentina, current director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency; Rebeca Grynspan, a former vice president of Costa Rica and current secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development; Olara Otunnu of Uganda, a former UN under-secretary-general; Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, Guyana's permanent representative to the United Nations; Macky Sall, a former president of Senegal.
Current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' term expires at the end of this year. His successor is scheduled to take office on Jan. 1, 2027. ■

Colombia resumes power exports to Ecuador
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
07:33:48 CST
08:33:48 KST

QUITO, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa announced Friday that Colombia has resumed electricity exports to Ecuador, whose power system is under strain amid dry conditions.
In a post on X, Noboa thanked Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella for resuming electricity exports and underscored cooperation between the two countries.
Colombia suspended commercial electricity exports to Ecuador in recent weeks amid concerns that the intensifying El Niño phenomenon could increase the risk of domestic power shortages.
The resumption of electricity supplies will help ease pressure on Ecuador's power system, which has been strained by reduced river flows feeding its hydropower plants. A lack of rainfall in southern Ecuador has caused drought conditions, affecting reservoir levels at the Paute Hydroelectric Complex, which supplies about 35 percent of the electricity fed into Ecuador's national interconnected system.
The power interconnection with Colombia can cover about 10 percent of Ecuador's peak demand, providing a backup when hydropower generation is low.
While the government has ruled out power cuts for households, industries connected to medium- and high-voltage networks face up to 72 hours of power cuts per week as authorities seek to ease pressure on the system. The measure has drawn opposition from business groups over concerns about its potential impact on economic activity and employment.
In 2024, Ecuador experienced an unprecedented energy crisis, resulting in power outages of up to 14 hours a day. ■

Albanian PM blames ‘foreign hands’ for unrest as student protests intensify

Albanian PM blames ‘foreign hands’ for unrest as student protests intensify
Riot police clash with protesters for fourth day, as young Albanians protest corruption and poor university conditions
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has blamed “foreign hands” for the increasingly violent student-led protests that are calling on him to resign.
Riot police clashed with protesters outside the education ministry for the fourth day in a row, as thousands of young Albanians marched through the capital, Tirana, on Friday to protest government corruption and poor university conditions.
“This is not a student phenomenon,” Rama said in a video address on Friday. He said there were “foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace”.
Rama insisted that the protest had “absolutely nothing to do with the hardships, problems or legitimate aspirations of anyone who desires a better life”.
Police officers used water cannon and tear gas as demonstrators hurled rocks.
The protests have spread beyond the capital to Elbasan, Shkodra and Korca, where demonstrators broke windows and set fire to rubbish bins, local media reported.
The ongoing escalation follows months of mostly peaceful demonstrations, originally sparked by the sale of part of Albania’s coastline to a luxury resort development linked to Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.
Days of unrest have increasingly targeted banks and government buildings. Protesters hurled bricks and concrete blocks at the education ministry on Tuesday. They also set fire to several buildings across the city, including the prime minister’s office, the finance and justice ministry buildings and branches of several banks.
According to a police statement, 160 people were detained over alleged acts of violence on Thursday evening.
The EU question
Demonstrators are demanding Rama’s resignation, as well as electoral and education reforms.
The prime minister, whose government denies corruption, said he would be ready to discuss rising education costs but rejected the calls to resign.
He said on Thursday, “My responsibility is to listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward.”

Corruption scandals have complicated Albania’s efforts to join the EU. Analysts say the country is a hub for gangs seeking to launder money from drugs and weapons trafficking.

Grynspan holds lead for next UN chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
23:16:30 UTC
08:16:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Grynspan holds lead for next UN chief as race enters decisive stage
An informal poll by the United Nations Security Council on Friday placed former Costa Rican Vice President Rebeca Grynspan as the narrow frontrunner in the race to become the 10th UN secretary-general, two people close to the process said.
But there was no clear winner as all candidates received two or more opposing votes from the ultimately decisive five permanent members of the council — Russia, China, the US, France and Britain — opening the door for new candidates to join the race, diplomats and observers said.
Whoever wins will have to tackle multiple crises, including several wars, cutbacks in American contributions to the UN, and the 193-member body's declining political relevance as Washington has pulled out of dozens of its agencies.
This was the sixth secret ballot organized by council officials, who have less than three months to pick the successor to UN chief Antonio Guterres, whose term ends on December 31.
Securing the council's recommendation requires at least nine positive votes of the 15 countries and no "discourage" votes from the five permanent members.
The race has entered a decisive stage, as Friday's poll for the first time used color-coded ballots revealing whether a veto power opposes a candidate.
Four of five polls in recent months showed Grynspan, 70, narrowly ahead, with one poll in August placing Guyana's UN ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett in the top spot.
This dynamic did not fundamentally change on Friday, with Grynspan receiving nine "encourage," five "discourage" and one "no opinion" vote, with two of the five opposing votes coming from the Security Council's permanent members, people close to the process said.
Rodrigues-Birkett received eight votes in favor, six against, and one "no opinion," with two opposing votes from the permanent members.
Rafael Grossi, director general of the UN nuclear watchdog, received a near-identical result to Rodrigues-Birkett, but with one fewer permanent member supporting his bid.
Four more former UN officials and senior diplomats are vying for support, but they have received more opposing than supporting votes, indicating waning enthusiasm for their candidacies.
Diplomats say several senior figures, including former and current foreign ministers and country leaders, are considering entering the race. Any new entrant will face a steep challenge of convincing the divided council in short order.
On the question of new contenders joining the race, Washington's envoy to the UN, Mike Waltz, said after the vote: "Countries, if they want to put more candidates in, that's certainly within their sovereign rights."
When Guterres was chosen in October 2016, it took six straw polls for the council to reach agreement.
In the more than 80-year history of the UN, there has never been a female secretary-general.
In an interview with Reuters on Thursday, Grynspan said she "wouldn't be surprised" to receive a veto and said that it would be just the start of negotiations as such blocking votes have been overcome by winning contenders in past races.
"The game is not over -- we will have to continue working," she said.
The Costa Rican economist added that the UN has become too risk-averse and its next leader must be prepared to bear the cost of diplomatic failure and try again.
She also said the UN must cut top jobs, curb bureaucracy and stop agencies duplicating work, arguing that cost-cutting alone would not revive an institution struggling with shrinking resources and declining political clout.

Uncovering the secrets of New Zealand’s elusive ‘jungle penguins’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
23:15:14 UTC
08:15:14 KST

Deep in the misty fjords of New Zealand’s South Island, a team of researchers is trying to catch one of the world’s most elusive penguins: the forest-dwelling tawaki, or Fiordland crested penguin.For weeks, researchers stand sentry each day over a burrow on Eleanor Island, hoping to corner the female bird so they can retrieve data from its tagging device.
But this penguin has developed a clever exit strategy – digging multiple tunnels to elude its captors.
“It took us about four days to recapture that bird,” says Dr Thomas Mattern, a research fellow at the University of Otago and chair of the Tawaki Project, a scientific initiative established to study the population.
“We plugged all the holes around the nest so that it could not escape, until we finally could recover that device,” he adds.
In a first for the species, Tawaki Project researchers are conducting long-term population counts, unlocking secrets about the bird’s breeding and foraging habits, and what threats they might face.
The project is New Zealand’s most comprehensive mapping of tawaki nests. Over September, it mapped 93 nests across two islands in Fiordland, and has now mapped 1,200 nests across nine fjords in the past 12 years. Its mapping shows the tawaki population is roughly three times bigger than earlier surveys suggest, says Mattern, pictured below at Precipice Cove.
The Māori name for crested penguins, tawaki, is a catch-all for several species around New Zealand and the sub-Antarctic region, but the focus of this annual voyage is on the declining species that inhabits remote Fiordland, New Zealand’s largest national park, which is Unesco heritage listed.
Until German-born Mattern and his wife, Ursula Ellenberg, founded the volunteer research project in 2014, almost nothing was known about Fiordland’s tawaki, which stands half a metre tall, and features prominent yellow eyebrows.
“Tawaki are a ghost,” Mattern says of the penguin’s enigmatic behaviour.
But “they are the most amazing penguin species … They do not fit any penguin mould. What we know about penguins, you throw it all out of the window.”
Unlike most penguins, the Fiordland tawaki do not breed in colonies, preferring instead to build single burrows deep in dense rainforest, sometimes at high elevations. While some other species can nest in forests, tawaki are unique because they nest exclusively in forests, Mattern says, describing them as “proper jungle penguins”.
Its hunting habits are also unusual. Some groups fish entirely within the fjords, while others hunt in the ocean.
“When you think you have them nailed down, you go to a different fjord, and they show behaviour that just does not conform to any of the ideas you have developed so far,” Mattern says.
‘Absolutely zero sense’
Tawaki have also become infamous among scientists for their baffling journey to feed before they go through their annual “catastrophic moult” – the scientific term for when animals shed and replace all their feathers in one go.
All penguins moult after breeding season and before they do, they eat vast quantities of food to put on weight. Despite an abundance of food around the fjords in December (when breeding season ends), tawaki undertake a 5,000 to 7,000km return trip to the sub-Antarctic region to feed.
“These emaciated tawaki, that have just said goodbye to their chicks, hop in the water and travel halfway to Antarctica, which makes absolutely zero sense because there should be more than enough food in the water just outside their breeding area,” Mattern says.
“They are running a marathon, while trying to gain weight.”
Mattern believes tawaki are likely acting on ancient instinct, heading to grounds where all other crested penguin species feed.
The Tawaki Project is funded by public donations and international grants, and supported by local volunteers, such as
Richard Abernathy, the owner of tourism company Fiordland Expeditions, who donates his boat and time to the expedition for several weeks a year.
“Since 2018, we’ve been chasing penguins all over Fiordland,” says Abernathy whose ability to find nests in surprising places has earned him the nickname “sniffer dog”.
Together, their efforts have “shed light on the most understudied species” in New Zealand, Mattern says.
In 2020, the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List moved tawaki up in status from “vulnerable” to “near-threatened” because the researchers were able to develop a better picture of their populations, estimated to be in the region of 12,00 to 15,000 mature birds.
But risks remain, including from commercial fishing practices.
“[We’re] looking at survival rates … to determine whether the population is stable,” says Mattern.
“If they’re going down, then we need to kick into gear to improve the situation for them.”

China’s tourists flock to experience a pretend typhoon as ‘dark tourism’ flourishes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
23:15:14 UTC
08:15:14 KST

When Leon Lv was looking for somewhere to travel last year, she turned to the Chinese social media app RedNote for ideas. The algorithm took her to videos of people struggling to survive typhoon-strength winds and flash floods.
“I never experienced a typhoon. I don’t know how it will feel and what will happen. I just have seen it on the news,” says the 28-year-old from Chongqing in south-west China. “So that’s why I want to go there to have a safe place to experience it and learn something.”
She travelled more than 1,300km to Hangzhou in the east, and joined a group of 20 to take part in a disaster simulation that featured a typhoon-fuelled flooding scenario.
Standing in a simulated flood, her mind momentarily went blank as hundreds of tonnes of water swept people off their feet, and carried them towards a safety barrier. As the surge hit, she forgot she was in a simulation. “One thing I learned is how to stay calm and protect myself during a flood. I learned how to use the right body position to stay safe,” she says. “No book and no school [can] teach me like that.”
Across Chinese social platforms phrases like “paying to suffer”, or “paying to buy fear” are trending online as part of a wave of interest in experiences known as “dark tourism”.
Lvxing Base, a company in Hangzhou offering simulated disaster experiences has gone viral. The founders spent 10 years making documentaries in some of the world’s most extreme environments.
At a 200,000 square metre facility, which opened in 2024, they simulate extreme weather conditions like typhoons and mudslides, giving participants the experience of what it would be like in a disaster.
“I don’t deny that many people come because they want excitement,” says general manager Wang Kuanghan. They want to see what this place is like, what a real typhoon and torrential rain feel like, and whether they themselves can withstand it. Most of our individual customers are between 20 and 30 years old.”
It plans to open five more centres across China within the next three years. It also plans to create earthquake and fire simulations.
The offering are not limited to private companies. At Beijing’s Haidian public safety museum, tourists experience simulated earthquakes, tsunamis and fires using a 4D theatre, equipped with moving platforms and sound effects. Last year the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou opened a five-storey centre to teach visitors how to respond to emergencies and disasters. Its earthquake simulator can recreate ground shaking equivalent to a 7.2 magnitude quake.
Extreme weather has become increasingly common in China. In 2025, China recorded its highest number of hot days since records began, and was hit by 10 typhoons, well above the long-term annual average. China’s ministry of emergencies reported that 67 million people were affected by such disasters across the country.
In 2024, local governments were instructed to promote immersive disaster education, instructing safety centres, museums and training bases to use simulations to teach people how to respond in a real crisis.
‘A new generation of travellers’
“The new generation of Chinese travellers want to experience a place rather than simply see famous attractions,” says Robert Li, director of the School of Hotel and Tourism Management at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.
But some travellers have found a way to blend the two approaches; rather than indulging in the white-knuckle ride of a simulated typhoon, they are travelling to real sites of death and destruction.
In May 2008 a magnitude 8.0 earthquake devastated towns in China’s Sichuan province, killing more than 70,000 people. Alice*, a 30-year-old writer from Sichuan walked around Beichuan, one of the affected towns, the ruins of which the government had preserved. Metal beams hold collapsed buildings in place for the public to visit. She saw the site where schools collapsed, crushing students inside.
In Yingxue close to the epicentre, a broken clock surrounded by the remains of a middle school is frozen at 2.28, the moment the earthquake struck.
“I felt scared because of the power of nature and how many children and students could not escape from it,” says Alice, who plans to start a Chinese language Substack account detailing her journeys into tragedy. “Everything was so broken. It became like a ghost town, because nobody lives in the old town any more.”
Alice believes dark tourism helps a country reconcile with its past, even if the government decides what can be remembered.
In recent years, tour guide Samantha Wang has seen an increase in Chinese tourists attending the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall. In 1937 the Japanese Imperial army captured Nanjing, and Chinese official accounts say 300,000 civilians and soldiers were killed over weeks of massacres. Japan’s official position is that it acknowledges that large numbers of civilians were killed but says the number of victims is “difficult to determine”.
Entry to the hall is free but tourists must book online The local government reserves 25,000 places a day. In August, tickets to attend the museum are frequently sold out in advance, she says.
“There are more tragic sites in China, and I see more people interested to know about that. That’s a new trend” says Wang.
Inside the memorial hall hang photos of victims. “They [visitors] feel sad when they see those pictures, when they see those kids who were killed … After the visit, they feel relieved, and they feel encouraged that they should work harder to make China stronger,” she says.
*Name has been changed
Additional reporting by Yu-chen Li in Taipei

Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
00:07:18 BST
08:07:18 KST

Trial of German steakhouse heiress that sparked a huge spy scandal
- Published
It is a trial that has gripped Germany, with a wealthy heiress in the dock for months and a case that triggered the country's biggest espionage scandal in recent history.
Christina Block, heir to a popular chain of steakhouses, is accused of ordering an Israeli security firm to carry out the violent abduction of her children from Denmark, following a bitter custody battle with her former husband.
There are allegedly connections with at least two former secret agents, from Germany and Israel.
In the latest twist, investigators in the case stumbled across evidence that has led to Germany's former intelligence chief, August Hanning, being arrested this month for treason and espionage.
Hanning's arrest stunned the intelligence community. Although his case has nothing to do with the Hamburg trial, he has denied allegations of involvement in an earlier attempted abduction of the children.
There was enormous media interest in Germany when Christina Block and six others went on trial in a high-security courtroom in Hamburg in July last year.
Block House restaurants, specialising in steak and baked potatoes, are a feature of many German towns. Their success over the past half century has helped make Christina Block's father Eugen a multimillionaire.
Prosecutors allege that she and a family lawyer, Andreas Costard, organised the forcible abduction of two of her children, who were staying with her former husband, Stephan Hensel, at his home in Denmark.
They say the operation was carried out by a 36-year-old Israeli citizen named only as Jonathan G and five others.
The abduction took place during the New Year celebrations of 2023-24, as the two children and their father were watching a firework display, according to the indictment.
Prosecutors say several men ambushed and beat up Stephan Hensel, and dragged the boy and the girl, then 10 and 13 years old, into a car.
On the approach to the border with Germany, they are alleged to have changed vehicles, taped up the children's mouths and tied the girl's hands.
The group are then said to have travelled on to Baden-Württemberg in a campervan. Prosecutors say the children were held there against their will until their mother arrived to pick them up on 2 January 2024 and took them to her home in Hamburg.
Christina Block, Andreas Costard and Jonathan G are charged with the abduction of minors, grievous bodily harm and unlawful detention.
Block's partner, a former TV sports presenter called Gerhard Delling, and three others are charged with aiding and abetting.
All of them deny wrongdoing, except for Jonathan G, who has admitted his involvement. However, he told the court he thought he was taking part in a rescue operation.
The trial comes after years of legal battles between Christina Block and her former husband, Stephan Hensel, over who had the right to look after the children.
Immediately after their separation, all four children lived with their mother in Hamburg. Hensel, who remarried, later moved to Denmark, where they regularly visited him.
In 2021, the two youngest children went to visit their father in Denmark, but then were not brought back to Hamburg as agreed.
A court in Hamburg ruled that Christina had custody and that the children should be returned. However, in February 2023, a Danish court ruled that, although the boy and the girl had been brought to Denmark unlawfully, they could not be taken back.
In May 2023, Hensel was charged with the abduction of minors, in a case which is still pending.
He has accused Christina of being violent with the children, charges she denies. She told the court Hensel wanted to take revenge on her.
She also denied knowing anything about plans for the abduction of the children from Denmark. Her defence argues that the Israeli security team had acted on its own initiative.
She told the court it was "a catastrophe" and that she had never wanted anything like that.
The head of the Israeli security team, David Barkay, who is not on trial but faces future legal proceedings, told the court that Christina Block and Costard had known about the planned repatriation operation.
Barkay, who was described by another witness as a former agent with Mossad, the Israeli secret service, said he had not shared all the details because he "didn't trust them."
The alleged connection with Germany's former spy chief, August Hanning, relates to accusations of an earlier attempt to abduct the children and bring them back from Denmark in 2022.
Prosecutors have said Hanning was responsible for arranging security staff sent to Denmark with Christina Block. His lawyer denies the accusations. Hanning has not been charged over the current Block court case.
However, while investigators were searching his home, they came across evidence to suggest Hanning was involved in buying some 2,000 documents from his former chief of staff and then passing on state secrets to foreign powers.
Which foreign power and who he is alleged to have given the secrets to is unspecified, but it has prompted widespread speculation.
Now 80, Hanning is in custody charged with treasonous espionage. His lawyer says he is being "unjustly persecuted" and that the charges are "unfounded".
Meanwhile the trial against Christina Block is currently on hold for two weeks - one of numerous delays and extensions over the course of the past 15 months.
The latest delay is because a witness, Stephan Hensel's new wife, failed to appear in court.

Drone strike kills 30 at cattle market in Sudan's Darfur

Breadcrumb
Drone strike kills 30 at cattle market in Sudan's Darfur
A drone strike on a cattle market in Sudan's Nyala killed 30 people on Friday, AFP reported, in one of the deadliest attacks on the paramilitary stronghold in the western Darfur region.
The Rapid Support Forces blamed the attack on the army, while a military source acknowledged an uptick in strikes on the area, without claiming responsibility.
Both the RSF and the army, at war since April 2023, have increasingly used drones to launch far-reaching attacks without sacrificing their fighters.
Nyala, Sudan's second-largest city and the capital of South Darfur state, serves as the seat of the self-declared administration established by the RSF last year.
"The drone strike on the city's cattle market today killed 30 people and wounded 47 others, who are receiving treatment at the hospital," a medical source at Nyala Hospital told AFP on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to brief the media.
The source did not say who was responsible for the attack.
The strike hit the livestock market on a Friday morning, when traders and shoppers typically crowd the area and roadside stalls serve grilled meat, a popular breakfast in Darfur.
The RSF accused the Sudanese army of carrying out Friday's attack using a Turkish-made drone.
In a statement, the paramilitary group said the strike targeted a densely populated civilian area, adding that preliminary reports indicated 17 women and five children were among the dead.
A military source, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP that the army had intensified strikes against RSF positions inside Nyala on Friday.
The source said the military had also targeted Nyala airport 48 hours earlier, adding that all attacks were aimed at military objectives.
Drone warfare
Sudan's war, now in its fourth year, has killed tens of thousands of people, displaced more than 11 million and triggered what the United Nations has described as one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.
More than 1,100 people were killed in drone attacks across Sudan during the first half of this year alone, according to the UN.
Nyala has come under repeated drone attacks in recent months as the army seeks to challenge RSF control over Darfur.
The paramilitary group seized most of the region last year after capturing El-Fasher, the last major Darfur city previously held by the army, in an offensive that UN experts said bore "the hallmarks of genocide".
The latest strike comes as fighting intensifies in several parts of the country, including the strategic Kordofan region linking Darfur to central and eastern Sudan.
On Thursday, an army Antonov aircraft struck a house in the paramilitary-controlled village of Abu Zaeima in North Kordofan, killing five children from the same family and wounding their mother, according to the rights group Emergency Lawyers.
Recent attacks in Kordofan have also hit a shelter for displaced people and a university dormitory, killing at least 15 people, the group said.

Ukraine could strip critical workers of draft exemptions – PM
Ukraine could reduce mobilization exemptions for employees of companies deemed critical to the country, Prime Minister Sergey Koretsky has said, arguing that employers are exploiting the current system.
The country declared mobilization shortly after the escalation of the conflict with Russia in February 2022, barring most military-age men from leaving the country.
However, approximately 1.4 million Ukrainians currently hold employment-based exemptions from military service, according to Economy Minister Aleksandr Kravchenko.
Speaking during a Q&A session in the Ukrainian parliament on Friday, Koretsky said the government is considering stripping critical-sector employers of the right to exempt 100% of their staff. He cited cases in which companies had significantly expanded their workforces, with all employees automatically shielded from conscription.
“Unfortunately, there are many abuses, and additional exemptions continue to be granted every month,” Koretsky said.
“If you have a 100% exemption, it means you can expand your workforce indefinitely and exempt people from mobilization, regardless of whether they actually work as repair technicians, energy workers or in other roles. Unfortunately, this practice has already become widespread,” he added.
Koretsky said some companies had received blanket exemptions despite not meeting the criteria for being classified as critical. As an example, he cited an unnamed contractor for Ukrenergo, the national power grid operator. “When we looked into the details, it turned out that only 20 out of 100 employees were actually working for Ukrenergo. Yet all 100 were exempted,” Koretsky said.
The prime minister called for audits to determine how many employees at a given company perform tasks essential to its operations and the country’s needs. He added that stricter criteria could be applied to businesses as a whole, with only those supporting Ukraine’s defense capabilities and other essential state functions qualifying as critical.
Earlier this week, opposition MP Yaroslav Zhelezhnyak published what he claimed was a draft of the proposed changes, reducing exemption quotas for defense and energy companies from 100% to 85%, and for housing and utility companies from 75% to 60%.
Multiple lawmakers and businesses have warned that such measures would exacerbate existing staffing shortages in critical industries.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian outlet Strana UA reported on Thursday, citing sources, that relations between Koretsky and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky had deteriorated. The outlet claimed that Zelensky could dismiss Koretsky in the spring of 2027 and blame him for government failures during the winter months.
Koretsky, who was appointed prime minister in a government reshuffle in July, has been linked by local media to disgraced businessman and former close Zelensky associate Timur Mindich, who fled to Israel amid an investigation into an alleged $100 million embezzlement scheme involving state nuclear power operator Energoatom.
According to Strana UA, Koretsky has defied Zelensky’s expectations by developing political ambitions, disregarding some of his requests and communicating directly with European partners without Zelensky’s involvement.
Amid mounting battlefield losses and desertions, Ukraine’s conscription drive has been marred by incidents of draft officers forcibly detaining military-age men on the streets, sparking spontaneous protests, clashes and outrage on social media.
While Kiev does not regularly publish figures on its battlefield losses, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk claimed last month that Ukrainian forces had recently been suffering around 27,000 killed and wounded per month. Russia’s Defense Ministry, meanwhile, claimed that Ukrainian casualties reached 500,000 in 2025 alone.

Sky closed over Moscow multiple nights in row as Ukraine resumes refinery strikes
Flights over the city of Moscow were restricted for the sixth night in a row on Oct. 16-17, according to flight-tracking data and updates from Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya).
The latest restrictions coincide with President Volodymyr Zelensky's announcement on Oct. 15 that Ukraine would no longer hold back from attacking Russian oil refineries. That same night, flights were grounded in both Moscow and St. Petersburg.
Rosaviatsiya announced late in the evening of Oct. 16 that three of Moscow's four major airports — Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovksy — were suspending operations due to security risks.
"Temporary restrictions have been introduced on the arrival and departure of aircraft," the agency said. "These restrictions are necessary to ensure flight safety."
Earlier in the day, Russia's Transportation Ministry said that civil aviation operations in Moscow Oblast had been placed under "special monitoring" by the ministry and Rosaviatsiya. The previous evening, Rosaviatsiya announced that flights were grounded at all four of Moscow's airports as well as at Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg.
While the agency did not at first announce restrictions at Moscow's Sheremetyevo Airport the night of Oct. 16-17, independent flight-tracking data indicated that the facility was also experiencing disruptions and delays.
According to aviation monitor Flightradar24, Sheremetyevo Airport is currently the fifth-most disrupted airport in the world and is experiencing "major problems."
Rosaviatsiya then announced temporary restrictions at Sheremetyevo Airport at around 2 a.m. local time.
Meanwhile, Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported that nearly 30 drones bound for the capital have been intercepted as of 1:30 a.m. local time on Oct. 17.
The latest closure marks the sixth consecutive night that restrictions have been imposed on air travel over Moscow, leading to long passenger queues and hundreds of flight delays. Russia's Transportation Ministry said it was deploying additional staff to the capital's airports in response to the situation.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that Ukraine fired nearly 500 drones at the region overnight on Oct. 13-15, all of which he said were intercepted by Russian air defense units. The following night, he claimed nearly 100 Ukrainian drones were shot down over Moscow.
Ukraine had refrained from strikes on Russia's refineries for three days to accommodate demands from U.S. President Donald Trump, who unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow.
Trump has claimed that Ukraine's refinery strikes are driving up oil and diesel prices worldwide, despite evidence that the U.S. war in Iran is in fact the primary culprit.
While Zelensky attempted to accommodate Trump — who threatened to withhold intelligence from Ukraine and struck a deal with Russian President Donald Trump to buy diesel from Moscow — Russia hammered Ukrainian cities and energy infastructure in large-scale attacks.
On Oct. 15, Zelensky said Ukraine's refinery attack pause was over.
"We're done," he said.

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Escalating hostilities in Yemen have cut access to Taiz City, preventing women and girls from receiving essential maternal care, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said Friday.
More than 147,000 women and girls of childbearing age in Taiz have been cut off from life-saving care. Only five of the city's 27 emergency maternal and newborn care hospitals are partially functioning, said OCHA, citing the UN Population Fund.

The office reiterated its call on all parties to protect civilians and to allow "safe, rapid and unimpeded" humanitarian access to reach people in need. ■

China willing to deepen cooperation with Croatia: Chinese FM
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:42:54 CST
07:42:54 KST

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, holds talks with Croatian Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Gordan Grlic Radman in Zagreb, Croatia, Oct. 16, 2026. (Xinhua/Peng Ziyang)
ZAGREB, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- China is willing to work with Croatia to achieve greater outcomes in bilateral cooperation, said Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi when holding talks with Croatian Minister of Foreign and European Affairs Gordan Grlic Radman here on Friday.
Wang, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that Croatia, an important stop on the ancient Silk Road, has once fostered mutual learning between Eastern and Western civilizations. This marks the first visit to Croatia by a Chinese foreign minister in 33 years, and serves as a reciprocal visit following Radman's trip to China last year.
The China-Croatia relations have developed in a mature and steady manner over the years, setting an example for the relations between countries of different sizes, Wang said.
The success of bilateral relations rests on equality, mutual respect and trust, win-win cooperation and friendly exchanges between the two peoples, Wang said, adding that these ties inject more certainty and stability into a complex and volatile international landscape.
China is willing to work with Croatia to take next year's 35th anniversary of establishing diplomatic relations as an opportunity to draw on experience and chart a course for stronger ties over the next 35 years, Wang said, calling on the two sides to work together for following high-level exchanges and bring bilateral ties to a new high.
Wang stressed that China respects Croatia's sovereignty and territorial integrity and supports its constructive role in international and regional affairs. China also appreciates Croatia's longstanding commitment to the one-China policy, which has strengthened the political foundation of bilateral relations and opened up broad prospects for cooperation, he added.
Wang said China is ready to work with Croatia to leverage "three major engines" to drive further progress in bilateral cooperation. First, at the bilateral level, the two sides should focus on infrastructure and renewable energy as key areas, while expanding cooperation into new sectors such as nuclear energy, ports, telecommunications, and artificial intelligence. Second, at the regional level, China-Croatia cooperation can be advanced through the broader framework of China-EU (the European Union) cooperation, as the Peljesac Bridge serves as an example of successful trilateral cooperation between China, the EU, and Croatia. Third, at the sub-regional level, the two sides should promote cooperation between China and Central and Eastern European Countries (CEECs). Croatia has been a builder, contributor, and beneficiary of this cooperation mechanism. China stands ready to work with CEECs to plan the next phase of engagement and deliver more tangible results.
Emphasizing that China and the EU share extensive common interests, Wang said that both sides advocate multilateralism, uphold the central and leading role of the United Nations and are committed to resolving international and regional disputes through political dialogues. China and Europe also share common ground on global issues such as climate change, he added.
Recent progress at the second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism has shown that bilateral differences can be resolved through dialogues on an equal footing, he said.
China is willing to deepen its comprehensive strategic partnership with the EU and hopes that Croatia, as an EU member, will play a constructive role in advancing China-EU relations, Wang said.
Radman said that Croatia attaches great importance to its relations with China and respects China's sovereignty and territorial integrity. Croatia has consistently adhered to the one-China policy and will continue to uphold it firmly, neither participating in nor supporting any "Taiwan independence" activities, he added.
Croatia is willing to take the 35th anniversary of establishing diplomatic relations as an opportunity to elevate bilateral ties, and will work to expand cooperation with China in areas such as transportation and logistics, renewable energy and automobile manufacturing, Radman said.
He added that China has played an important role in maintaining world peace and stability. As key partners, the EU and China share responsibility to jointly safeguard international order and promote global security and development.
Croatia values the cooperation framework between CEECs and China, Radman said. He thanked China for organizing activities under the framework and expressed hope that further cooperation would yield more results and bring greater benefits to the peoples of both sides.
During their talks, Radman also shared his views on the situation in the Western Balkans. Wang said that Croatia is an important country in the region, adding that China does not interfere in the internal affairs of Balkan countries and respects the choices made by their peoples.
China is willing to be a friend and partner of these countries and hopes they will foster harmonious relations and work together to build a shared future, Wang said. ■

====================================================================================================

World Insights: EU summit ends with mounting bills, unresolved divisions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
06:42:43 CST
07:42:43 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The two-day European Union (EU) summit concluded in Brussels on Friday without a breakthrough on the bloc's long-term budget, as rising security commitments and soaring energy costs exposed a growing gap between Europe's ambitions and its ability to deliver.
Behind the summit's limited progress lay three pressing challenges: a budget difficult to agree upon, a growing security bill complicated by tensions with Washington, and an energy crisis testing Europe's economic resilience.
TOUGH BUDGET NEGOTIATIONS
The European Commission has proposed a nearly 2-trillion-euro (2.24 trillion U.S. dollars) budget for 2028-2034, seeking to increase investment in competitiveness, defense and technology.
The Irish presidency's latest compromise would reduce the Commission's proposal by around 141 billion euros (158 billion dollars), yet the revised plan has drawn resistance from opposing camps.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned that the compromise would cut budgetary flexibility by half, leaving 99.5 percent of funds predetermined.
"This proposal puts us in a straitjacket," she said.
According to Brussels-based think tank Bruegel, six fiscally conservative countries led by Germany favor a smaller budget, while 17 "Friends of Cohesion," including Italy and Spain, seek to protect agricultural subsidies and regional development funds.
Brussels-based think tank Bruegel argued that both camps supported greater investment in common European priorities but placed national interests first.
It said that the Irish plan as the "worst possible compromise," warning that it could leave emerging priorities, including competitiveness and defense, severely underfunded while protecting traditional spending.
Fabian Zuleeg, chief executive and chief economist of the European Policy Centre, has likewise argued that Europe's expanding investment needs cannot realistically be financed through national budgets alone, calling for innovative financing arrangements, including new common borrowing.
The disagreements leave European Council President Antonio Costa facing a difficult task as he seeks a budget agreement by year-end.
GROWING SECURITY BILLS
Europe's fiscal pressures are compounded by a growing security bill and differences with Washington over Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said at the summit that the war would cost Ukraine 155 billion euros (173 billion dollars) in 2027 and requested at least another 70 billion euros (78 billion dollars) in assistance.
The EU has already agreed on a 90-billion-euro (100 billion dollars) loan covering 2026-2027. However, Ukraine's additional financing needs remained under assessment, with European leaders seeking further input from the Commission and international financial institutions.
In its final conclusions, the European Council explicitly expressed regret over the U.S. decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel, a move also criticized by Zelensky.
Meanwhile, recent restrictions on the U.S.-controlled Starshield satellite communications service disrupted Ukrainian military operations, exposing another vulnerability in Europe's security capabilities.
"Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine, and unfortunately in the short term Europe can't replace this capability," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas acknowledged on Friday.
Analysts noted that this episode highlights Europe's reliance on critical U.S. military technologies even as transatlantic differences over Ukraine become more pronounced.
For Europe, the dilemma is increasingly apparent: greater security responsibilities require additional resources, while some of the capabilities underpinning those commitments remain beyond its immediate control.
SOARING ENERGY COSTS
Energy has become another source of financial strain. According to von der Leyen, the Middle East conflict has added 106 billion euros (119 billion dollars) to the EU's fossil fuel import bill, highlighting Europe's vulnerability to external energy shocks.
The International Energy Agency is accelerating the release of emergency oil stocks, including diesel, with plans to bring another 100 million barrels to the market over four months, while Brussels is pursuing temporary support for energy-intensive industries and measures to improve refining capacity.
Yet the summit exposed divisions over how far climate policies should be adjusted to ease immediate costs.
Italy, Greece and the four Visegrad countries pushed to postpone the EU's second emissions trading system, ETS2, until 2030, arguing that carbon pricing would impose further burdens on households and businesses.
However, Nordic countries resisted, concerned that weakening the system would undermine investment certainty and longer-term climate objectives.
The summit ended without an agreement on further postponement. Leaders instead requested an updated assessment of ETS2's design, impact and safeguards.
Researchers at the European Council on Foreign Relations argued that Europe's green transition was facing growing political resistance shaped by economic insecurity, competing national interests and the distribution of costs.
The dispute reflects a difficult choice: easing today's energy pressures could weaken incentives for long-term investment, while maintaining ambitious climate policies risks adding to the burden on businesses and households.
For European leaders, agreeing on common goals remains easier than deciding who should bear the costs of achieving them. ■

The newly elected parliament is scheduled to convene for its first sitting on Nov. 3, when it will begin its term. ■

Authorities are investigating a shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, where a 16-year-old shooter killed four people before being shot dead by a bystander.
The shooting took place on Thursday afternoon at Silver Rail elementary school, about 125 miles (200km) south-east of Portland.
Here is what we know so far about the four victims, including three children aged five, eight and 11, and a 25-year old teacher, as well as the two people injured.
Rhoam Summer
In a Facebook group post, Rhoam Summer’s father Kelik Summer posted about his five-year old son’s death, saying that Thursday was “the worst day of my life.” He added: “My son Rhoam was killed in a school shooting. We are broken and lost, but are surrounded by friends and family who are keeping us safe.”
Rhoam’s grandfather Bryan Jolly also confirmed his grandson’s death to the New York Times. Jolly described the tragedy as “senseless and a shock”, adding that Rhoam was “in my house a lot and in my garden with me and wrestling with me on the couch”.
“He was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear,” Jolly said.
A separate GoFundMe page that appears to have been set up by friends of Rhoam’s family said: “In the wake of an unimaginable tragedy, the Summer family is grieving the heartbreaking loss of their sweet five-year-old son, Rhoam. There are no words that can ease the pain of losing a child, and no family should ever have to experience a loss like this.”
Bend police also confirmed Rhoam’s identity on Friday afternoon.
Eight-year old boy
Police are not releasing his identification at his family’s request.
Eleven-year old boy
Police are not releasing his identification at his family’s request.
Megan Lambert
Twenty-five-year old Megan Lambert, a teacher at the school, was identified as another victim killed in the shooting, Bend police said on Friday.
In a statement shared with Bend police, Lambert’s family said: “Megan was a native central Oregonian. She grew up in Bend. She had a passion for playing sports, especially volleyball. She was a volleyball coach. She actually turned down pay for her first season as a coach, so families who couldn’t afford to participate could have the chance to play the sport she loved.”
“Her goal was to be an educator, and teach in the school district she loved growing up in … Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher, though she subbed there for many years … She loved Silver Rail. This was her dream job. Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart,” her family added.
The Central Oregon Volleyball Club website lists Megan as a local high school coach and describes her as a “blessing” who has done “so much for her team”.
Saylor Graham
Seven-year old Saylor Graham was injured in the shooting, according to several GoFundMe accounts set up by co-workers and friends of her family. “The family is focused on being at the hospital while their child fights for their life,” one account said.
“Right now, they are carrying the impossible weight of traveling to and from the hospital, staying near their child, caring for their other child, trying to keep up their household, and missing work during this crisis,” it added.
A business partner of Saylor’s mother, Danielle Graham, declined to be interviewed but confirmed Saylor’s identity to the Guardian.
Meanwhile, Bend police said on Friday that a seven-year old girl who was shot “is receiving life-saving care” at Oregon Health & Science University hospital in Portland, adding: “She is in serious but stable condition.”

Brazil: Amazon deforestation lowest in nearly 40 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
22:30:00 UTC
07:30:00 KST

Brazil: Amazon deforestation lowest in nearly 40 years
October 17, 2026
Brazil has recorded the lowest level of deforestation in the Amazon rainforest in nearly 40 years.
According to data released by the Brazilian space research agency Inpe on Friday, between August 2025 and July 2026, 3,335 square kilometers (1,288 square miles) of forest were cleared, the lowest level witnessed since records began in 1988.
The numbers showed a nearly 42% decrease from last year's figure of 5,731 square kilometers.
The Amazon is the world's largest tropical rainforest and one of its most biodiverse ecosystems, most of which lies in Brazil.
It also extends into parts of Peru, Colombia and other South American countries. Deforestation and the illegal exploitation of resources have been pushing it closer to a climate tipping point.
Drop hailed as 'historic achievement'
"It's an absolutely stratospheric drop...it's like a dream," said Environment Minister Joao Paulo Capobianco at a press conference in the capital, Brasilia.
"Our goal is to achieve zero illegal deforestation by 2030," said President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a post on X.
"The figures released today are a historic achievement," said Marcio Astrini, executive secretary at climate advocacy group Observatorio do Clima.
"They put Brazil at the forefront of the forest protection agenda and show the world that, with political will, it is possible to stop the chainsaws and curb greenhouse gas emissions," Astrini said on his organization's website.
Observatorio do Clima said the figures were the result of a "sustained commitment" to protecting the environment by the government, which introduced greater monitoring and stiffer penalties for illegal logging.
The news comes ahead of the October 25 runoff election between Lula and conservative senator Flavio Bolsonaro with the two running neck and neck according to polls.

Teacher and armed parent teamed up to stop Oregon school shooter, police say
BEND, Oregon, Oct 16 - A 16-year-old boy who shot and killed a teacher and three children in an Oregon special-needs classroom was stopped by another teacher who tackled him and an armed father who fatally shot him, officials said on Friday.
Their actions on Thursday saved other lives, the local police chief told a press conference.
A day into their investigation of the latest US school shooting, police released new details of the scene at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, where three schoolchildren aged 5, 8 and 11 were killed along with 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
A 7-year-old was wounded and listed in serious but stable condition, and another teacher suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police said.
TEACHER 'HELPED PREVENT MORE BLOODSHED,' POLICE SAY
The unidentified teacher who stopped the shooter on Thursday threw her phone at him, tackled and fought him. A 36-year-old father of two students then rushed in with a legal .40-caliber pistol and fired at the suspect multiple times, killing him just before police arrived.
This teacher, who was not injured, "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz, at times choking back emotion, told a press conference.
"The teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that's true heroism," he said, without identifying her.
Kenda Freeman told the New York Times that her son Kaylub Giamanco, whose two daughters attend the school, killed the shooter, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement.
"He is not seeking recognition but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said, adding that he asked for privacy and did not want to speak to the media.
The shooting traumatized much of Bend, a city of about 100,000 people some 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, including 9-year-old fourth-grader Kalani Journeigh and her classmates, who heard the gunshots from a nearby classroom.
"All of us were screaming and we were all, like, really scared," Kalani told Reuters, adding that she feared, "We might die."
"My heart was beating really fast and after the couple of gunshots that we heard, it just stopped and we never heard it again," she said.
A friend of hers was going to get therapy, she said, because "that was really traumatizing to her."
Officials identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, a 16-year-old former special-needs student at the school who was armed with a shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom and had another 44 rounds on him, police said.
Police were trying to determine what motivated the shooter and how he obtained a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun, Krantz said.
"Everyone wants to know why, including us," the police chief said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it."
VICTIMS MOURNED
Just before the shooting, the assailant was seen throwing his weapon over the school fence and then climbing after it onto school grounds. The driver of a truck passing by verbally confronted the boy, who opened fire on the vehicle.
The assailant shot through locked glass doors and stormed a class of mixed-grade special-needs students. Police arrived within three minutes of the first call, and the shooter was already dead, Krantz said.
People in Bend gathered near the school to mourn on Friday morning, placing flowers and candles outside yellow-crime scene tape that cordoned off the scene.
"Thank God for that father," Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just blocks from the school, said through tears. "He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and our prayers should go out for him because he has a lot on his mind today."
The family of the slain teacher, Lambert, said working at Silver Rail was a "dream job" for her.
"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," the family said in a statement that was read aloud at Friday's news conference.
Lambert's family also praised Giamanco and expressed gratitude to him.
"We think he is a hero," the family said, according to the statement.
US school shootings have become more frequent in recent years. Since the start of this year, 118 people have been wounded or killed in 149 incidents involving a gun fired or brandished in a school, or gunshots striking school property, according to the K-12 School Shooting Database, a nonprofit online tracker.
A separate online database, the Gun Violence Archive, has recorded 371 mass shootings since January 2026, defining mass shootings as four or more people being struck by gunfire, not including the shooter. Three of those, including the Bend incident, occurred in public schools, the archive said. REUTERS
