Moscow’s alternative teens have made a downtown nightlife district their weekend hangout. Drunken fights are driving customers away — and police are targeting the teenagers for how they dress.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
21:27:23 UTC
06:27:23 KST

Moscow’s alternative teens have made a downtown nightlife district their weekend hangout. Drunken fights are driving customers away — and police are targeting the teenagers for how they dress.
In the summer of 2025, media outlets first reported on the “nefors” of Kitay-Gorod — teenagers in unusual clothes who hang out in this central Moscow neighborhood. Around the same time, local café and bar owners noticed they were getting fewer customers: The rowdy young members of alternative subcultures had scared them off. A year later, police began rounding up the “nefors,” handling teenagers roughly as they detained them, sometimes without explanation. Police go mainly by how they look. Sometimes, though, there are grounds for police intervention: The “nefors” get drunk, shout, and fight, or lie on the ground after overdosing on drugs. Some also hold far-right views. Bereg, a cooperative of independent journalists, spent two nights in Kitay-Gorod — one in the summer and another after the school year began. Meduza is translating its report in full.
Caution: This article contains extensive profanity, as well as xenophobic statements (which are important to understanding the story’s context).
August
‘Back in our day, it was six nine’
Late in the evening, several teenagers sit on the sidewalk in a quiet lane in Kitay-Gorod, in central Moscow. They’re dressed in black, their once brightly dyed hair now faded and grown out. One girl, wearing ripped fishnet tights and a short skirt, looks for something to prop her smartphone against as she gets ready to film a TikTok. Another, in an oversized hoodie, talks loudly on a video call. Several boys nearby roar with laughter.
Girls with bright makeup and faces whitened with unnaturally pale foundation or powder; boys with bob haircuts or long bangs; many in tall platform shoes, some with extensive piercings and tattoos, including on their faces and necks — people who look like this are called “nefors.”
Those particularly fond of them often use the affectionate diminutive “neforyata” — many are under 18. They belong to a range of youth subcultures and often look very different from one another, making any general description difficult. One thing is certain: They stand out from other Muscovites.
Since the spring of 2025, Kitay-Gorod has become the main hangout for young “nefors.” Nowhere else in the city has so many of them. Groups of teenagers from different subcultures, immediately recognizable by their distinctive clothes, emerge from subway stations and fan out through the neighborhood.
Two boys turn into a courtyard near the Moscow Choral Synagogue on Bolshoy Spasoglinishchevsky Lane. Both wear black T-shirts; one has a keffiyeh wrapped around his head and mismatched sneakers.
“Fuck!” one of them blurts out. There’s a police car in the courtyard they were heading for, and an officer is smoking a little farther away.
Since the summer of 2026, police and the Russian National Guard have been patrolling Kitay-Gorod more frequently. They used to focus on fining people for drinking alcohol where it wasn’t permitted. Now they may turn a blind eye to people carrying beer bottles. They pay much more attention to teenagers.
Patrol cars are a frequent sight on the streets, with police vans here and there. From Friday through Sunday, the number of police vehicles in the neighborhood rises noticeably. Officers may drive past the same spot several times in an hour.
Red barrier tape is strung across the entrance to a courtyard with several bars and cafés. Two athletic-looking men stand nearby, both in civilian clothes and balaclavas. They barely pay attention to adults, even those arriving with large backpacks. But the moment they spot “nefors,” they spring into action, blocking the entrance, ready to demand ID. The “nefors” aren’t eager to engage with the guards: They quickly turn around and leave.
— So they’re only keeping schoolkids out? a man of about 40 in a white shirt asks one of the bar’s patrons.
— Yeah. If they can see you’re normal, they let you through.
The man nods knowingly: All last summer, teenagers in unusual clothes crowded around the bar, and customers were “not thrilled” with them.
Other customers felt uncomfortable around the “nefors,” who got drunk, shouted, and sometimes threw up right beside the benches where they hung out. The schoolkids didn’t go into the bars themselves, except to look for a bathroom. They brought their own alcohol and snacks: There are plenty of liquor stores nearby, and locals say the staff sometimes don’t ask customers for ID.
The patrons keep discussing the teenagers, mostly dismissively. They joke that you don’t need ID to tell how old “kids like that” are — just ask them to read an analog clock or finish a line from the song “Nu gde zhe ruchki” (“Where Are Those Hands?”).
— Or that meme, “six-seven”! If [someone] does this — that’s it, fuck off, says the man in the white shirt, moving his hands up and down like a scale to demonstrate the signature gesture.
— I know that meme too, and I’m almost 40. So what? another patron replies.
— But you wouldn’t do that with your hands.
— No. Back in our day, it was six nine!
In the bar next door, the conversation is also about teenagers and screening people at the door. The bartender and his customer reminisce about their youth: There were subcultures back then too, but they “stood for something.” Now, they think, teenagers are simply being obnoxious.
“I was actually pleased once when I heard a Deftones track, ‘My Own Summer’: Wow, they’re starting to learn the basics!” the bartender says. “Turns out it’s just some short video that went viral on TikTok and has nothing to do with Deftones! They’re just [milking] it, and nobody’s planning to learn [to play guitar] or even find out what it is.”
The customer recalls recently seeing a teenager on the subway wearing an Aria band T-shirt, with a skateboard under his arm and a fresh scar on his face, probably from falling off the board. The bartender decides the younger generation isn’t a lost cause — there’s just “something wrong” with the “nefors” who come to Kitay-Gorod to have fun.
‘All of Kitay-Gorod can see people constantly having it out, drinking, smoking, doing drugs, and screwing’
“People have become afraid to come to Kitay-Gorod, because before 9 [p.m.] it’s one crowd, and afterward it’s a completely different one,” Albert (not his real name) tells Bereg. He owns a business in the neighborhood and is now in his second year of watching the crowds of teenagers who hang out here.
At first, Albert says, there were no problems: Teenagers in unusual clothes gathered in the courtyards, but they behaved “perfectly reasonably” and people were simply curious about them. Gradually, the alternative crowd grew to include people who got drunk and behaved indecently, for instance relieving themselves in the street. By the middle of the summer of 2026, Albert says, this behavior had become the norm for them.
“They like to shout and act really obnoxious. Their favorite pastime is pepper-spraying each other. They get into fights every day,” Albert says. Although this “aggression” wasn’t directed at bystanders, the bar’s customers felt unsafe and stopped coming to Kitay-Gorod.
“Customers told us straight out: We love you, we appreciate you, we respect you, but we’re scared to come into your neighborhood on Fridays and Saturdays, because things are totally out of control here,” Albert says. In the summer of 2025, his business’s revenue was 40% lower than the year before.
When teenagers fought or used pepper spray, Albert, his employees, and other Kitay-Gorod business owners called the police. Sometimes they had to call several times in an evening. But their complaints went nowhere: The police would arrive and shrug.
Albert says officers told business owners that “dealing with minors is a pain in the ass,” especially since there were dozens of them here and, as he understood it from what the officers said, only one patrol car. The bar owner believes getting away with it only encouraged the teenagers.
Everything changed after March 20, 2026. That evening, several unidentified people attacked students leaving the Moscow Choral Synagogue. “Across the street is Gorka Park. People who look pretty rough gather there every day, especially on Fridays. They’ve had a few drinks, and sometimes they go looking for trouble,” the synagogue’s communications director, Dmitry Drigailo, said of the attack.
Whether any “nefors” were among the attackers is unknown. But several Muscovites who often spend time in Kitay-Gorod tell Bereg that this was when the National Guard and OMON riot police began patrolling alongside the police.
The roundups of “nefors” began after that. One of the largest took place on July 3, when officers detained and beat dozens of people, including teenagers. “Suddenly I was hit on the back of the neck, forced to my knees, grabbed by the arms, punched in the face, and then hit in the leg,” one person detained that day told Bereg.
“All of Kitay-Gorod can see people constantly having it out with each other, drinking, smoking [marijuana], doing drugs, and screwing,” Albert says:
All of Kitay-Gorod is turning into a public toilet — I look [at the sidewalk] and realize the toilet is here now, and here, and here. Things have gotten out of control. If it hadn’t gone this far, I wouldn’t even pay attention to these teenagers. But I’m certainly not going to make excuses for these kids, because I’ve seen all this over and over.
In the evenings, especially on Fridays and weekends, broken glass is scattered throughout Kitay-Gorod, and the air smells of urine.
Police raids forced the teenagers out of the parks and small public gardens where they used to hang out and into the lanes and courtyards. Albert says “now it’s other people’s problem,” and he “doesn’t envy them.”
Intensive care ambulances driving past are a sign to pedestrians that teenagers are still partying nearby. Bereg’s correspondent spotted several of these vehicles in Kitay-Gorod, including ones marked “pediatric intensive care.” Albert says that “at least 20 times” he has seen teenagers overdosing and watched as ambulances were called for them.
Albert says there have always been young people who “show off for each other” and try to express themselves through unusual clothes and bright makeup — and that’s normal. But the bar owner struggles to sympathize with the “nefors”: He has witnessed their “out-of-control behavior” too often. “These aren’t the sweet, innocent kids they’re made out to be on Instagram,” he tells Bereg.
Albert says their behavior is the only reason he feels negatively about these teenagers. “I hope they figure out what they love as soon as possible and find the confidence to pursue it,” he says. “And above all, I hope they have the sense and instincts to avoid stupid mistakes and not ruin their lives for no reason.”
‘There were these loud chicks right there — they left them alone and picked on us’
It’s easy to find where the “nefors” hang out in Kitay-Gorod — just follow someone in unusual clothes. You can also find specific spots through Instagram and TikTok videos; sometimes the creators even post GPS coordinates in the comments under their videos.
The most popular places have names: the “drunk courtyard,” the “puck,” and several “zigas” — “upper,” “lower,” and “old.” One of the first “zigas” is near the rock merchandise store Zigzag.
The teenagers call Danilovskaya Alley the “old ziga.” It’s a tiny park with a Soviet-era playground, screened from the road by rows of trees. Apparently counting on that cover, the people at the “old ziga” don’t even try to keep the noise down. All you have to do to find the visibly intoxicated young people is follow the sound.
Several groups have gathered in the courtyard, surrounded by empty bottles, cigarette butts, pill blister packs, and other trash. A rental e-scooter lies in a puddle beneath the pull-up bars.
A tall blonde girl in wide-mesh fishnet tights and a long-haired boy sit down on a bench. Both look about 16. They discuss their search for the places in Kitay-Gorod where groups of teenagers gather. Both are annoyed: Their acquaintances gave them only vague descriptions, so they had to figure it all out themselves. They don’t like the police raids either, but their desire to be part of the scene outweighs their fear of getting caught in a roundup.
“The riot cops are the worst — there’s no reasoning with them at all,” the boy says. “Whether you’ve got connections or not, nobody gives a fuck: They’ll just beat you up, and that’s it.” He can’t understand why officers behave so differently at big events, such as soccer games.
— I went to a Spartak game — everything was fine, they were polite there. Here, though — it’s just fucking insane, they’re murderers and fucking psychos.
— Like the country’s got no other problems — so they come to Kitay-Gorod, his companion says with a smirk.
— That’s what I’m saying. Don’t they have anything better to fucking do?
The girl says she ran into a raid a few hours ago but managed to get away while police were checking her friends’ IDs. “There were these loud chicks right there — they left them alone and picked on us,” she says. The boy doesn’t seem impressed by her story — he smirks and says he witnessed a “real roundup” that same day:
Today, near the “puck,” in the courtyards, I went up to a group. I said, “Guys, a paddy wagon just pulled up.” They go, “What’s a paddy wagon?” Then bam — five seconds later, a whole bunch of cops in body armor come in. Everyone’s yelling, “Pigs, fucking run!” And I slowly stepped aside, pressed myself against the fence — and they left me alone.
The boy says that when he’s sure there’s nothing to detain him for, he tries to act as though nothing’s happening — and it works. “I get the fuck out when I’m either high or drunk,” he says. Right now, he’s “a little drunk.” But even if he were sober, he thinks he could still get in trouble if detained:
The booze doesn’t fucking matter, but weed takes two weeks to clear your system, and if they take me to the station and test me, I’m fucked. If they find anything — drug treatment clinic, injections, parents. But if you’re sober and they definitely won’t find anything, just act normal and pray.
A loud belch comes from the far end of the courtyard, followed by a burst of laughter.
— Bless you! a male voice calls out.
— I need to puke, another replies.
— Well, go over there, in the bushes.
The courtyard goes quiet.
— What’s your name again? I forgot, the long-haired boy asks the girl sitting beside him on the bench.
— You never asked.
The boy is surprised that she’s perfectly comfortable hanging out with him when she doesn’t even know his name. She admits she “knows everything about him”: Before they met in person, she looked up his Telegram username with a bot that searches for personal information. Their conversation makes it clear that Telegram is where they met.
— You were willing to spend 200 rubles on that?
— I bought a bunch of searches at once a while back — about 15 rubles each.
— I think doxxing is cringe now.
— Well, I mostly use it if I need to call someone urgently and don’t have their number. Or if I forgot their name.
The teenagers move on from roundups, drugs, and personal data searches to complaining about their parents. The boy boasts that he managed to get his mom to let him stay out until 1 a.m. But his “bros” have “strict parents,” so he has to find new people to hang out with. “I want to get drunk, unwind — and they’ve got to be home by 10,” he says.
The group on the next bench is planning to keep the night going at someone’s apartment. They discuss how to get there (the subway has already closed) and what cover story to tell their parents.
— Business [a Business-class taxi — Bereg] or the bus? asks a short girl with red hair.
— I need to get drunk, or there’s no point taking the bus, another girl’s voice says with a laugh.
A phone rings. “Got any pepper spray?” the same voice asks into the phone. “Yeah, bring me some.” The girl moves the phone away from her ear, and the screen lights up her face. She’s blonde, with many facial piercings.
— Got anything on you? someone asks the blonde cryptically. It’s too dark to see the speaker’s face.
— No, not even any vodka left, bro.
— A lighter?
— Definitely got a lighter. A fancy one, too.
The girl takes out a lighter shaped like a gold bar.
— That’s cool! a boy says admiringly.
— Check it out, check it out! her red-haired friend says.
“Ah, who gives a fuck, we bought a pack at Sadovod for 600 [rubles] — there’s like 20 in there, for fuck’s sake,” the blonde brags. “We said we’d bring [the money] later.”
— So, did you?
— No! It burned down, fucking Sadovod.
The teenagers roar with laughter. When Bereg’s correspondent asks whether they feel safe in this courtyard, they say “the pigs never come here.” Soon the group leaves in a taxi.
A couple — a boy and a girl — comes running up to take their place. It’s too dark to make them out.
“Holy fuck, why are there old people sitting here?” the male voice mutters irritably, referring to Bereg’s correspondent.
The couple moves over to the playground merry-go-round, where their friends are already sitting. The teenagers discuss concerts and festivals and swap gossip about performers.
A high-pitched male voice sings:
- You jerked me off with your hands,
- My dick wouldn’t get hard.
- Fucking sick of all the calls,
- This way and that.
People in another part of the courtyard pick up the tune and sing along. Nearby, a boy in a hoodie sits on a playground slide, leaning on his knees with his head hanging down. He’s clearly unwell, but he refuses Bereg’s correspondent’s offer of help. The singing teenagers pay him no attention.
A few minutes later, a National Guard vehicle drives past the courtyard. It stops nearby, but no one gets out. After waiting a little while, it drives away.
* * *
By the end of August, officers had finally turned their attention to the “old ziga.” Local residents say there was a fight “involving knives,” after which forensic specialists came to the playground. Residents saw them taking fingerprints from bottles scattered around the courtyard. Bereg could not confirm through publicly available sources that such a fight had occurred.
In September, the playground entrance was closed.
October
‘Cops aren’t our bros!’
It’s been pouring all evening. But the teenagers pay no attention, walking around without umbrellas or their hoods up. Despite the start of the school year and the nasty weather, they still gather in Kitay-Gorod on Fridays.
Two dark-haired girls in thick-soled shoes enter Gorka Park between Bolshoy Spasoglinishchevsky and Petroverigsky Lanes and head confidently down a path. A few minutes later, they emerge onto a playground. At least a hundred young people in “nefor” clothes are there, ranging in age from about 12 to 20. This place is called the “new ziga.”
“Maybe we’ll find someone we know after all,” a girl of about 14 says hopefully to her friend. Her friend shrugs. Even if there are familiar faces here, finding them will be hard: Parts of the courtyard are packed, and most of the teenagers keep moving around.
Several people are shouting and tossing someone into the air — light-colored sneakers flash above the crowd’s heads. It’s very loud, with music playing from all directions: everything from Kai Angel and 9mice — teen favorites the crowd sings along to — to, for some reason, lezginka dance music.
— You sober? a boy in a black hoodie asks me and a girl standing nearby.
— Yes.
— Pfft, he snorts, walking away as he laughs loudly and exchanges glances with his friends.
Different boys approach Bereg’s correspondent and other girls with similar questions several more times. They react much the same way when told the girls are sober. Some don’t bother speaking: They simply lift the edge of a girl’s sweatshirt hood, look into her eyes, and walk away disappointed. They’re checking her pupils: If they’re unnaturally dilated, she’s probably under the influence of synthetic drugs or psychiatric medication. These boys aren’t interested in sober girls.
— So, how do you like the zoo? a curly-haired teenager in baggy black jeans and a leather jacket asks, stopping in front of me. Apparently, my age and “normie” clothes make me stand out.
— Why a zoo?
— Just look at them, he says, spreading his arms and swaying a little.
He says you can sometimes find “normal people” here, and “there’s always something going on.” Mark (not his real name) is 16. He says he spends every weekend here and recognizes many of the “new ziga” regulars. Right now, he’s trying to find the “bros” he arranged to meet, but they aren’t answering.
“Give me back the vodka, for fuck’s sake!” a short girl with long dark hair screams behind him. She looks no older than Mark. Boys have crowded around her and are playing keep-away, tossing a vodka bottle to one another so she can’t get it.
— I’m telling you, it’s a total zoo! You can’t stand being here drunk or [sober].
— But you’re here anyway.
— Well, I’m on a bender — my girlfriend dumped me.
The bottle flies over Mark’s head, narrowly missing him, and lands in the bushes. The girl who was trying to catch it runs screaming after it.
Mark says he plans to party all night and go home in the morning once he’s sobered up. He says his parents don’t mind him spending weekends in Kitay-Gorod. “They get that I’m 16, I want to hang out,” he says. “What am I supposed to do, sit at home on TikTok? That’s boring.”
As a child, Mark practiced martial arts, often won competitions, and was passionate about it. But then he was injured and had to quit. On top of that, conflicts with classmates escalated into bullying, and he began having mental health problems.
Mark says he spent time in a psychiatric hospital and calls himself “suicidal”: Several times, he stood at the edge of a roof, but something stopped him each time. Once, for instance, his mom called, and the call made him change his mind — Mark was afraid his death would “really traumatize her.”
Now Mark wants to train as a surveyor. “First, the pay’s good; second, you basically don’t do anything at work; third, I really like math,” he says. “And it’s a cool job: If I do well in school and get hired somewhere building tunnels, someone’s life will depend on my calculations.” He says that “as someone who’s suicidal,” he understands “the value of life.”
“Something’s keeping me here, apparently,” he says, continuing to recall his attempts. “Maybe I’ll be some really great family man, maybe I’ll have some really great kids — I don’t know, but there’s got to be a reason for all this.”
While Mark reflects on his purpose in life, the teenagers around us start to get restless. He raises his head and peers into the distance. “Oh, cops,” he says matter-of-factly. “Let’s get the fuck out of here, because shit’s about to go down.”
Someone bolts and starts climbing the fence, but most of the teenagers walk confidently along the path toward the exit. The path narrows, and in the crowd it starts to feel as if we’re leaving a concert or some other big event — everyone is packed in practically shoulder to shoulder, but they try to stay calm and avoid pushing.
— What are they gonna do to us, anyway? a male voice asks behind me.
— Beat the shit out of us! another replies.
— For what?
— Everything.
— We’re not even drinking!
Mark offers to show me the “puck” — that’s where the “nefors” go after officers drive them out of the “new ziga.” He says they try to take different routes to avoid attracting police attention. “Cops aren’t our bros!” he says with a smile.
“Sieg Heil! Sieg Heil! Sieg Heil!” someone in the crowd chants loudly. It’s unsettling. The only response from those around us is to joke that the riot police might come after the “nefors” too.
I ask Mark if it’s true that gatherings here often end in fights. He nods emphatically. “There was even shooting here a few days ago!” he says excitedly. “It’s the kind of [round] that could easily go right through someone, but luckily they fired into the air.”
Mark says he himself was once “grabbed for fighting” in Kitay-Gorod. According to him, there was no fight — he was just teaching a girl he knew how to wrestle. They had to tell the officers they knew each other and were just practicing. Police checked their IDs on the spot and didn’t take the friends to the station. “We got lucky, that rarely happens,” he says.
One such fight, he says, ended in a death. He says he watched a crowd beat a 19-year-old man to death as punishment for raping a 13-year-old girl. The Telegram channel Podslushano Kitay-Gorod was among those that carried accounts of the incident; Bereg could find no other corroboration. Mark thinks the “nefors” “did the right thing.”
On the way to the “puck,” Mark keeps spotting friends and greeting them by name. He says this is what teenagers value about Kitay-Gorod — “it’s easy to connect with someone for a bit, but you can find good friends too.” Mark’s test of a good friend is whether they’d be willing to get him home when he’s “absolutely shitfaced.”
‘They take you in for looking alternative — you have to explain why you’re dressed like that’
Twenty minutes later, we’re at the “puck.” It’s a tiny courtyard on Pokrovka, with a huge circular flower bed in the center, edged by a wide curb. Menu booklets from a nearby café are neatly arranged all along the curb.
Within minutes, the courtyard fills with teenagers. Three boys notice the menus, grab the booklets, and try to tear them up, but can’t — the pages are laminated. Instead, swearing loudly, they rip pages out of the booklets and start throwing them in all directions. After destroying several menus, they settle down and move over to a bench.
I take out my cigarettes, and teenagers immediately surround me. Among them is a short boy in a beige jacket. Mark says he’s 12.
The teenagers boast to each other about what cigarettes they usually smoke — the stronger the cigarettes, the cooler you seem. Mark, too, smokes the strongest ones in his brand’s lineup: “I’ve smoked so much, nothing gives me a buzz anymore,” he says. Asked how he buys alcohol and cigarettes as a minor, he says he gets older friends to help.
“I can tell you’re kind people, good souls. Can you spare a cigarette?” A boy with peach-colored hair appears out of nowhere. He looks at least 18.
Beside him is a friend dressed in black, with long dark hair, tattooed hands, and a large silver-colored pendant around his neck. “Sorry, that was the last one,” I say truthfully, showing him the empty pack.
Mark starts making excuses, and the boys laugh at him.
— What’s with the flashy fit, bro? the boy in black suddenly asks, his expression changing as he looks at Mark’s jeans, which are covered in white marker drawings.
— I did these myself, can you believe it?
“You did?!” the boy shrieks, reaching out to shake his hand. “Get [over] here, you fucking designer! Fucking designer shit!”
— I’ll do your jeans for a pack of cigarettes! I’ve got acrylic markers with me.
— Damn, no, I don’t want to mess these up, they’re my brother’s — my brother died, I wear his jeans.
The boys discuss whether it’s a good deal and ask what exactly Mark can draw; it’s hard to tell whether they’re joking.
— Can you slap a fucking swastika on there?
— On the ass, sure.
“By the way, this is my personal bodyguard,” the boy in black says, abruptly changing the subject and turning to his peach-haired friend. “Man, show us what you’re packing! Kid, get that shit out.”
His friend unzips his jacket and takes a signal pistol out of an inside pocket. Half the cylinder is already empty.
A siren gives a low-pitched warning blast from the street. Everyone at the “puck” turns to look: A police car is escorting a motorcade of several black foreign-made cars. “Whores!” one of the “nefors” shouts at the police car, to approving cries from the crowd.
At the far end of the courtyard stands a man in a bright orange jacket. He looks about 40 and stands out sharply from the teenage crowd. From time to time, teenagers approach him, exchange a few words, shake hands, and walk away.
“Some guy, a bro of mine, tried to sell me Lyrica today, can you believe it? One blister pack — 2,500 [rubles] cash,” Mark suddenly says, catching my eye. The peach-haired boy is interested in the offer. Their conversation suggests it’s a good deal: The drug usually costs much more on Telegram channels.
— My bro works at a hospital. They write prescriptions in old people’s names, then sell the stuff, Mark says.
“Any way to hook up with them and start dealing?” asks the boy in black. “I’ve got zoliki, tramadol, alprazolam, shit like that — I’ve got everything.”
— So do they.
— Seriously, any way to hook up with them and build a drug-dealing empire?
— I don’t know, ask him!
The boys get the contact information and leave to buy beer. Someone is holding a half-liter (17-ounce) plastic bottle of some cheap fruit-flavored cocktail; a group of boys nearby drinks liqueur from 200-milliliter bottles (about 7 ounces) and discusses where else to go in Kitay-Gorod.
— Remind me, what’s the name of that fucking sleazy dive you love so much? a boy with short hair and a black track jacket asks his friend.
— Klub Klub. But they’ve renamed it Knizhny [Book] now.
— Book club? Does anyone actually read there? the boy in the track jacket laughs.
Mark complains that he’s starting to sober up. He excuses himself and walks over to the lawn, where he throws up on the grass. When he returns, he says he won’t drink any more — at least not today.
A short girl with long black hair, a pale face, and burgundy lipstick enters the courtyard. She looks no older than 16. She’s carrying a yellow “Caution: Wet floor” sign, the kind usually put out in shopping malls during cleaning. She proudly says she stole it from the nearest “McDonald’s” (now Vkusno — i Tochka, the chain that replaced McDonald’s in Russia), then runs into the teenage crowd, declaring, “I’m the fucking coolest person here.”
A tall, thin young man with very short hair and a black windbreaker stands out in the crowd. He invites various groups back to his place, but says that “unfortunately, there’s no mephedrone” at home. He’s a local TikTok celebrity who calls himself Lyokha Neforyuga. He’s 19.
Lyokha used to have long hair and belonged to PMC Redan, but at the end of the summer he decided to give up his alternative look. He cut his hair, switched to more neutral clothes, and began saying he was now a “normie.” Lyokha has repeatedly been detained and held in jail for drinking in public and fighting. He also says he is registered as a patient at an addiction clinic, which he claims is why the military enlistment office refused to let him enlist as a contract soldier.
Teenagers nearby discuss Lyokha Neforyuga, saying “half of KG [Kitay-Gorod — Bereg] wants to smash his fucking face in.”
— What for? one boy asks another.
— He does stupid shit: yells at everyone, gets drunk.
— Well, let him drink. So he drinks — big deal.
— And yells!
— Nah, the yelling’s not cool.
Right now, Lyokha is very drunk. He looks as though he’s taken drugs as well: His movements are jerky, and he grinds his teeth and bites his lips.
— Lyokha, what did they cut your hair off for? the boy in the track jacket calls out to him.
“Who are you?” Lyokha replies suspiciously. “I got it cut myself, bro. How do you know me?”
— You’ve got a TikTok.
“Oh, yeah, I’ve got 2.5 million [views],” Lyokha says, relaxing and starting to smile. “Damn, he actually knows me!”
Someone distracts Lyokha, and he heads back into the crowd. Another siren blasts a warning from the street. Several police cars are patrolling the neighborhood, and the officers inside can be seen scrutinizing the people at the “puck.” The cars drive past, but a few minutes later they return and pull over. Several officers get out of each car.
“They take you in for looking alternative — you have to explain to the cops why you’re dressed like that,” a male voice tells someone behind me.
— We’re leaving! Mark commands.
— Stay put, stay put, stay put, I don’t think they’re here for us, the boys on the next bench say, trying to reassure everyone.
— No, they’re definitely here for us, I tell the boys, meaning everyone in the courtyard.
— But you’re at least 18, aren’t you? one of them asks, puzzled. It turns out this is his first time here, and he doesn’t yet know that police can detain anyone.
Mark suggests heading to Chistoprudny Boulevard. He says “nefors” gather there too, but usually no one gets detained. Other teenagers follow his lead, but as before, the crowd splits up: Some walk down Pokrovka, while others cut through residential courtyards. We’ve barely left the “puck” when someone in the crowd lights a joint.
— Was anyone at the “puck”? asks a boy in a white T-shirt with light, wavy hair who has been at Chistye Prudy this whole time.
— Yeah, the cops just showed up.
— Were there even any people there?
— Thirty, at least.
— Ah. Well, I guess most of the others are at Ustinsky Square. There are skins there now, though. Other than that, nothing interesting.
Less than a minute later, next to the boy who complained about skinheads, a group of boys starts discussing how many times each of them has beaten up migrant workers from former Soviet countries. The boy in the white T-shirt gives them a sidelong glance and moves farther away.
“I’m right-wing too,” a fair-haired boy with a short haircut says, approaching the group. He boasts about his experiences in detention. He says he recently got out of a pretrial detention center — though it’s unclear whether he’s confusing it with a temporary police holding facility or a jail for administrative offenses.
“No fucking way!” “Fuck, for real? You’re the man!” “What a guy!” “White pride!” — the boys shout over one another, shaking their new acquaintance’s hand and clapping him on the shoulder.
“Glory to Rod, death to the freak!” shouts the boy who recently “got out of a pretrial detention center,” raising his right arm. The group takes up the slogan and gives Nazi salutes too.
A bottle shatters nearby, and I start to feel uneasy — almost everyone here has talked about fights involving weapons, and there have been repeated stories about broken bottles used as weapons too.
The rain gets heavier, and I decide it’s time to go home.
— Haven’t there been fewer people in KG since the school year started? I ask Mark as we say goodbye.
— Yeah, there have. But I still get drunk every day.
— How’s school going?
— Loving it! I can do both.
— So if there are fewer people, it’s not because school’s started and their parents won’t let them out anymore?
— Oh, that’s only how it works for dumbasses. People who want to get drunk come here to get drunk. We’ve got goals.

Russia Seeks New Gas Buyers in Africa After Losing More Than Half of Gazprom’s Exports

06:19:47 KST

- Category

Russia Seeks New Gas Buyers in Africa After Losing More Than Half of Gazprom’s Exports
Russia is turning to African countries in search of new markets for Gazprom after the state gas giant lost more than half of its exports outside the former Soviet Union following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, The Moscow Times reported on October 16.
Russian Energy Minister Sergei Tsivilev announced that Moscow was prepared to supply gas to African countries while offering exploration, extraction, and broader energy infrastructure services.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Our country can offer a comprehensive solution: modernize existing hydroelectric plants, build solar and thermal power stations, lay networks, supply substations and transformers, and create power-system management and dispatch centers,” Tsivilev stated.
Tsivilev added that Moscow views Africa as a “long-term market,” The Moscow Times reported.
The push comes as Gazprom struggles to replace European customers lost since 2022. According to estimates from Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development cited by The Moscow Times, Russian gas exports are expected to total about 77 billion cubic meters in 2026, down from 185 billion in 2021 and roughly 200 billion at the end of the 2010s.
The ministry projects exports falling further to 72 billion cubic meters by 2028, after the EU gas embargo takes effect. The Moscow Times noted that this would return Russian gas exports to levels last seen in the second half of the 1980s.
Russia has also struggled to secure a major new gas agreement with China. The Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, has sought to increase annual supplies to China to as much as 100 billion cubic meters, but negotiations have stalled over pricing.
According to sources cited by the South China Morning Post, Beijing wants Russian gas priced at around $50 per thousand cubic meters, close to what Russian households pay, or roughly $120-$130 for industrial consumers.
Moscow, however, wants pricing closer to the approximately $250-$260 per thousand cubic meters China currently pays for gas delivered through Power of Siberia 1. That price already represents a discount of roughly 40% compared with Gazprom’s contracts with other foreign customers, which average about $420 per thousand cubic meters.
The Moscow Times reported that negotiations over the proposed Power of Siberia 2 pipeline, which Putin has renamed “Power of Baikal,” are currently suspended because of the disagreement over price.
On October 13, Zelenskyy warned that Russia’s blockade of maritime routes could trigger food shortages across parts of Africa, Asia, and the Middle East within one to two months by restricting Ukrainian grain exports.

Zelensky’s diesel burnout, Nord Stream on trial, Russiagate revived: RT stories that shaped the week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

Zelensky’s diesel burnout, Nord Stream on trial, Russiagate revived: RT stories that shaped the week
Zelensky’s diesel-fueled burnout
This week did not start well for Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky, who was apparently blindsided by US President Donald Trump’s decision to suspend sanctions on Russian diesel supplies after talks with the Kremlin. The deal won’t alleviate the global diesel shortage, but it’s already cooling speculative markets and easing pressure on Trump ahead of next month’s midterm elections.
For Zelensky, it’s a “diplomatic nightmare,” as Russian analyst Sergey Poletaev wrote for RT. Trump rubbed salt in the wound on Saturday when he openly suggested that Ukrainians “get a new leader who can make a deal” and halt attacks on Russian oil refineries. Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump went on to claim, “wants to make a deal more than Zelensky.”
Backed into a corner, Zelensky began throwing haymakers. Accusing the American president of empathizing with dictators, Zelensky demanded air defense missiles from the US before vowing to continue his drone campaign against Russia’s refineries – with or without American support.
The US apparently sent a warning signal to Zelensky by throttling the Ukrainian military’s access to SpaceX’s high-speed Starlink and Starshield satellite communications services, which are vital tools in guiding attack drones used against Russia, and in detecting incoming retaliatory strikes. Neither Trump nor SpaceX CEO Elon Musk would take responsibility for the communications drop-off, but even if they had, their message would likely have fallen of deaf ears.
Zelensky escalates the energy war
The Ukrainian leader followed through on his promise to keep hitting Russian refineries, despite Trump’s announcement of an “energy ceasefire” between Moscow and Kiev (which neither side confirmed). Ukrainian forces attacked facilities in Russia’s Saratov and Ryazan regions on Wednesday, before firing a barrage of four long-range Flamingo cruise missiles and 69 fixed-wing kamikaze drones at the Ryazan refinery again on Thursday.
Debris from an intercepted UAV triggered an intense fire at the facility, according to the Russian Defense Ministry.
Retaliation was swift, from both Moscow and Washington. Russian forces used missiles and drones to strike six power plants in Kiev, Kharkov, and the surrounding regions, as well as military logistics hubs and data centers. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that it shot down four missiles out of 39, confirming reports that Zelensky launched the refinery strikes knowing Ukraine lacked adequate air defense supplies to repel the retaliation.
Trump went on to savage Zelensky in a Newsmax interview on Thursday. “I’m not a big fan of Zelensky. They’ve destroyed that country,” he said, before accusing the Ukrainian leader of selling missiles given to him by the US “on the open market.”
“Zelensky is not a good guy for us to deal with,” Trump concluded.
Nord Stream trial begins
As Ukraine doubles down on its infrastructure war, the costliest infrastructure attack in history is finally being litigated in a German courtroom. Sergey Kuznetsov, a Ukrainian military officer, went on trial in Hamburg this week, accused of leading the team that sabotaged the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines in September 2022, an act that German prosecutors consider a “war crime.”
Kuznetsov is staying silent, refusing to admit or deny a role in the bombing. The evidence against him is circumstantial, and his lawyers are confident that without a confession, he “cannot be convicted.”
As RT has explored in depth, the prosecution’s version of events is riddled with plot holes and inconsistencies. However, to pick apart the alternative story – that the pipelines were destroyed in a CIA operation – would call the relationship between Washington and Berlin, the foundation of the postwar liberal order, into question.
While a guilty verdict against Kuznetsov would directly implicate the Ukrainian military in a war crime against its largest foreign donor, the trial, at least at this stage, appears set up to avoid this outcome.
Russiagate resurrected
Speaking of reopening old wounds, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham dug up the bloated corpse of ‘Russiagate’ this week to bolster his efforts to undo the 2016 Brexit referendum and rejoin the EU. Burnham claimed that he had “clear” evidence that Russia interfered in the vote, in which Britons voted by 51.89% to 48.11% to leave the union.
Just as the original ‘Russiagate’ claims against Trump fell apart under questioning, Burnham’s allegation crumbled once subjected to some basic scrutiny. The British PM was unable to back up his accusation when grilled in Parliament, and his foreign secretary, Stephen Doughty, humiliated himself on national television when he attempted to evade questioning on the claim.
The final nail in the coffin came when Burnham’s own domestic intelligence chief cautioned against exaggerating “Russian influence” on Brexit, arguing that debating the influence of “Russian trolls” on the vote “play[s] into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.”
However, Burnham couldn’t be faulted for his timing and opportunism. As he spoke of Russian bots and influence campaigns in Parliament on Monday, Zelensky, his Polish and Baltic backers, and his army of internet supporters claimed that a Ukrainian strike on a Yandex data center in Russia the previous day had wiped thousands of “Russian bots” from social media.
As it turned out, none of this was true. The strike interrupted the activity of Yandex’ web crawler bots, which archive websites for search users, but with the help of an AI-created graph and some creative interpretation of the word “bot,” the hoax made it all the way to the Warsaw Security Forum.
French riots spread
French students took part in a fifth wave of demonstrations this week, which they say are aimed at securing more school funding and better learning conditions. Every wave of protests thus far has descended into rioting and vandalism, and this week’s marches were no different, with participants torching cars and battering police officers with cobblestones and fireworks in Paris.
RT’s Nadege Abderazzak watched heavily armored police baton-charge crowds of rioters in the French capital on Wednesday, noting that officers now outnumber protesters two-to-one at some rallies.
With French President Emmanuel Macron determined to increase military spending and continue arming Ukraine, France’s financial situation is in dire straits, and right-wing National Rally leader Marine Le Pen is on track to win the country’s next presidential election.
Meanwhile, Albanian students have taken a page out of their French counterparts’ book. After large protests demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama and opposition leader Sali Berisha over corruption allegations, a crowd of students breached the fence of the Education Ministry in Tirana on Wednesday and torched the building.
Rama’s response has also drawn from the Western playbook, with the Albanian PM accusing protesters of waging “hybrid war” against the country.
What we’re watching
Zelensky may be in Trump’s bad books, but he can still count on the support of Macron, Burnham, and the rest of his European backers, whom he met in Brussels on Thursday and Friday. In his address to the European Council on Friday, the Ukrainian leader asked for another “70 billion euros” for ammunition, missiles, and air defense. Should Ukraine “fall,” Zelensky warned, another 20 million Ukrainian migrants will flood into the EU.
We’ll be keeping an eye on what kind of promises the cash-strapped Europeans make after this blatant shakedown.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will fly to Tehran on Monday for talks with his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi. The two diplomats are expected to focus on de-escalating the simmering US/Iran conflict in the Middle East, and any progress on this front will likely be reflected in global energy markets.
Lavrov will also meet Serbian Interior Minister Ivica Dacic on Friday, ahead of critical parliamentary elections on October 25. Amid student protests, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic called the election early and stepped down to run as prime minister, a high-stakes move that turned the vote into a referendum on his nine years in power. With pro-Western students and right-wing ‘patriotic’ forces squeezing Vucic from either side, we’ll be keeping an eye out for polls, protests, and interference from the usual suspects.
For more on all of these stories, stick with RT.

Israeli settlers beat up and rob WaPo journalist in West Bank (VIDEOS)
Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine has been badly beaten by Israeli settlers and stripped of her equipment while covering attacks on Palestinians harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank.
The assault occurred on Friday near the village of Abu Falah, the latest in an ongoing string of attacks staged by organized settler groups. Masked settlers have repeatedly attacked Palestinian villages, hurling stones and setting orchards on fire in an apparent effort to disrupt the autumn harvest. The Israeli military, which is usually present, has taken little to no action against the settlers.
Levine, a veteran photographer who has covered conflicts across the Middle East and elsewhere for decades, was caught in a settler charge on the Palestinians. The mob threw the journalist, who was wearing a blue protective vest clearly marked ‘PRESS,’ to the ground, repeatedly kicking her while stealing her cameras and phone.
“They just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times,” Levine told reporters after the incident.
Footage from the scene shows the immediate aftermath, with Levine seen prone on the ground after the settlers were repelled by the villagers. The journalist was badly shaken but apparently spared more serious injuries thanks to her protective vest and helmet.
Severe settler + soldier attack on olive harvesters in Abu Falah. American WaPo journalist Heidi Levine badly wounded. Machine gunfire—at least one Palestinian shot. Tear gas. Soldiers assaulting journalists. pic.twitter.com/He61cNYk0c
— jasper nathaniel (@infinite_jaz) October 16, 2026
The photographer was evacuated by Palestinian paramedics and treated at a hospital in Ramallah for her injuries. Later on, another group of journalists was reportedly pelted with stones by settlers at the site. Oren Ziv, a journalist who also witnessed the attack, reported that at least one Palestinian was wounded by gunfire. It was not immediately clear whether Israeli settlers or the military fired the shots, but the IDF reportedly did nothing to stop the violence.
The Washington Post strongly condemned the attack and called for a full investigation. “While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities,” Matt Murray, executive editor of the Post, said in a statement.
Ten days earlier, veteran Palestinian photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh, who has been working with AFP, suffered a similar assault during a settler raid on Palestinian olive farmers. The journalist, marked as press, was attacked by armed Israeli settlers, who beat him with rifle butts and robbed him of his equipment. The violence was reportedly witnessed by an IDF unit that did not intervene.
Journalists documenting settler violence have increasingly become victims of it. The Committee to Protect Journalists documented at least 16 incidents involving 35 Palestinian, Israeli, and international journalists in the first eight months of 2026 alone, with the figures already surpassing those recorded in 2025.

Meta employees say Lula’s accounts restricted in Brazil election: Report
The messages, reported by a Brazilian daily, say the platform recommended Bolsonaro’s profile and his WhatsApp channel.
Employees at Meta have acknowledged in internal communications that the Instagram accounts of Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva were negatively affected by restrictions during the country’s election, media reports say.
The messages, reported on Friday by Brazilian daily Folha de S Paulo, also acknowledged the platform recommended the profile of Lula challenger Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, as well as his WhatsApp channel. Folha, the Sao Paulo-based paper, cited messages it had reviewed.
Meta told the Reuters news agency that the technical issues cited in the report were already public and the conversations it referenced related solely to the severity of the issues, not political interference.
“Any suggestion that Meta favors one side is false,” it added in a statement.
Lula, the left-wing incumbent, will face right-wing challenger Bolsonaro in a presidential runoff on October 25, following a stronger-than-expected performance by the senator in the first-round vote earlier this month.
Friday’s report came on the heels of a Brazilian court ruling on Thursday that ordered Meta to immediately adopt measures to provide equal treatment of the two candidates ahead of the runoff.
The ruling by a judge in Brazil’s top electoral court was made shortly after Lula filed a complaint that accused the tech giant – which owns Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp – of using biased algorithms and AI restrictions to favour opposition candidate Bolsonaro ahead of the election.
Justice Marco Aurelio Bellizze ruled that Meta cannot reduce the distribution of political content, restrict searches or remove posts in a way that creates an imbalance between Lula and Bolsonaro. His ruling also orders the company to ensure its artificial intelligence tool applies identical criteria to both candidacies.
Bellizze said in his ruling that Meta must pay a fine of 500,000 reais ($98,700) per day if it fails to comply.
According to Lula’s party, some of his posts appeared without a share button and had reduced reach. Options for reactions, sharing, audio or accelerated speed were also missing.

The case featured harrowing testimony about violence and sex parties he called “freak-offs”. It was a forceful reckoning for one of music and entertainment’s most influential figures.
In September, NBC News reported that Combs was continuing to enjoy aspects of his millionaire lifestyle at FCI Fort Dix, smuggling in Hennessy cognac; having fellow inmates cook, clean, make his bed and give him massages; and using a contraband cellphone to view social media and an ex-girlfriend’s nude selfies.
TMZ on Wednesday then reported that Combs was injured in a fight with another inmate at Fort Dix and had to be taken out of the prison for treatment. In a rare rebuttal, the BOP refuted TMZ’s report, telling the AP: “The story you are referring to is false and did not happen.”
In the wake of the NBC report, Combs was placed in the prison’s special housing unit, a heavily secured part of the facility away from the general population for inmates with disciplinary issues or security concerns. He has also been docked 41 days of good-conduct credit, pushing his release date back to 2 March 2028, according to the person familiar with the matter who spoke to the AP.
The second US circuit court of appeals in April heard arguments in Combs’s effort to overturn his conviction and sentence, which his lawyers argued was too harsh. The court has yet to rule.

In Brazil, deforestation in the Amazon has fallen to its lowest level ever recorded, earning praise for the president
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
00:00:37 EEST
06:00:37 KST

In Brazil, deforestation in the Amazon has fallen to its lowest level ever recorded, earning praise for the president
Kyiv • UNN
Over the year, deforestation in the Amazon fell to 3,335 km² — the lowest level since 1988. At the same time, the number of fires in the state of Amazonas increased by 253%.
Brazil recorded a record reduction in deforestation in the Amazon rainforest. Over the past year, the area of destroyed forest decreased by 41.8%, reaching its lowest level since satellite monitoring began in 1988. Bloomberg reported this, citing Brazil's Ministry of the Environment, writes UNN.
Details
According to official data, 3,335 square kilometers of forest were cleared in the Amazon over the 12 months through July 2026. This was the result of the strengthened environmental policy of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who returned to power in 2023.
His administration revived the operations of the Amazon Fund, stepped up the fight against illegal mining and land clearing, and expanded protected areas. In 2023, deforestation fell by more than 20%, and in 2024 by a further 31%.
Record reduction in deforestation accompanied by large-scale fires
Our goal remains to achieve zero deforestation by 2030
At the same time, the situation with forest fires remains difficult. In the state of Amazonas, the number of fires increased by 253% compared with last year. Climate change, the El Niño phenomenon and human activity are cited among the causes.
Environment Minister João Paulo Capobianco said that the authorities were investigating a possible link between deliberate arson and the presidential elections. Special rescue units were deployed to fight the fires.
The new environmental figures were released ahead of the second round of the presidential election, in which Lula is set to face Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro. Under the latter's rule, deforestation in the Amazon reached a 15-year high.

The United States holds the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership globally, making it the world's most heavily armed society.
Persistent mass shootings in the US have repeatedly heightened public calls for stricter federal gun control measures.
Despite repeated calls over the years, the US Congress has yet to enact such restrictions.
"America's gun violence crisis is killing our babies. Enough is enough," gun-control group GIFFORDS said on X.

Griffin's neighbours told AFP they had seen his mother taken away from the house she shared with the suspect on Thursday afternoon in a police patrol car.

The government of Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has accused former president Joseph Kabila of planning a "general attack" after he teamed up with M23 rebels to take on Kinshasa's forces.
Kabila "has decided to formalise his widespread attack against the Republic," government spokesman Patrick Muyaya told AFP news agency on Friday, adding that "the choice to take up arms means killing Congolese in order to try to conquer territories".
"They want to launch a movement to give themselves a new face, but in reality the intentions, the macabre plans, the modus operandi are known," Muyaya said in an interview.
"The players remain the same, the nature of the movement remains the same," he added.
Kabila on Monday joined forces with the M23 rebels to head a new outfit, taking a more direct role in the insurgency ravaging the DRC's volatile east.
The new group — the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN) — was presented as a "politico-military" outfit that will "pool their strengths, resources and means" with the aim of "putting an end to tyranny by any means, including force."
It will be headed by Kabila with M23 rebel chiefs serving as deputies.
Kabila was condemned to death in absentia a year ago for "complicity" with the M23 rebels.
The 55-year-old Kabila, who ruled from 2001 to 2019, is accused by DRC authorities of being an initiator of the Congo River Alliance (AFC), the now dissolved political wing of the M23.
Kabila has denied the allegations.
Volatile time
After several years outside the country, Kabila reappeared in May 2025 in the major eastern city of Goma that is now controlled by the M23 rebels. He has since made regular visits to rebel-held territory.
In early 2025, an offensive led by the M23 rebels in the eastern DRC resulted in the capture of Goma and Bukavu.
Since then, the front line has stabilised, though fighting continues — at times intense, involving drone strikes and artillery barrages — particularly in South Kivu province.
Kabila's return to the political scene comes at a volatile time.
Opposition rallies in June and September protested against a proposed constitutional amendment that could pave the way for a third term for the current president, 63-year-old Felix Tshisekedi.
Tshisekedi, who succeeded Kabila, reaches the end of his second and constitutionally last five-year term in 2028.
The main opposition coalition has so far kept its distance from Kabila.
Kabila however has expressed support for the opposition.
In a speech posted online on Friday, he criticised the government for being "motivated solely by its own perpetuation in power".

KFC is dropping Pepsi in favor of Coca-Cola: PepsiCo could lose $500 million a year
Kyiv • UNN
KFC in the United States will replace Pepsi with Coca-Cola. PepsiCo could lose approximately $500 million in annual sales and some restaurant partnerships.
The American fast-food restaurant chain KFC has decided to stop serving Pepsi beverages and switch to Coca-Cola products at its U.S. locations. Analysts forecast that, due to the loss of its long-standing partner, PepsiCo could miss out on approximately $500 million in annual sales. Reuters reports, according to UNN.
Details
According to estimates by Bank of America analysts, ending its cooperation with KFC could lead to an approximately 3% decline in sales of Pepsi beverage concentrates in North America. At the same time, Coca-Cola could increase the corresponding figure by 2.5% thanks to the new partnership.
KFC's decision has created an additional challenge for PepsiCo, which is already facing weak demand and rising costs in the North American market. The company's return to profitability is progressing more slowly than expected, forcing it to step up cost-cutting measures.
Why the loss of KFC could become a problem for PepsiCo
Jefferies analysts believe that the main threat to PepsiCo lies not so much in the financial losses as in the weakening of the brand's position and the possible review of other long-standing contracts with restaurant chains.
The fact that a longtime Pepsi customer is switching to a competitor raises the question of whether other partners that previously seemed out of reach could now also change suppliers
Richard Exon, founder of the independent creative agency Joint, also believes that investors view KFC's decision primarily as a signal of changing competitive positions in the market, rather than as a critical financial loss for PepsiCo.
Thus, KFC's switch to Coca-Cola could have broader implications for the U.S. soft-drinks market, as it draws attention to the stability of PepsiCo's other partnerships with major restaurant chains.

Ukraine has accumulated record-high gas reserves in six years ahead of winter — Naftogaz
Kyiv • UNN
Gas reserves in underground storage facilities have reached 16 billion cubic meters — the highest level since 2020. Naftogaz has additionally contracted more than 1 billion cubic meters.
Ukraine has accumulated 16 billion cubic meters of gas in underground storage facilities ahead of the heating season. This is the highest level since 2020, despite intensified Russian attacks on energy infrastructure. Acting Chairman of Naftogaz Serhiy Fedorenko said this in an interview with Reuters, reports UNN.
Details
According to him, during 2026, Russia attacked the company's facilities more than 400 times—twice as often as last year. Oil and gas production, processing, and transportation facilities, as well as thermal power plants in frontline regions, came under attack.
This year, most of our facilities have been hit
Will Ukraine have enough gas for the winter?
The current reserves exceed the minimum volume of 13.2 billion cubic meters that the government has deemed necessary to get through the winter. For comparison, Ukraine began the previous heating season with reserves of less than 14 billion cubic meters.
At the same time, gas consumption in the country is declining. According to Fedorenko's forecast, it will amount to about 20 billion cubic meters in 2026, compared with 21 billion last year. One of the reasons was the shutdown of some industrial enterprises due to Russian shelling.
To provide additional security for the heating season, Naftogaz has already contracted imports of more than 1 billion cubic meters of gas, 25% of which will be liquefied natural gas. The supplies are scheduled for the period from December to March.
Ukraine has also offered the European Union the use of its underground gas storage facilities, whose total capacity is about 30 billion cubic meters. A third of this capacity is ready to be allocated to European partners.
Despite the record reserves, Naftogaz is cautiously assessing the prospects of getting through the winter because of the constant threat of new Russian strikes and possible damage to energy infrastructure.

In Russia's Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug, a fire broke out at the Viktor Chernomyrdin Condensate Stabilization Plant, owned by Gazprom, following a drone attack. The facility is located near Surgut, more than 2,000 km from the Ukrainian border. ASTRA reports this, citing the results of an OSINT analysis, writes UNN.
Details

ASTRA OSINT analyst examined the available materials, including data provided by the Supernova+ channel, and established the probable location of the strike. According to the analyst's conclusions, the fire started at a technological facility in the central part of the plant's industrial zone.

Armed with a .40-caliber pistol he is licensed to carry, Giamanco pulled over, followed the gunman into the school and witnessed the shooter in a scuffle with a teacher. Giamanco then fired his weapon, killing the assailant, police said.
“The tragedy at Silver Rail elementary has devastated the Bend community,” Giamanco’s family said in a statement, asking for privacy and declining further media interviews. “He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support.”
Speaking briefly to reporters on Friday, Giamanco’s mother read the statement from her phone and said her son appreciated the support but wanted to remain private.
“Yes, my brother shot the shooter in yesterday’s events at the Bend elementary school,” Kameron Giamanco wrote in a public Facebook post on Friday that reiterated the family’s request for privacy in the aftermath of the traumatic event.
“He’s an absolute HERO. However, we are not speaking to media at this time. He’s not ready, nor is the family.”
Though she did not name him, Oregon’s governor, Tina Kotek, praised the man who followed the shooter into the school during a news conference on Thursday.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life,” she said, “your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well.”
Authorities are still investigating what led to the deadly attack, and have not released a motive. The suspect was using a pump-action shotgun purchased by his mother, according to reporting from the Associated Press.
“This is going to be a long investigation,” Bend’s police chief, Mike Krantz, said, adding that the police would maintain a large presence at the school for the next few days.
This story was updated on 16 October 2026 to correct the name of the shooter. His name was Griffin J John II, not John Griffin II.
Anna Betts and Abené Clayton contributed reporting

Hurricane Isaias knocks out Gulf Coast power, NASA images show
Isaias became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season on October 8 and made landfall near Destin, Florida, on the evening of October 9 as a Category 2 storm, with maximum sustained winds of 105 miles (170 kilometers) per hour, NASA’s Earth Observatory reported.
Isaias brought heavy rain, flash flooding and damaging winds to parts of the southeastern United States, including Alabama and the Florida Panhandle. Fallen trees and power lines left many residents without electricity.
Using data from the NOAA-20 satellite’s VIIRS instrument, NASA’s Black Marble HD product captured changes in nighttime lighting before and after the storm. Images from October 11 showed sharp declines in nighttime lighting around parts of Pensacola and along the U.S. Route 98 corridor toward Destin, suggesting widespread power disruptions.
A comparison of images from October 11 and 12 showed nighttime lights beginning to return in some areas. By October 14, lighting patterns appeared similar to pre-storm conditions.
Ranjay Shrestha of NASA’s Black Marble science team said the high-resolution imagery helps identify where outages persist and recovery is progressing, supporting emergency responders in prioritizing resources. However, satellite observations complement ground-based outage reports rather than replace them.
NASA’s Disasters Program is also supporting the Alabama Red Cross and the Alabama Emergency Management Agency in their response to Hurricane Isaias, in coordination with FEMA and the USGS Coastal Storms Team.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that NASA scientists had developed a more precise method to track Earth’s shifting center of mass, revealing how seasonal changes in water, ice and air subtly alter the planet’s balance.

Elka Rоuskov is the newest among “Bulgarian Woman of the Year” laureates
Lyutvie Gencheva named “Audience Favourite Bulgarian Woman”
Friday 16 October 2026 22:26
Friday, 16 October 2026, 22:26
Elka Rouskov with the Bulgarian Woman of the Year award
PHOTO BTA
Font size
For the 15th time, the Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad has presented its “Bulgarian Woman of the Year” award to one of the many Bulgarian women who devote their energy, knowledge, emotion and a significant part of their personal time to causes aimed at preserving and strengthening the ties between Bulgarian communities around the world and their homeland. This year, 29 Bulgarian women from 11 countries were nominated.
At a special ceremony in the Maxima Hall of the University of National and World Economy in Sofia, the jury presented the St Zlata Meglenska Award to Elka Rouskov from the United States. She received a bronze statuette and an icon of the saint, the heavenly patroness of Bulgarians abroad.
“I am absolutely delighted to be the newest little bird in the flock of women honoured with this prestigious award,” Ms Rouskov said, dedicating the distinction to Bulgarian schools, folk organisations, libraries, community centres and cultural clubs in the United States and Canada.
“For me, ‘Bulgarian Woman of the Year’ means connection, communication, a bridge and a bond with Bulgaria, as well as great responsibility and love. I cannot sum up this moment or my work for my country in a single word, but it is about connection, a bridge and love for Bulgaria,” she said emotionally in an interview with Radio Bulgaria immediately after the award ceremony.
With Elka Rouskov’s support, a number of ongoing cultural programmes and groups have flourished. They include the Bulgarian Voices women’s choir in Seattle, the Seattle Cheta folk ensemble, the Medena Pitka children’s folk group and the Glagolnitsa literary circle. Through their work, Bulgarian culture is not merely a memory of the past, but a living experience passed down from one generation to the next.
The concerts, theatre performances and cultural events she organises in New York, Chicago, Los Angeles, Phoenix, San Diego, Las Vegas and Seattle build bridges between Bulgarians in different parts of America and showcase the richness of the Bulgarian spirit to a wider audience.
Elka Rouskov also makes a point of engaging young people. At her initiative, the Little Bulgarian School in Chicago organises the Bulgarian poetry recitation competition How Beautiful You Are, My Homeland.
Elka Rouskov with Zivka Bubalova-Petrova, Director of the Little Bulgarian School in Chicago
PHOTO Joan Kolev
“What matters to me is that we continue our work in support of Bulgarian organisations abroad,” Elka Ruskova said. “They need this support enormously because they are involved in educating Bulgarian children abroad every day. I can say this because I have witnessed their work for years. I believe that, particularly in the United States, we should strive to work together with Bulgarian organisations, community centres, libraries, folk ensembles, festivals and schools. This will be my next mission to bring people together, and I am glad and hopeful that I will have the strength and support to pursue it, as I have had until now.”
Ms Ruskova added that she would be happy to support initiatives that could unite members of the newly established Club of Bulgarian Woman of the Year - St Zlata of Meglen laureates around shared causes.
Plaques recognising contributions to the promotion of the Bulgarian language, folklore, culture and spirituality abroad were presented to Elisaveta Yordanova, founder and choreographer of the Gorana ensemble in New York; Teodora Mileva, representing the management of the Sts Cyril and Methodius Bulgarian Cultural and Educational Organisation in Vienna; Elka Rouskov, one of the co-founders of the Bulgarian Cultural Centre in Seattle; and Yana Belichka, head and choreographer of the Zornitsa ensemble in Montreal.
PHOTO Joan Kolev
To mark the 15th presentation of the Bulgarian Woman of the Year - St Zlata Meglenska 2025 award, special lifetime achievement distinctions for promoting Bulgarian culture and spirituality around the world were presented to Diana Glasnova of Zagreb, Croatia, editor-in-chief of the Rodna Rech magazine, and Violeta Zhelyazkova of Boston, United States, who helped establish a Bulgarian cultural centre in the city 25 years ago.
Special recognition was also given posthumously to Kamelia Ilieva, editor-in-chief of the Bulgarian magazine Roden Glas, published in the Czech Republic. Her husband, Sasho Iliev, accepted the plaque on her behalf.
Once again, the “Audience Favourite Bulgarian Woman” award was also presented. This year’s recipient was Lyutvie Gencheva of Freiburg, Germany, founder and driving force behind the folk dance ensemble Mladost na Megdana (“Youth on the Village Square").
The Executive Director of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, Raina Mandzhukova, presents Lyutvie Gencheva with the "Favorite Bulgarian of the Audience" award
PHOTO BTA
The ensemble brings together Bulgarian school pupils and young people aged 15 to 25 from Germany, France, the Netherlands, Spain, England and Sweden. It came into being spontaneously at the end of the tenth edition of the Na Megdana na Drugata Bulgaria (“On the Village Square of the Other Bulgaria”) festival, held in Lyon in 2025. Today, its members have already performed at an impressive number of events in Bulgaria and across Europe.
“We hardly dared to dream that it would develop this way,” Ms Gencheva admits, listing some of the dance troupe’s upcoming appearances: in London on 24 October, in Arbanasi on 30 October, and in Sofia on 31 October, when it will perform at the National Palace of Culture alongside the Trakia ensemble. 
On 7 November, the group will take part in a concert marking the tenth anniversary of the Association of Bulgarian Folk Ensembles Abroad.
Lyutvie Gencheva with the "Audience's Favorite Bulgarian" award
PHOTO Joan Kolev
“The award means a great deal to me because the Audience Favourite is a woman people have voted for, and people vote only when they know someone and are familiar with what she does. I am grateful to everyone who voted for me, especially as there were 29 Bulgarian women nominated this year.
“Metaphorically speaking, each one of them is a storm wherever she lives, striving in her own way and drawing on her own strengths to preserve the Bulgarian community or guide it in a particular direction. I would very much like these women to have the opportunity to unite around common goals in the future, so that they can move things forward together and 29 storms can become a hurricane.”
Anita Ekenova, Lyutvie Gencheva, Radoslava Nedyalkova
PHOTO Joan Kolev
The Executive Agency for Bulgarians Abroad established the Bulgarian Woman of the Year - St Zlata of Meglen award in 2009. According to tradition, Zlata was a young Bulgarian woman who, during Ottoman rule, refused to renounce her Christian faith despite the cruelty inflicted upon her. She died a martyr and is now revered as the patron saint of Bulgarians living abroad.

US deficit hits $2T in a year, highest level since 2021
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
20:31:15 UTC
05:31:15 KST

The US budget deficit has grown to almost $2 trillion over the past year, reaching its highest level since 2021.
The expansion comes amid growing worries about the massive $40.3 trillion US debt load, rising inflation, and climbing borrowing costs.
Refunds of the Trump administration's tariffs, after they were overturned, have further widened the budget gap.
The federal deficit, which occurs when government spending exceeds its revenues, rose to $1.99 trillion in fiscal year 2026, the Treasury Department said.
This marked a 12-percent increase from the prior year, when the shortfall came in at $1.78 trillion.
A key driver of expenditures was the rising interest paid on public debt, which jumped $144 billion to a record $1.36 trillion.
Interest costs on around $32 trillion in publicly held US debt have been ballooning in recent years, and climbing bond yields have sparked further concerns.
Treasury bond yields, which influence interest rates for mortgages and auto loans, have jumped this year, with steeper borrowing costs adding to pressures that US voters face ahead of November's midterm elections.
Treasury data released Friday showed $145 billion in customs refunds over the year, primarily from tariffs, erasing significant gains from Trump's duties.
Overall, government revenues climbed by three percent to $5.40 trillion in the latest fiscal year, which ended September 30.
But spending was much higher, rising by six percent to $7.40 trillion.
War risks
The Trump administration has pledged to cut deficits and government spending since it returned to the White House last year.
Besides slashing the federal workforce and foreign aid, the Republican-controlled Congress pushed through cuts to the Medicaid health insurance scheme and moved to shrink the federal food assistance program too.
But they also extended expiring tax cuts and provided fresh funding for administration’s migrant deportation drive.
The latest data released on Friday showed that higher tax collections from individuals and customs revenues were offset by more refunds and lower corporate tax collections.
Among other sectors, spending on defence military programs increased by $48 billion, or six percent, over the year to $917 billion.
Taken together, a Treasury official estimates the US deficit-to-GDP ratio is around 6.2 percent, up from 5.8 percent last year.
This stands in contrast to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's previously stated goal of bringing the deficit down to three percent of GDP, alongside other targets like spurring economic growth of three percent.
The latest budget figures come less than three weeks before US midterm elections, where US President Trump's Republican party is fighting to retain control of Congress.
Ahead of the crucial vote, both Republicans and Democrats have raised ideas that could widen the budget shortfall further.
Democrats say they are looking to reverse Medicaid cuts and revive health care tax breaks.
