Author
Krasimir Martinov
Report
Bratislava marks 100 years of academic study of Bulgarian
The Bulgarian National Radio is a media partner of the celebration
Friday 16 October 2026 21:35
Friday, 16 October 2026, 21:35
The building of the Philosophy Faculty of Comenius University in Bratislava
PHOTO facebook.com/fphil.uniba
Font size
A scientific conference on Bulgarian-Slovak intercultural dialoguewas held at Comenius University, Slovakia’s largest and oldest higher education institution. The university’s Moyzes Hall also hosted a celebratory concert entitled The Mystery of Bulgarian Polyphony, performed by the Bulgarian vocal quartet Svetoglas. The occasion is the centenary of the beginning of academic studies of the Bulgarian language in Bratislava.
The two-day academic forum is held under the patronage of H.E. Snezhana Yoveva-Dimitrova, Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Republic of Bulgaria to the Slovak Republic, and Prof. Dr Marian Zouhar, Dean of the Faculty of Arts at Comenius University. Bulgarian is taught within the university’s Department of Slavic Philologies.
“Marking this impressive anniversary is important for the development of Bulgarian studies worldwide as a whole,” Bulgaria’s ambassador to the Slovak Republic, Snezhana Yoveva-Dimitrova, told Radio Bulgaria in an interview.
H.E. Snezhana Yoveva-Dimitrova
PHOTO facebook.com/Bulgarian.Embassy.Slovakia
“The Bulgarian Embassy in Bratislava has been actively involved in preparing and organising both the celebratory concert by the Svetoglas quartet and the logistics of the international academic conference and its accompanying events at Comenius University. These include presentations of specially prepared documentary and facsimile exhibitions dedicated to Bulgaria’s cultural and historical heritage, the country’s ancient treasures and its monuments inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List. We are implementing these projects in cooperation with partners such as the Institute of Balkan Studies with the Centre of Thracology at the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences, the State Institute for Culture at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Bulgarian National Radio and others.
We believe that this celebration will help strengthen interest in Bulgarian studies. That is why we are also encouraging pupils from the Hristo Botev Bulgarian Secondary School to take a more active part in various accompanying initiatives. They are among the potential future students of the university’s Faculty of Arts,” Ambassador Yoveva-Dimitrova said shortly before the opening of the academic forum Bulgarian-Slovak Intercultural Dialogue at Comenius University.
The major academic event marking 100 years of Bulgarian studies in Slovakia features a series of lectures and discussion sessions held simultaneously in different halls of the university’s Faculty of Arts.
Topics under discussion include the history, development and future of academic Bulgarian-language studies abroad, as well as literary interactions between Bulgaria, Slovakia and the wider Slavic world. Ethnological research on the Bulgarian community in Slovakia is also presented, alongside other issues of bilateral and international academic interest.
Asked how ties between Bulgarian and Slovak scholars influence relations between the two countries, HE Snezhana Yoveva-Dimitrova said that the Bulgarian and Slovak Academies of Sciences had maintained an excellent partnership for many years.
“This cooperation is based on inter-academic agreements, which are due to be updated very soon,” the Bulgarian ambassador continued. “Just a few months ago, the President of the Slovak Academy of Sciences, Prof. Martin Venhart, paid an official visit to Sofia, where he met with Prof. Evelina Slavcheva. Updating the agreement between the two academies was one of the topics discussed. They also addressed the exchange of expertise and the links between science and business.
We should point out that Bulgarian scholars are well recognised within Slovakia’s academic community and take part in various projects under European and other programmes. Students, too, participate actively in initiatives such as the Erasmus programme. All of this helps strengthen ties between Slovak and Bulgarian researchers, students and academic communities.”
In her interview with Radio Bulgaria, H.E. Snezhana Yoveva-Dimitrova also spoke about the untapped potential of bilateral relations between Bulgaria and Slovakia, the Bulgarian Embassy’s role in raising Bulgaria’s profile in Slovakia, and the development of the Bulgarian Cultural Institute in Bratislava, which will mark the 55th anniversary of its establishment in November.
The full interview with Bulgaria’s ambassador to the Slovak Republic will be broadcast in the coming days on the Bulgarian National Radio and Radio Bulgaria.

EU leaders regret US decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:41:50 UTC
04:41:50 KST

Melike Pala
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
European Union leaders on Friday expressed regret over the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel, reaffirming their continued support for Ukraine.
"The European Council regrets the United States’ decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel," they said in conclusions adopted after a two-day European Council meeting on Oct. 15-16 in Brussels.
Last week, US President Donald Trump said he struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia to address high fuel prices.
The leaders called for the immediate restoration of safe passage for all civilian and commercial vessels in the Black Sea, describing attacks on shipping, including in the exclusive economic zones of Bulgaria and Romania, as "unacceptable and constitute a serious violation of international and maritime law."
They urged for stronger measures to counter hybrid threats, protect critical infrastructure and improve preparedness, saying further restrictive measures and tighter visa requirements for Russian nationals would be considered urgently.
On European security, the leaders underlined the need to strengthen the EU's defense capabilities while maintaining NATO's role as the foundation of collective defence for its members. 
Middle East, ICC
On the Middle East, the leaders voiced concern over escalating tensions and called for diplomatic efforts to prevent further destabilization, stressing the importance of freedom of navigation and maritime security.
They strongly condemned threats to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and called for any arrangements concerning the waterway to comply with international law.
The leaders also condemned Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and civilian shipping in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait, urging an immediate halt to military operations.
On Gaza and the occupied West Bank, they expressed grave concern over the worsening humanitarian crisis, condemned illegal settlement expansion and "continued and growing settler violence" against Palestinian civilians.
The leaders called on Israel to reverse illegal settlement plans, including the proposed construction in the E1 area.
"It (European Council) reiterates that businesses should not bid for construction contracts for E1 or other settlement developments and underlines the legal, economic and reputational consequences for businesses and financial institutions participating in settlement construction, including the risk of serious breaches of international law," the declaration said.
They also regretted US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), urging Washington to reverse the measures and reaffirming the EU's readiness to protect the court and ensure its continued access to financial and other services.

Nirit is travelling 14,000km to vote in Israel's election. She's not alone
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:38:26 UTC
04:38:26 KST

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.
Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.
Nirit Eylon immigrated to Australia 21 years ago. This month, for the first time, she’s flying back to Israel specifically to vote.
The country does not allow citizens living abroad to vote from outside its borders.
But with an election many view as the most consequential in its history fast approaching, estimates from the US-based Fly&Vote initiative, which helps facilitate their travel, suggest as many as 53,000 Israeli expats are expected to return.
Eylon is among them.
"There is a perception that this election is about right and left. I don't believe it's so. I believe it's between right and wrong," the 52-year-old, who lives in Melbourne, tells SBS News.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Eylon believes Israel is at a crossroads. She views the election as a contest between competing visions of the country’s future: one grounded in liberal democratic values, and another shaped by religious nationalism.
She believes Israel's leaders must be held accountable for failures surrounding the October 7 attacks, and that political change is necessary for Israel to begin to heal.
Eylon is far from alone in viewing this election as pivotal.
Israeli political science expert Shahar Burla, a contributing editor at The Jewish Independent, is one of more than 11,000 Israeli-born people living in Australia.
He tells SBS News he knows around 20 people in his immediate circle who are planning to return to Israel for the election — a circumstance he describes as "very unusual".
"I think that the main motivation is fear," he says.
There is a fear that if the Netanyahu bloc will win again, that will be the end of Israel as we know it as a democratic, liberal, free state.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government has pursued sweeping changes to Israel's institutions, including moves to curb the judiciary’s oversight of government decisions, while pushing increasingly hardline policies towards Palestinians and expanding Israeli military operations across the region, including in Lebanon and Iran.
Ongoing geopolitical tensions and fractured alliances mean the election will be watched closely by many outside Israel too.
SBS News has spoken with nine people from Jewish, Israeli, Palestinian, Lebanese and Iranian communities in Australia about what is at stake for them in this election, as conflict continues to reverberate across the Middle East.
While their views on peace, security and coexistence vary, they share one common belief: that Israel cannot continue on its current path.
For Palestinian Australian academic Shamikh Badra — who lost his father, his brother and his brother’s family to the war in Gaza — a change of government would be welcome, but he cautions it's not a simple fix.
"I am not saying that [the] next government will automatically be better, but removing this government is the first step," he says.
The electoral landscape
Netanyahu, as leader of the Likud party, has served as Israel's prime minister for nearly 20 non-consecutive years since he was first elected in 1996.
In the lead-up to the 27 October election, a relatively new, centrist party called Yashar has been polling neck and neck with Likud.
Former Israel Defense Forces (IDF) chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot leads the party, which takes its name from the Hebrew word for 'straightforward' or 'honest'.
Eisenkot is Netanyahu’s primary challenger to lead the country, and has a personal stake in Israel's ongoing conflicts, having lost both his son and nephew in the Hamas-Israel war.
He's running on a platform of accountability for the October 7 attack, promising to restore trust in Israel's institutions and strengthen national security.
But neither party is close to winning enough seats for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.
That means coalition-building will be crucial to forming government.
Currently, Israel’s parties are divided over their willingness to govern alongside Netanyahu rather than splitting along traditional left-right lines. Two distinct camps remain: those willing to join a Netanyahu-led coalition, and those who may be willing to join one led by Eisenkot.
But neither bloc appears to have a clear path to a parliamentary majority, raising the prospect of political deadlock.
Burla notes that while Eisenkot has positioned himself at the political centre, his prospective coalition spans the political spectrum and includes right-wing parties.
That limits how far a new government could go on issues such as recognising Palestinian statehood and negotiating territorial compromise.
Among Israel's major Jewish-led parties, support for Palestinian statehood remains limited. Yair Golan, leader of the left-wing Democrats, is the only major party leader to have endorsed a future two-state solution.
Burla believes changing Israel's leadership could remove a "first obstacle" to peace with Palestinians, but does not expect significant progress in the coming years.
"None of them will speak about a Palestinian state at this stage, or any territorial compromise with the Palestinians.
"But I think that Eisenkot has at least the potential, the political potential, to move forward some kind of a peace process."
High stakes for those with a vote — and those without one
Yasmeen Abu Fraiha is a medical doctor who works with humanitarian missions in the Middle East.
She's one of roughly two million Palestinian citizens of Israel, a group that makes up around 20 per cent of the country’s population.
Fraiha tells SBS News many "feel the urgency in these elections". She believes Palestinian voters will turn out in higher numbers than they have for previous polls.
Palestinian citizens of Israel have historically voted at lower rates than the wider population. In the 2022 election, just over half of Arab and Druze voters cast a ballot, compared with more than 70 per cent nationally, according to the Israel Democracy Institute.
Fraiha, too, feels democracy is at stake. But for Palestinians, she says, the consequences are more fundamental.
"I don't know if it will be necessarily better if [Netanyahu] loses, but it will definitely be worse if they win again," she says.
It’s really a matter of life and death for us as Palestinians, for sure in the West Bank and Gaza, but also inside Israel.
Yet many Palestinians who will be directly affected by the election’s outcome will have no say in it.
Badra, the Sydney-based researcher and community organiser from Gaza, says his family paid the ultimate price under Israel’s current government. His priority is to see it removed from power.
Beyond that, a path to peace will not be easy. But Badra says any lasting solution must address Palestinian rights and security, including an end to occupation and settlement expansion.
"Security for Palestinians means being able to live in your home without fear of bombing. It means children have food, medicine, education. It means people being able to move freely and live with dignity," he says.
"It also means real political and human rights for Palestinians."
On 7 October 2023, Hamas killed 1,200 people and took another 251 captive during its attack on southern Israel.
Israel's retaliatory bombardment of Gaza has decimated much of the strip and killed more than 74,000 people, including more than 1,400 since a ceasefire began last October, according to the local health ministry.
The humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire, with critically limited access to food, water and essential services. UNICEF estimates nearly 84 per cent of Gaza’s population continues to live in overcrowded displacement sites or damaged shelters.
Far from Israel, but close to home
The election’s outcome will be felt far beyond Israel. For many Australians like Sam Hoballah, the results will be deeply personal.
Born in southern Lebanon, in a town close to the Israeli border, the Sydney-based interpreter moved to Australia 40 years ago.
However, much of his family still lives in Lebanon, a country scarred by civil war and decades of regional conflict.
As a child, Hoballah says he grew accustomed to periods of recurring war and insecurity. Last August, before Israel launched its ground invasion of southern Lebanon, he returned to his hometown to visit family.
"This time it was different," he tells SBS News of the conflict in recent years.
"While [they] have been living in a difficult, insecure situation in that part of Lebanon, this time it is catastrophic."
Following the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023, a new chapter began in the decades-long conflict between Israel and the Lebanese militant group Hezbollah.
Despite a ceasefire in November 2024, the conflict flared again in March this year, after Israel and the US initiated war with Iran.
The Iran-backed Hezbollah fired rockets at Israel in support of its ally, triggering a major Israeli air and ground offensive in Lebanon.
More than 4,300 people have since been killed in Lebanon, according to the country’s health ministry, while dozens of Israelis have been killed in the conflict.
Israel’s occupation and bombardment of southern Lebanon has flattened villages and displaced hundreds of thousands of people.
Hoballah says his own siblings are among them; parts of his hometown, Shaqra, have been reduced to rubble.
"It's a total misery there now," he says.
"So you can imagine the psychological impact this has on our community here [in Australia]."
The 66-year-old says he can’t recall a time in his life when people in southern Lebanon felt safe under any Israeli government.
"To be honest, there was some differences, but no major difference."
He has little faith the election will bring meaningful change, but hopes to see Israel led by a more moderate coalition.
I'm a person who believes that people of different nationalities, race, faith, they can live together, and we can live with the people in Israel.
For Australians with ties to Iran, the war has also brought Israel's political future into sharp focus.
Suren Edgar, vice president of the Australian Iranian Community Alliance, says the conflict has affected many in his community very personally.
"You are consistently checking the news, trying to contact people and worrying about what may happen next," he tells SBS News.
He says decisions made by Israel’s next government "could have direct consequences" for his friends, family and the wider region.
"For me, what is at stake is whether the region moves toward another cycle of war, or towards greater stability."
Edgar hopes Israel's next government will balance its security concerns with the need to protect civilians and infrastructure, recognising that long-term security cannot come from permanent regional conflict.
"I hope it understands that weakening the Islamic Republic and weakening Iranian society are not the same thing."
Across different diaspora groups, the election is also being viewed as a vote on the direction the country will take in managing its foreign relationships and conflicts into the future.
Ric Benjamin is chair of the New Israel Fund Australia and a longtime organiser within Australia’s Jewish community.
He says many Jewish Australians feel "strongly connected to Israel" and are passionate about its elections, even if they can’t cast a ballot.
Benjamin points to the work of Jewish and Palestinian Israelis who continue to cooperate despite the conflict, such as those in the health and humanitarian sectors, as a rubric for Australians navigating their own divisions.
"If it's possible for people who are on the ground in the conflict, who have on both sides lost people through war or terror, if they are able to come together, why is it that our communities, 15,000 kilometres away, can't find that when they cry out for help?
Let's focus on the common causes and the common issues we have, and through that build trust and and build an acceptance.
That desire to break the cycle of conflict at the ballot box is one of the reasons Israeli Australian Limor Fayena has extended her trip to Israel. It will be her first time voting in Israel in 20 years.
The Sydney-based 50-year-old software engineer, who is also Burla's partner, says she hopes her vote will help bring about a "more responsible government" — one that will consider the future being created for the nation's children and grandchildren.
"How can we minimise the option of another war and sit down and think about the future — not the current and not the past?"

European Union leaders called on Israel to immediately reverse plans to expand illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and warned businesses against bidding for construction contracts, citing serious legal, economic and reputational risks, according to a statement issued Friday following a two-day summit in Brussels.
In conclusions adopted at the Oct. 15-16 European Council meeting, EU leaders condemned Israel's continued expansion of illegal settlements and escalating violence by Israeli settlers against Palestinian civilians in the occupied West Bank.
The leaders specifically demanded that Israel abandon plans for new settlement construction in the E1 area, a controversial development project that threatens to further fragment Palestinian territory and undermine prospects for a viable Palestinian state.

Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, are illegal under international law. The International Court of Justice reaffirmed this position in its July 2024 advisory opinion, which found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territories unlawful.

EU vows satellite support for Ukraine but cannot yet replace Starlink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:34:21 UTC
04:34:21 KST

The European Union has pledged to help Ukraine reduce its dependence on US-owned satellite communications, while acknowledging that it cannot replace Starlink in the short term.
Speaking at an EU summit in Brussels on Friday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said services were still being restored after disruptions he described as “a very unpleasant and dangerous surprise”.
Ukraine reported restrictions this week on some Starlink internet terminals, saying they had hampered its ability to defend against Russian forces.
The disruption came amid renewed tensions between Kiev and Washington even as US President Donald Trump denied ordering temporary disruption of Starlink service for Ukraine’s military.
EU leaders rallied around Zelenskyy but acknowledged limits to the support Europe could immediately provide.
“We are working hard to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself through satellite imagery and early-warning systems, which are much needed,” French President Emmanuel Macron told reporters after the talks.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned that Europe had no readily available replacement.
“Starlink is really necessary for Ukraine, and unfortunately in the short term Europe can’t replace this capability,” she said.
Europe’s satellite plans
EU countries currently pool and share satellite communications capacity through GOVSATCOM, a programme in which the bloc wants to fully include Ukraine, EU spokesperson Thomas Regnier said.
The EU also plans to incorporate commercial services into GOVSATCOM early next year to help meet military needs while it develops its own satellite network.
That network, known as IRIS², is intended to rival Starlink. Launches are planned for 2029, with full operations targeted for 2030.
Ukraine uses SpaceX’s military satellite service, Starshield, for battlefield communications, mid-range strikes on Russian-controlled territory and interceptor drones.
It also uses the company’s civilian Starlink system, though not for offensive operations.
SpaceX owner Elon Musk, whose stance on Ukraine has shifted repeatedly since 2022, said this week that any disruption was the responsibility of the US government, not his company.
Limited alternatives
European support extends beyond EU programmes. France’s Eutelsat already provides satellite communications services to Ukraine through its OneWeb network, although it has disclosed little about government and military uses.
Its constellation of 648 satellites, however, is far smaller than Starlink’s network of more than 10,000.
According to specialist publication Via Satellite, OneWeb cannot support drone and ground robot operations because of limited capacity and a lack of compact satellite terminals.
Kallas said the European Defence Agency had identified critical capabilities that Europe lacked, stressing that those gaps needed to be filled “as soon as possible”.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also underscored Ukraine’s dependence on the service.
“Starlink is the key for Ukraine, actually, to fight or fight back,” he told reporters. “It takes time for us to have the same capabilities. We do have it, but not enough.”
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said he had discussed Starlink with Macron on Thursday, including how European countries could provide more such services in the near future.

West Bank: US journalist injured by Israeli settlers
October 16, 2026
Washington Post journalist Heidi Levine was injured on Friday after being attacked by a group of Israeli settlers while on assignment in the occupied West Bank, according to the publication.
The Post said that the incident took place near the village of Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah, and involved "dozens of masked Israeli settlers" who attacked Palestinian villagers gathering the autumn olive harvest.
Washington Post says Levine clearly identifiable
Matt Murray, the paper's executive editor, called for an investigation into the incident.
"This morning, a Washington Post photographer, Heidi Levine, was attacked by Israeli settlers while reporting in the West Bank,” Murray said. Levine is a US citizen.
"She was wearing visible markings clearly identifying her as a journalist. While we are relieved that Heidi has received medical care and is safe, we are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities."
Speaking from a hospital bed later, veteran photojournalist Levine, who is in stable condition, said: "I was attacked, pushed to the ground. Luckily I had my flak jacket and helmet, otherwise I probably wouldn't even be here, because they just kept kicking me and kicking me."
Blogger Andrey Khrzhanovskiy filmed the incident and told The Post that the settlers beat Levine with sticks while journalists and villagers were forced back.
Netanyahu's office says facts 'remain unclear'
The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a statement saying it was not yet clear exactly what had happened.
"The facts surrounding the confrontation near Abu Falah, during which Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine was allegedly assaulted, remain unclear and are under investigation.
Netanyahu's office went on to say there were reports that "some 200 Arabs and far-left activists confronted approximately 40 Israeli youths." It said that there was footage of masked individuals from both sides "hurling objects."
"Other footage appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual. The investigation must establish the facts, including who initiated the violence," Netanyahu's office said.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said that both the IDF and the Israel Border Police attended the scene.
"Foreign media personnel were present at the scene and a female journalist was injured during the confrontation. All details of the incident will be examined. Upon arriving to the scene, the forces acted to disperse the confrontation using riot dispersal means," the IDF said in a statement on X.
"The IDF strongly condemns this incident. Attempts to incite friction between populations undermine security in the area," the IDF said.
US condemns 'criminal violence'
The US said it condemned "criminal violence by any party" in the occupied West Bank.
"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and support appropriate investigations as well as legal accountability for those responsible," the AFP news agency quoted a State Department official as saying, on condition of anonymity, without directly criticizing the settlers.
"The Department has reached out to the Washington Post to offer consular assistance," the official told AFP.
US Democratic Senator Chris Coons of Connecticut, in a post on X, called the attack "appalling" and said "there must be swift justice and accountability for perpetrators of violent extremism in the West Bank, which stands in the way of regional peace and is escalating an already unpredictable and dangerous situation."
Attack condemned by press association and advocacy group
The Foreign Press Association represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories and said Levine's passport, phone, wallet and equipment were stolen by the attackers.
"This is the latest in a long line of violent attacks by Israeli settlers against journalists and other civilians in the occupied West Bank," it said.
"Yet our repeated calls for action to confront this lawlessness have been ignored by Israeli authorities," it added.
International press watchdog Reporters Without Borders strongly condemned the attack and called on Israeli authorities to "put an end to this impunity and prosecute the perpetrators of this heinous assault."
"This brazen violence... is evidence of the impunity with which extremist Jewish settlers operate, often under the protection of Israeli armed forces," added the advocacy group, known by its French initials RSF.

Major lender in Bathla development sells debts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:30:19 UTC
04:30:19 KST

Major Bathla lender La Trobe sells $31.2m loan as private credit firms seek to recover funds
In short:
La Trobe Financial has sold its senior loan facility, tied to a Bathla Group development, to investors through a fund managed by 360 Capital.
The $31.2 million purchase would give 360 Capital greater influence over the Marsden Park project.
What's next?
Morningstar expects private credit fund growth to slow substantially.
The fallout from the collapse of property developer Bathla Group continues to reverberate through Australia's private credit market, with lenders taking matters into their own hands to recover money tied up in the failed construction giant.
In one of the latest deals, property investment and funds management group 360 Capital has revealed it acquired a senior loan facility for about $31.2 million through its private credit fund, funded by private investors and entities within the 360 Capital group.
A senior loan facility is the first mortgage debt in a commercial investment and ranks highest in repayment priority.
The ABC understands the debt was acquired from major private lender La Trobe Financial, relating to a Bathla development at 137 South Street, Marsden Park, in Sydney's north-west.
The Marsden Park project comprises 72 apartments and is nearing completion, according to two sources close to the construction.
Half of the apartments have already been pre-sold under contracts worth $25.8 million (excluding GST), 360 Capital said in a statement.
In August, La Trobe disclosed it had $38.1 million in loans to Bathla, comprising four residential loans and one development loan.
The ABC understands through this deal, La Trobe has sold its development loan, recovering all outstanding principal, interest and late-payment charges and significantly reducing its exposure to the collapsed developer.
Deal gives 360 Capital greater control
360 Capital's ASX-listed mortgage investment trust, the 360 Capital Mortgage REIT, already held an $8.9 million loan secured against the development, which ranked behind La Trobe Financial for repayment.
The trust has invested a further $5.2 million in the deal.
"The step was not taken lightly, but is very important to protect the value of the trust's subordinated position," the company said.
The deal means entities associated with 360 Capital now control both the first and second mortgages over the development, giving them greater influence over how the project is completed and the debts recovered.
Morningstar equity analyst Winky Tan said lenders holding first mortgages were in a much stronger position to recover their money, while mezzanine lenders further down the repayment queue risked losing most, if not all, of their investment.
"When you're able to finish the project, you can sell it as a finished product, which will have a much higher valuation than a half-finished project," she said.
Following the purchase, advisory firm Wexted was appointed as receiver, with a focus on speeding up the process of obtaining occupancy certificates and settling the 36 pre-sold apartments.
360 Capital executive chairman Tony Pitt said the group expected to recover the full amount owed to it under the loan.
Ms Tan cautioned that the ultimate financial outcome for any lender would depend on whether the remaining apartments could be sold and at what price, particularly given the downturn in the property market.
'Perfect storm' unfolding in private credit sector
Lenders including Centuria Bass and CVS Lane suspended withdrawals from some funds in August amid concerns about their exposure to Bathla.
MA Financial, which says it has no exposure to Bathla, also introduced withdrawal limits on some of its funds amid concerns more investors could seek to pull out their money.
Major private credit manager Metrics Credit Partners, which also says it has no exposure to Bathla, suspended withdrawals from some unlisted funds amid scrutiny of asset valuations.
Corporate regulator ASIC has previously warned of poor practices across the private credit sector, including questionable asset valuations, opaque fees and inadequate disclosure.
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said the Bathla collapse highlighted the need for stronger oversight, warning the industry was now "beyond warnings" and should prepare for enforcement action.
Ms Tan described the sector as facing "a perfect storm" of higher interest rates and falling property prices, with developers potentially struggling to refinance their debts just as nervous investors sought to withdraw their money.
Morningstar expects growth in private credit funds to slow substantially in the near to medium term, potentially make it harder for developers to secure financing and further worsening Australia's housing shortage.

Russian band Shortparis releases ‘Iliada,’ its first album since the death of singer Nikolai Komyagin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:13:20 UTC
04:13:20 KST

Russian band Shortparis releases ‘Iliada,’ its first album since the death of singer Nikolai Komyagin
On October 9, Shortparis released “Iliada” (“Iliad”), their first album since vocalist Nikolai Komyagin died in February 2026. Its sound is unusual for the band, and its lyrics are probably the most candid in their catalog. Music critic Artyom Makarsky explores how “Iliada” differs from the band’s earlier recordings and how some of its lyrics might be interpreted.
There aren’t many Russian-language posthumous albums. Records by Andy Cartwright and Yung Trappa came out almost immediately after their deaths — both musicians left plenty of finished, unreleased material. In rock, collaborators usually spent a long time finishing the musicians’ work, and most of these recordings revealed a different side of the artist: Kino’s “Cherny albom” (“Black Album,” 1991) drew on house and electronic music, while Yanka’s “Styd i sram” (“Shame and Disgrace,” 1991), completed by Yegor Letov, was more jittery and tense than her other work. There was also Sergei Kuryokhin’s “Detsky albom” (“Children’s Album,” 1998), on which he sang for the first time and ventured into dance music.
Shortparis also change their style on “Iliada.” Acoustic keyboards increasingly replace synthesizers, with horns appearing here and there as the band moves toward epic rock. In 2018, their cover of the glam rock song “All the Young Dudes,” written by David Bowie, was an anomaly in their catalog. After “Iliada,” that experiment seems like a logical step — Shortparis are now releasing music in the vein of early Sparks, Bowie himself, or the unfairly overlooked Soviet art rock band Aprelsky Marsh. Only “Gvozd” (“Nail”) and “Zanovo” (“All Over Again”), with rhythms more typical of the band, recall the old Shortparis.
Still, this change will really surprise only those who missed everything the band has released since keyboardist Alexander Galyanov left in 2023. The tenderness of “Kolybelnaya” (“Lullaby”) and “Proshchalnaya” (“Farewell Song”) has its roots in their soundtrack to Anna Melikyan’s film “Chuvstva Anny” (“Anna’s Feelings”). Straightforward rock was already there on the EP “Grozdya gneva” (“Grapes of Wrath,” 2023), and horns appeared on “Rodnaya zemlya” (“Native Land”), a song from Kirill Serebrennikov’s film “Ballada ob Edichke” (“Limonov: The Ballad of Eddie”).
The band released nothing in 2024 — perhaps they had probably already begun work on ‘Iliada’ by then. They seem to have devoted the past two years to the project, with a pause after Komyagin’s sudden death in February 2026. That summer, the magazine Pravila Zhizni tried to get drummer Danila Kholodkov to open up about what would happen next, but he said only that “right now, nobody’s even trying to think about [new releases].” Still, the band released an album: “Iliada” became their final statement, a monument to Komyagin, and a way to work through their grief.
“Iliada” has three main lyrical themes: death (and, with it, war), silence, and doubt.
Death appears in the opening song’s very first line: “The dead will no longer fall into line.” The theme develops in “Poy so mnoy” (“Sing With Me”), which describes two scenes: birch trees stained with soldiers’ blood and advertisements featuring dead soldiers in the subway. And though fireworks go off — perhaps for Victory Day? — nothing lets you forget death.
Yet the world of “Iliada” is largely closed off: everything that happens to the album’s narrator takes place in Russia. The soldiers have already returned — they lie buried in their native soil. “Russkaya toska, ili Pesnya slabaka” (“Russian Melancholy, or a Weakling’s Song”) recreates a storyline from Alexei Balabanov’s film “Gruz 200” (“Cargo 200”). Another coffin arrives in “Pobeda” (“Victory: Song for a Children’s Funeral Orchestra”) — this time carrying a father rather than a fiancé — as jubilant propaganda contrasts with a sense of catastrophe. Here, too, Ukraine is evoked through allegory: “There the banks are jelly, there the sand is sugar, but the river flows not with water, but with bitter boiling water.” This place promises a soldier certain death.
Silence is the album’s second major theme. The protagonist keeps recalling how he said and did nothing: “I’ll be peaceful, I’ll be meek, I’ll be faithful, a galley slave”; “Do you remember the tear rolling from your eyes when you kept quiet for the first time?”; “Hear that growling? That’s our silence”; and “In the silence, whispers about the country.” He’s hardly happy about it. He’s forever questioning himself (the record’s third main theme): “Maybe these songs aren’t sung in vain?”; “What if I’ve been singing about all the wrong things? What if we’ve all been going the wrong way?” In the line “I’d sing only of love, but the country doesn’t want that,” Komyagin, who often sang of a coarse, gritty romanticism, suddenly realizes he needs to speak about something else after all. Now he’s gone, and these lines full of doubt have become darker still.
Shortparis never wanted to state their position clearly and directly, and Komyagin’s own interviews left the same impression. But war demands an answer. Komyagin understood that, and so “Iliada” became the band’s clearest album. Its lyrics are still full of contradictions, as in the closing lines of “Zanovo”: “All-o-ver-a-gain! You can’t start again! Start again! Everything all over again!” Or take “Molodost” (“Youth”), a song that touches on a possible revolution while telling the story of someone unprepared for it. But the album depicts such a bleak world that the band’s overall position is clear. Komyagin does, however, seem to mourn the Russian soldiers, asking in “Kolybelnaya”: “Who will remember all their faces? Could even you, Lord?” Not every listener will necessarily share that sentiment.
The band’s aptly named label, Fenix Music, stresses that the album should be heard in full, and its cohesion really does matter. But another contradiction emerges here: “Iliada” is clearly an unfinished album, as the titles of some tracks suggest — “Pervaya” (“First”), “Shestaya” (“Sixth”), and “Sedmaya” (“Seventh”). On “Pervaya,” the words are unintelligible, sounding more like a scratch vocal laid over the music for lack of finished lyrics. The two interludes are much the same, with the nonsense words on “Interlyudiya I” (“Interlude I”) clearly following the rhythm of the lyrics to “Poy so mnoy.” “Shestaya” ends the same way.
This unfinished quality seems to be the greatest strength of “Iliada.” Shortparis’ music used to be polished, perfect in many respects — even the noise was deliberate. Now that close listening reveals missing (or very quiet) syllables in Komyagin’s singing, the band’s songs come alive, feel more intimate, and become easier to understand.
Shortparis like to quote literary classics when talking about themselves. In 2025, for instance, they accompanied the news of their return from a European tour with a photograph of a page from Andrei Platonov’s “Chevengur.” It contained a passage about sparrows that don’t fly off to distant lands because they are proletarian birds. A fairly transparent metaphor. The epigraph to “Iliada” uses the same technique, quoting Nikolai Chernyshevsky’s “Chto delat?” (“What Is to Be Done?”):
It was a bold, spirited little song, and its melody was cheerful — there were two or three sad notes, but they were swallowed up by the tune’s overall brightness, disappearing in the refrain, disappearing throughout the final verse.
This reference is more complicated than it seems. The song in the passage is sung by Vera Pavlovna, the protagonist of “Chto delat?” Shortly after this scene, she learns that her husband has killed himself. The song is the French revolutionary song “Ça ira,” written by a former soldier and also known in Russian as “Akh, poydut dela na lad” (“Ah, Things Will Get Better”). Chernyshevsky freely translated this iconic song, which predated “La Marseillaise,” as follows:
We are coarse, but we ourselves suffer from our coarseness. We are full of prejudices, but we ourselves suffer from them, and we feel it. Let us seek happiness, and we will find humanity and become kind — things will get better — we’ll live on, we’ll live to see it.
That “we’ll live to see it” now feels especially bitter, while “Akh, poydut dela na lad” itself seems to hold the key to the record: despite all the contradictions, there is hope. This text mattered to Komyagin — back in 2023, he read it onstage, putting particular emphasis on “We’ll live on, we’ll live to see it.” And Homer’s “Iliad,” after all, tells of the final days of a 10-year war.

Details
At a press conference following the EU summit, von der Leyen said that the agreement reached with China would not resolve the structural imbalance. The EU's trade deficit with China in goods currently exceeds €1 billion ($1.12 billion) per day.

She said that the European Commission would develop a new instrument to swiftly restrict access to the EU single market when this is in the bloc's interests.
She also said that in December the European Commission would present a proposal for a new instrument designed to reduce EU companies' dependence on single sources of supply for certain critical goods.
In addition, the Commission will propose creating a "solidarity mechanism" to support countries or economic sectors that face coercion or retaliatory measures from states outside the EU.

Elon Musk approached US President Donald Trump with a proposal to limit the speed of Starlink satellite communications in Ukraine, disrupting Kyiv’s ability to counter Russian drone attacks, The Telegraph reported on 16 October, citing four sources familiar with the discussions.
The restrictions had immediate consequences for Ukraine’s defenses, forcing some drone missions against Russian positions to be called off and threatening the ability to intercept Russian jet-powered drones as they targeted Ukrainian cities at the time.
According to The Telegraph, Trump agreed with Musk’s suggestion, paving the way for the Pentagon to impose restrictions on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s satellite network used by Ukrainian forces.
The report contradicts Musk’s public claim that the US military and ultimately Trump were responsible for deciding any limits on the system. However, Trump denied that either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing access, while an anonymous US official told AFP that the president had not requested the reduction in service.
The reported restrictions come amid tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. The episode has raised concerns about Ukraine’s dependence on privately controlled communications infrastructure and the risk that changes to US support could weaken its battlefield capabilities.
Starshield restrictions hampered Ukraine’s drone defenses
Starshield is the military-grade version of Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet network. It allows Ukrainian drone operators to maintain communications with aircraft moving at high speeds, supporting both defensive interception missions and strikes against Russian targets.
The speed limit imposed on Ukrainian drones using Starshield was around 160 kph, making it difficult for them to intercept Russian jet-powered drones and missiles traveling at roughly twice that speed.
According to The Telegraph, a senior source said Musk had become concerned about potential backlash from European consumers following the restrictions. A high-ranking European official and two Ukrainian sources reportedly corroborated the account that Musk and Trump were both involved in the decision.
The Pentagon has not publicly explained the restrictions. The report’s account also remains disputed: Trump said on 16 October that he did not believe either he or Musk was responsible for Ukraine losing access, while an anonymous US official cited by AFP said the president had not requested the reduction.
“Trump and Musk must be held accountable”: US senator warns Starlink network failing over Ukraine could cripple its shield against Russian missiles and drones
Ukraine says Starshield capabilities are being restored
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 16 October that restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite communications system had disrupted several military operations, including efforts to intercept Russian jet-powered Geran drones attacking Ukrainian cities.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine did not use Starlink to support attacks inside Russia, but relied on the system to intercept drones targeting civilians, conduct mid-range strikes against Russian military targets in occupied Ukrainian territory, and deliver food and water to frontline troops using drones.
“When the speed was reduced, we were unable to intercept a certain number of jet-powered ‘shaheds,’ [Gerans - ed.]” Zelenskyy wrote on X, adding that Ukrainian forces had lost the ability to carry out some operations while the restrictions were in place.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s Defense Ministry was in contact with partners and had received signals from the White House that the capabilities would be restored. However, he stressed that speeds had not yet returned to their previous levels, although restoration was underway.
Europe warns against dependence on Musk’s network
The latest episode has renewed European concerns about relying on Musk and SpaceX for critical communications infrastructure. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski warned Musk on social media that European customers were watching his actions, The Telegraph reported.
The European Union is developing its own satellite communications system, IRIS², intended to provide an alternative to Starlink, according to The Telegraph. The system is planned to become operational by 2030, leaving Ukraine and European governments dependent on existing providers in the meantime.
The report adds to concerns that decisions made in Washington or by private technology providers could directly affect Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.

GUANGZHOU, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Guangdong Provincial Government recently approved an investigation report into a fatal fire that killed 12 people, with those responsible referred to judicial authorities.
The fire broke out on Dec. 9, 2025, in a self-built building housing a hardware and electrical appliance store on the first floor in Chaonan District, Shantou City. Spreading across 150 square meters, the blaze resulted in the deaths of 12 people.
The direct cause was a lit mosquito repellent stick on the first floor of the building that ignited nearby combustibles, causing lithium-ion batteries stored indoors to explode and triggering the deflagration of other hazardous materials, including polyurethane foam sealant, butane canisters for portable stoves, spray paint and rust remover.
The investigation pointed to a number of problems exposed by the accident, including poor safety management at the store involved, lax government oversight of unpermitted construction, weak routine inspections, ineffective fire safety campaigns and lax quality review of a third-party fire hazard assessment.
Guangdong Building Fire Facilities Inspection Center Co., Ltd. bore responsibility for serious failures in its assessment work and seriously distorted report.
The company and related responsible personnel have been transferred to judicial authorities for handling in accordance with the law. Clues and materials concerning public officials' performance of duties discovered during the investigation have been referred to disciplinary and supervisory authorities. ■

Li Huifang, the person in charge of the Heshi Peixin Kindergarten in Maiji District, and Zhu Jinglin, the executive principal, instructed and organized the addition of toxic materials to food served to children and staff, to make it appear more colorful and attractive for marketing.
According to a verdict issued by the Intermediate People's Court of Lanzhou City in Gansu, Li was sentenced to life imprisonment, deprived of political rights for life, and had 500,000 yuan (about 74,000 U.S. dollars) in personal property confiscated. Zhu received 15 years in prison and a fine of 300,000 yuan. Four kitchen workers were sentenced to between six and eight years in prison, each with fines, for carrying out the instructions.
According to a provincial investigation report released in July 2025, these pastries had been served to children and staff on a monthly basis since May 2024. Of 251 children tested, 247 had abnormal blood lead levels. All 247 children with abnormal blood lead levels received hospitalization or home-based nutritional intervention. By July 20, 2025, most of the affected children had completed their first treatment course and had been discharged from hospitals.
Clinical evaluation by experts demonstrated an average decrease of 40.21 percent in blood lead levels following treatment, achieving the projected therapeutic targets.
According to the July investigation report, provincial disciplinary authorities have investigated 10 local officials, including the provincial health commission director and Tianshui city leaders. The Gansu provincial government has pledged full support for the children's medical care. ■

Director-General of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Qu Dongyu (R) presents the 2026 Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Achievement Award to Wu Bingfang, a researcher at the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS) at the closing ceremony of the World Food Forum, in Rome, Italy, Oct. 16, 2026. The Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS) won the 2026 Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Achievement Award on Friday for developing the CropWatch, a global cloud-based crop monitoring service platform. (Xinhua/Wang Kaiyan)
ROME, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- The Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (AIRCAS) won the 2026 Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) Achievement Award on Friday for developing the CropWatch, a global cloud-based crop monitoring service platform.
The award was presented at the closing ceremony of the World Food Forum, hosted by FAO in Rome, Italy.
Developed by a team led by Wu Bingfang, a researcher at AIRCAS, the platform has helped more than 40 countries and regions monitor crop conditions and supports food security policymaking based on scientific data, according to the research team.
In announcing the award, FAO recognized the platform for transforming complex crop monitoring into an accessible, open cloud service and making it widely available around the world.
According to the research team, the platform has been integrated into FAO's Hand-in-Hand Geospatial Platform and the Group on Earth Observations (GEO) Knowledge Hub. It serves as an important channel and an independent source of timely crop monitoring information for users worldwide.
The team also regularly publishes the CropWatch Bulletin based on the platform, providing the public with a reliable source of agricultural monitoring information. The bulletin has served users in 173 countries and regions to date, said the team.
Speaking to Xinhua after receiving the award, Wu said the recognition affirmed the team's more than three decades of dedication.
"This is not the end, but a milestone on a new journey ahead," he said.
Wu said the team would continue to enhance the platform's innovative capabilities, ease of use and capacity to serve international users, while deepening cooperation with FAO and other international organizations. The team aims to help more countries strengthen their independent crop monitoring capabilities and contribute to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly the goal of "zero hunger."
The FAO Achievement Award recognizes individuals or institutions for outstanding achievements in areas including fisheries, forestry, climate, land and water, and animal and plant health, particularly in sustainable agriculture and rural development and food security. ■

News analysis: Experts urge action on root causes of Red Sea humanitarian crisis
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-17
03:03:22 CST
04:03:22 KST

by Xinhua writers Habtamu Worku, Liu Fangqiang
ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Following yet another deadly shipwreck off the coast of Djibouti, international experts emphasized that the escalating humanitarian crisis along the Red Sea migration corridor demands targeted preventive measures beyond reactive emergency responses.
The eastern migration corridor continues to claim hundreds of lives each year, with more than 900 migrants dead or missing along the route in 2025 alone. However, the number of people who undertake the journey is increasing, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
ESCALATING HUMANITARIAN CRISIS
In one of the deadliest shipwrecks recorded on the route in recent times, at least 139 migrants died last week, while 84 remain missing after their boat, carrying 305 people toward war-torn Yemen, capsized off the Djibouti coast. Only 82 people survived. Another shipwreck in March this year left nine people dead and 45 missing.
Frantz Celestin, IOM regional director for East, Horn, and Southern Africa, expressed deep sorrow over the catastrophe.
"Given the number of days that have passed since the tragic event, we do not expect to see anyone alive, but we might still see (bodies) coming to the shore," Celestin told Xinhua recently.
"What is happening is very heartbreaking. It is difficult to hear, when we have a conversation with those who are affected, what they went through, and how some of them are even suffering survivor's guilt," he noted.
"Parents have been contacting us, sending photos with their name and saying, have you seen my kid? Or, do the ones who were buried look like this person? Something like this is very difficult to hear from a parent," he added.
The IOM classifies the Red Sea route, also known as the Eastern Migration Route connecting the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, as one of "the busiest and most dangerous migration corridors" worldwide.
Each year, tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel through Djibouti and cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen, hoping to reach Gulf countries in search of safety, stability and employment.
Agnes Igoye, a migration expert with the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, an East African bloc, told Xinhua that the route is a key pathway for irregular migrants from Horn of Africa countries as they attempt to cross "harsh overland treks through deserts and risky sea voyages" in hopes of reaching Yemen, often seen as a gateway to Gulf countries.
Noting that the promise of work in Middle Eastern and Gulf countries continues to draw young people despite the grave risks, she said limited safe and regular migration pathways, coupled with economic hardships, leave many with few alternatives.
Highlighting an annual average increase of about 20 percent in movements along the route over the past four years, Celestin warned that this trajectory will continue unless root causes are addressed.
"If things do not change in their home countries, or their home communities, we can expect people to move," he said. "The only way to reduce the number of people on the move is to change the conditions that are forcing them to move."
BEYOND EMERGENCY RESPONSE
Experts urged to address underlying structural factors behind rising fatalities along the maritime corridor, including limited economic opportunities, socioeconomic inequalities and climate vulnerability.
According to Celestin, over 500,000 movements were recorded along the eastern route last year alone, while more than 130,000 migrants have landed in the war-torn Yemen so far this year. The number has already marked an increase of about 20 percent, compared to last year's total of 110,144, and more than doubled the 60,897 recorded in 2024.
"That is a lot of people moving. We need to find a way to reduce the likelihood of that many people moving, and the solution for people to move the regular pathways in a safe and regular manner," Celestin said.
Highlighting the search for safety, stability, and better socioeconomic opportunities as primary push factors, he argued that unproductive agricultural lands caused by climate change, insecurity and conflict, as well as limited employment and economic opportunities are forcing vulnerable populations to seek better conditions abroad.
Experts emphasize that addressing these deep-seated root causes requires comprehensive strategies focused on expanding domestic youth employment, enhancing vocational skills training, and building economic resilience across vulnerable communities in the Horn of Africa.
Sustainable solutions require interconnected initiatives, said Igoye. These include improving border governance, fostering cross-border collaboration, increasing protection services, investing in return and reintegration programs, and working with destination countries to establish safe, legal migration options and regulated employment opportunities.
Celestin called for robust structural reforms, international solidarity, and expanded regular migration pathways to curb dangerous irregular migration.
"We at IOM want to make migration a choice instead of a necessity, and this is what we are working on closely with governments and local communities -- to address the needs of those who tend to move," he added. ■

"Having been in quarantine, she was diagnosed early and is currently receiving supportive care, improving her chances of recovery while limiting the risk of further spread of the disease," the ministry said.

The ministry said additional cases among quarantined individuals remained possible until their monitoring period ended, but assured the public that any new cases would be swiftly detected and treated.
Kenya confirmed on Oct. 6 its first case of Ebola linked to the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, involving an individual who boarded a commercial flight to Nairobi on Oct. 3. A family member then took him to hospital, where medical staff immediately placed him in isolation.
Despite receiving supportive care, the patient died on Oct. 5 and was buried the following day in accordance with the country's safe and dignified burial protocols for viral hemorrhagic fevers. ■

The programs will cover the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region, the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, and three cross-regional groups linking northeast China, including eastern Inner Mongolia, with the Yangtze River Delta, Xinjiang with the Chengdu-Chongqing twin-city economic circle, and the Yellow River bend with the Central Plains.
The circular, jointly released by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, the Ministry of Finance and the National Development and Reform Commission, calls on participating cities to accelerate the implementation of four lists of priority tasks covering hydrogen technology and equipment development, industrial hydrogen projects, fuel cell vehicle promotion, and hydrogen refueling station construction.
Cities are also urged to strengthen industrial and supply chains, promote smooth domestic circulation and avoid local protectionism. The circular also calls for better planning of major projects, stronger safety management, and timely assessment of the pilot programs' economic, social and environmental benefits.
The three departments will assess the pilot programs, with the results serving as the basis for allocating central government reward funds. The funds must be disbursed promptly and used only to support hydrogen energy applications, helping lower hydrogen-use costs and pass the savings on to end users, according to the circular.
The initiative comes as China seeks to expand the use of cleaner energy in industry and transport. Hydrogen produced using renewable electricity can help reduce carbon emissions, although high costs and challenges in storage and transportation remain obstacles to wider adoption.
China is already the world's largest producer and consumer of hydrogen, with output exceeding 39 million tonnes in 2025, according to official data.
Under a policy issued in March, China aims to have 100,000 fuel cell vehicles nationwide by 2030, while each city cluster can receive up to 1.6 billion yuan (about 238 million U.S. dollars) in central government reward funds over the four-year pilot period. ■

====================================================================================================

From Terah to today: The many roads that lead Jews home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:56:53 UTC
03:56:53 KST

For thousands of years, Jews lived in exile, far from the land of our ancestors. Scattered across the world, we dreamed of returning to the country we had once inhabited. Wherever Jewish history carried us, our hearts remained attached to the same place.
We lived in countless countries, spoke different languages, and belonged to different cultures. Through centuries of wandering, one truth remained unchanged. There is only one Jewish homeland.
The first Zionist
Though there is only one Jewish homeland, there are many roads that lead home. This was always true. Terah, the father of Abraham, was raised in a world of idolatry. Yet he felt an inner tug to leave Mesopotamia, modern-day Iraq, and journey toward the Land of Israel. He received no Divine command. He did not believe in the one God, yet something stirred within him, drawing him toward a distant land.
Ironically, he was the first Zionist, the first person described by the Torah as setting out for the Land of Israel from his homeland. His motives are unknown. He gathered his son Abraham and other family members and traveled toward Canaan. Along the way, Terah settled in Haran, where he eventually died.
His son Abraham later heard the voice of God commanding him to continue the journey his father had begun. Abraham traveled to the Land of Israel with a religious mission: to spread belief in the one God. Yet his pagan father had begun the journey.
Evidently, God implanted within the Jewish soul an instinctive attachment to its homeland. He gave us the ability to respond to the pull of land, peoplehood, and historical destiny even without religious commitment or prophetic revelation. At history’s dawn, this attachment could awaken even in a heart that had not yet awakened to faith.
The age of “isms”
This ancient echo reemerged millennia later. The 19th century witnessed a dramatic weakening of organized religion. The Enlightenment and the Age of Reason promised to lift humanity out of the ignorance and suffering of the medieval world. Science, discovery, and individualism propelled humanity toward an era of progress.
Organized religion, and Christianity in particular, was increasingly blamed for centuries of human suffering. Its unholy alliance with monarchy and political power had contributed to bloodshed and feudalism. Religion’s walls were crumbling.
Into this widening void emerged new ideologies. Society abhors a vacuum, and ideologies rushed to replace religion. Socialism, utilitarianism, communism, and other movements competed for the hearts and minds of Europeans.
It was the great age of “isms,” as new systems of thought offered competing visions of human identity, social order, and historical progress.
Yet perhaps the most powerful “ism” of all was nationalism. Increasingly, people defined themselves primarily by their nation rather than their religion. “John” was no longer primarily a Protestant who happened to live in England, but a proud Englishman who happened to be Protestant.
“Gustave” was no longer primarily a Catholic who happened to live in France, but a proud Frenchman who happened to be Catholic. National identity swept across a continent long shaped by religion and religious rivalries.
A Jewish awakening
Unfortunately, Judaism did not fare much better than other religions. With Emancipation, for the first time in our long exile, we were invited to become full-fledged members of an enlightened European society.
Many combined these newfound freedoms with traditional Jewish observance, but others abandoned their Jewish roots entirely.
Many Jews look back with reverence upon the great age of the yeshivot, when brilliant young men devoted years, sometimes decades, to intensive Torah study. This remarkable era helped lay the foundations for the phenomenal growth of Torah study in the modern world.
Yet there was another side to this history. Far more Jews were drawn into the universities and intellectual circles of Europe than into its great yeshivot. For many, the door swung in only one direction: away from Jewish religious life.
Millions of Jews faced the threat of losing their Jewish identity and disappearing into the surrounding culture. Traditional religious appeals no longer spoke to them. If Jewish identity depended exclusively upon religious commitment, an enormous portion of the Jewish people was in danger of being lost to history.
As Jewish identity weakened across Europe, God awakened that ancient echo. In the age of nationalism, Jewish nationalism emerged, offering Jews a way to identify with their land, their people, and their history. It captured the hearts of Jews, including many who had drifted away from religious observance.
Secular Zionism was a Divine impulse, awakening an ancient attachment to our land and people that had lain dormant for centuries. As religious commitment weakened, God stirred a different form of Jewish consciousness. Millions of Jews today express their deepest connection to their people through their commitment to our national project of return and to the modern State of Israel.
Oct. 7 demonstrated how deeply the State of Israel stands at the center of contemporary Jewish identity and how much more vulnerable Jewish life would be without it.
This became even more evident in the subsequent eruption of anti-Zionism and its frequent convergence with antisemitism, which further underscored Israel’s centrality to Jewish identity and the Jewish future. Israel has become a powerful anchor of Jewish belonging, even for Jews whose connection to religious observance is limited.
Thousands of years ago, Terah felt the pull of our land without profound religious conviction. Thousands of years later, countless Jews, far less detached from God than Terah had been, followed a similar path. They felt drawn to the same land, the same people, and the same historical destiny.
Across the centuries, Jews have found their way home through countless different journeys, shaped by different convictions, circumstances, dreams, and personal attachments. There is one home, but there are many roads which lead home.
Another road home
The roads leading to our homeland are as varied as the Jewish people themselves. Some are paved with religious conviction, others with national identity and historical consciousness.
Many Jews harbor a lifelong dream of aliyah and eventually fulfill that dream by building their lives and families in Israel. Still other roads emerge unexpectedly, shaped by circumstances, personal attachments, and the bonds of family.
My mother, of blessed memory, passed away this past Sukkot. She took a different road to our one homeland. We were raised in a Zionist home, though not an especially ideological one, and Zionism was not a central part of our upbringing.
Our family grew up in Brooklyn during the 1970s, when it was a thriving center of Modern Orthodox Jewish life, with flourishing synagogues, schools, and communities.
Moving to Israel was never part of her plan. However, her children developed a deep attachment to Israel, and all eventually moved here and built their families.
Wanting to be close to her children, grandchildren, and eventually great-grandchildren, my mother and father moved to Israel at an advanced age.
Their aliyah was not the fulfillment of a lifelong dream. It was not driven primarily by ideology or Zionist conviction. It was driven by a deep love of family.
Yet leaving behind a familiar world and beginning a new life so late in life required enormous courage and determination. I will always be grateful to my Mommy for making that sacrifice and giving us those precious years together. My mother made that journey, and now she is buried just a few minutes from our home in Gush Etzion.
There are many roads that lead home. Some are paved with ideology, conviction, and Zionist dreams. Others are paved with something simpler and more personal: the love of family.
May God bless her soul, and may her love and devotion continue to inspire our family for generations.
The writer is a rabbi and educator at Yeshivat Har Etzion (Gush). Find his latest book, Echoes of Rashi: Bereishit, at mtaraginbooks.com

====================================================================================================

Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:56:50 UTC
03:56:50 KST

Deforestation in the Brazilian Amazon has fallen to its lowest level since records began, new government data shows.
But whether this globally important success is maintained or reversed is on a knife edge ahead of a presidential election run-off on 25 October between two candidates with sharply different visions for the future of the rainforest and how that affects relations with the US under Donald Trump.
The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, fell behind in the first round of voting despite an impressive record in slowing the destruction of the Amazon while also reducing poverty and food insecurity. He is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro.
The Prodes satellite data series, which is considered the most accurate measure of deforestation, showed forest clearance in the Amazon fell by 41.8% over the past year to 3,335 square kilometres, the lowest value since the start of such measurements in 1988.
This beats the previous record low by 1,236 sq km, equivalent to an area the size of Rio de Janeiro.
Since 2022, the year before the start of the Lula administration, the deforestation rate has slowed by 71.2%, according to the data collated by Brazil’s National Institute for Space Research. This was largely as a result of stronger enforcement measures and state investments in environmental agencies.
The Brazilian states with the worst records in 2026 were Pará, which registered 33.9% of all Amazon deforestation in the year, Mato Grosso (25.5%) and Amazonas (15.7%).
However, even in those places the figures were down by more than 45% on the previous year. The state where the problem grew worse (up 0.4%) was Roraima, which is a Bolsonaro stronghold.
Outside the Amazon, the neighbouring biome of the Cerrado – an area of savannah – registered its lowest annual deforestation since 2001, at 5,516 sq km. This is significant as the Cerrado has long been treated as an area of environmental sacrifice, where soya and beef producers could clear more forest than they were allowed to do in the Amazon. Over the past four years, Cerrado deforestation has fallen by 48.4%.
These spectacular results, which brought some conservationists to tears, stand in sharp contrast to the 2019-23 term of Jair Bolsonaro, who oversaw a 59.5% increase in Amazon deforestation, roughly equivalent to destroying more than a million trees a day, through cuts to forest protection agencies, reduced implementation of penalties for environmental crimes, and verbal encouragement for illegal miners, loggers and land grabbers.
Bolsonaro was then convicted for attempting a coup but his son has vowed to release his father and let him take any position in government that he chooses.
The younger Bolsonaro has followed his father’s example in courting support from predatory landowners in the Amazon and other extractivist interests while ignoring the climate crisis in his manifesto.
The former environment minister Marina Silva, who has arguably done more than anyone to defend the rainforest, has warned that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to finish his father’s “perverse project” to destroy the Amazon.
The stark contrast between the two candidates is evident in the electoral results map in the Amazon, where Bolsonaro secured the most votes near areas of degraded forest, mines, ranches and soya monocultures, while Lula’s support was higher in big cities or areas of forest where the vegetation was relatively intact.
It is also evident in their very different relations to the US. Lula has warned that Trump is trying to colonise the country and capture its resources. He defends the Amazon as a sovereign asset for Brazil, an important home for Indigenous peoples and an essential element in global efforts to stabilise the climate.
The Bolsonaro family, by contrast, has close ties to the US. Flavio’s brother Eduardo has lived in Texas since last year and called upon the Trump administration to impose punitive tariffs on his own country.
Jair has saluted the US flag and led chants of “USA, USA”. If the family secure power, they are expected to shift Brazil’s trade priorities, particularly when it comes to critical minerals, from China and Europe to the US.
The biggest difference, however, is likely to be the far right’s willingness to exploit natural resources in the Amazon and elsewhere in Brazil and then sell them to the highest bidder, regardless of environmental and social concerns.
Conservation groups said the new deforestation data showed how much was at stake in the presidential run-off.
Marcio Astrini, the executive secretary of the Climate Observatory, said: “The figure makes it clear that putting an end to forest destruction in Brazil is entirely possible.
“However, everything depends on the election result. The country will decide whether we move toward the end of deforestation or toward the end of the forest.”
