If the economic narrative doesn’t improve, things could get ugly for Labor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
If polls are right, voters are in a mood to send Labor into the wilderness
Labor's sprawling backbench has been a sight to behold ever since the 2025 electoral bushfire that consumed the Coalition, leaving behind a lot of empty stumps and toasted tussocks.
The view from the press gallery seats drives this home. Below the viewer sprawls the government's 94-seat majority. It dominates the green benches of the lower house, spilling across the chamber's centre line deep into what is normally opposition upholstery.
It's the literal embodiment of political weight. All those bums on seats.
But for the first time in this parliament's life — and we're pretty much at the half-way mark — those rows upon rows of Labor MPs this week looked more like one of those forests where too much fuel has accumulated.
A lot of wood ready to ignite.
Anecdotes galore of rattled and angry Labor MPs
If polls are right then voters are increasingly in a mood to light the match of a political conflagration. Many of those backbenchers would become oncers.
That was the underlying vibe this week in private conversations in the corridors of parliament, where there were stories and anecdotes galore of unhappy, rattled and angry Labor MPs venting their frustrations.
Some of this might be overblown, but the fact it's out there is new.
Discipline and internal unity have been a mark of the Albanese government, now in its fifth year. Yet for the first time in years, there are plenty of rumblings.
Some backbenchers have been eager to unload their feelings on journalists and several newspapers reported growing agitation across Labor ranks.
Even ministers are at it.
The whole nervous scene was bad enough for the prime minister to resurrect his old line to colleagues — he used it in the lead-up to the 2022 and 2025 elections — that despite how tough it feels now, they'll all be "kicking with the wind in the fourth quarter" come election time.
As the grizzling and fretting continued, the prime minister jumped on ABC Afternoon Briefing on Tuesday to put on a brave face.
"We need to be focused not just on — with due respect here on ABC 24 — on the 24-hour media cycle. We need to make sure as well that we're focused on where we are a year ahead, five years ahead, 10 years ahead," he told Patricia Karvelas.
"What I'm saying is that I'm not spooked by that … we act as an orderly government."
But gnawing at the government's storyline of competence is the ongoing effort to sort out the budget, which is now five months old.
Defeat in the jaws of victory
Legislation has been brought in to address a series of unintended consequences from the introduction of a 30 per cent tax on trusts.
The government says that was always the plan to bring on these changes later this year, given they're not slated to take effect until future years. But the whole thing is another reminder of how much unfinished and unanticipated business sits in the government's in-tray.
Then, at a dinner hosted by the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry on Tuesday night, the prime minister appeared to take all the credit for pushing the Australian Tax Office to delay its ban on credit card payments, even though the treasurer had indicated he was already moving to address that issue when it blew up late last week.
Amid talk of the prime minister throwing the treasurer under the bus, Anthony Albanese told parliament that "the whole premise of it is completely wrong".
"The treasurer and I had a discussion last week," he said. "We convened the expenditure review committee, and we unanimously, right across the leadership of the government, agreed that the decision by the ATO to have a limited period of pause on the ban that had been imposed needed to be extended so that there would be proper consultation with small business."
It's a solid explanation. And it would have normally sufficed. But with the government struggling to keep command of the political narrative, the negative headlines reinforced the sense that it keeps finding defeat in the jaws of victory.
The credit card surcharge issue was supposed to be a positive thing. Instead, it turned into a headache that reinforced a notion that Labor doesn't understand business or the economy.
Then, on Wednesday, the Senate pulled the rug out from under one of the government's bigger budget savings — the plan to wind back a rebate to over-65s for health insurance, a $3 billion measure that Health Minister Mark Butler said would be redeployed for aged care services.
Crossbench, Greens and Coalition senators joined forces to scupper the measure, which the government promptly reintroduced.
Loading
The Senate's growing hostility
There are different ways to read this clash.
The government says it shows the Coalition is not serious about finding savings, despite its rhetoric on the need for budget repair.
The Coalition reckons older Australians, pensioners in particular, shouldn't be made to pay for the broken budget.
Interestingly, Barnaby Joyce told this column on Friday that "Labor has a point" on the rebate issue.
"If that's not where you want the savings, then where do you want to find savings?" he said.
"You've got to move away from just talking about being financially prudent and put meat on the bones."
Either way, the Senate's growing hostility to the government's agenda is worth watching closely.
The Greens under new leader David Shoebridge have come out swinging, eager to throw sand in the government's wheels.
And some of that new mood of disruption is because all the big players are starting to focus on the next election. While not due until May 2028, its influence on political behaviour has already begun. Not least as the prime minister can always call an election early, perhaps for a year from now.
The Greens have already shown they're starting to rethink their approach. And the Liberals will have to make a threshold decision in coming months on whether they stick with Angus Taylor to lead them to the next election.
If they think he can't deliver, they'll need to give whoever they opt for time to prepare. For now he looks as safe as you'd expect of any major party leader struggling to reach a primary north of 20 per cent to be. Which will make the lead-up to Christmas a nervous time for him.
Labor will also eventually need to make strategic decisions in coming months, particularly about when and how to renew the frontbench, many of whose members have been in their portfolios since 2019.
If the economic and budget narrative doesn't improve, things could get ugly.
"Usually they're brilliant at discipline," Joyce told this column of Labor. "But we've had different views coming forward. When you see a little bit in public you know there's a lot going on behind closed doors."
Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

Could a whale really swallow a human? A marine scientist says yes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Just when you think it's safe to go back in the water, along comes Whalefall.
Based on Daniel Kraus's 2023 novel, the thriller follows Jay Gardiner (Austin Abrams), a young scuba diver who attempts to shake off the grief of his father's recent passing with a dive.
But his swim turns dangerous when Jay's diving gear becomes tangled with a giant squid that has been marked as lunch by a hungry sperm whale, and Jay is swallowed with his mollusc companion.
Stuck in the belly of a whale, Jay must figure out a way to escape in 60 minutes before the oxygen in his scuba tank runs out.
When the trailer for Brian Duffield's Whalefall film adaptation hit the internet this year, fans were thrilled to see Kraus's story of grief and acceptance hit cinema screens.
But a question remained: Could a human actually be swallowed by a whale and survive?
Dr Vanessa Pirotta, a lecturer and whale scientist in the Marine Predator Research Group at Macquarie University, has written books on the gigantic creatures and addressed the National Press Club in 2025 on the importance of ocean research to our wider environment.
She's currently conducting Australian-led research as a part of the Sydney Offshore Megafauna Surveys to find out how many of these gentle giants we have in our waters.
We're talking about Whalefall. But before we dive into it, I must ask: what is your favourite whale fact?
Oh, God, where do I start? I think the one I love is that whales have belly buttons because they're mammals. They live birth.
Wow, how big is a whale belly button?
I've done many whale necropsies where I've measured a whale but I never thought to measure the actual width of the belly button. I would say, focusing on an adult whale, maybe it's like the size of a clenched fist.
One of my favourite things and most interesting things to do as a whale scientist is understanding, working with pathologists and vets, to understand why the animals died. It sounds completely morbid, but the only opportunity for me really to see and learn about whale anatomy is by investigating dead whales and it's really the most interesting thing in my life that I do.
I've got to ask you the question on everybody's mind. Could a human be eaten and swallowed by a whale?
This is the billion-dollar question. So, when we're talking about Whalefall, the movie, it's a sperm whale.They're a toothed whale, as opposed to the humpback whale or toothless whales. They have baleen plates, which are hair-like strands hanging from the roof of their mouth.
They're designed not to bite down on food but to engulf lots of tiny, tiny food and water and then get rid of the water out the side of their mouth.
So, what I'm trying to say is, the biology of the whale that we're dealing with in this movie, you could potentially as a human go down the throat but whether you make it alive or not, I don't think anyone knows that.
Full disclosure: I have not yet done a sperm whale necropsy, but a human could easily fit inside their mouth and potentially be sucked into their throat.
Incredible. In the movie, Austin Abram's character is accidentally swallowed while tangled up with a giant squid, which the whale is hunting. Could this situation ever happen in real life?
This is where the movie is doing my head in. That feeding behaviour would usually happen kilometres, at least a kilometre or so, underneath the ocean, so there's huge pressure. The animal is equipped for pressure. So technically, if a sperm whale was feeding at that shallow a depth, then potentially you could. The sperm whale wouldn't use its teeth to crunch you up and bite you and chew you like what we would be doing.
They would simply use the teeth to grab onto you, like it's doing with the squid. The teeth are there to be like a fork. So, I would say that that's why it's doing my head in because, A, it's not usual to see a sperm whale feeding at this depth and, B, how has it miraculously followed a giant squid all the way to the surface? The squid would have been gone by that stage.
Humans are not part of a whale's diet, I must point out. So, these animals are not targeting humans. A human would be dead and implode by the time they get down to that depth.
Abrams is also covered in the plastic and metal of his scuba gear. Would a whale not realise that was not viable sustenance?
If that did all happen at the subsurface, my assumption would be that the whale would probably bite onto the tank attached to him and instantly know that something's not right.
There have been other divers that have been kayaking or swimming next to humpback whales or other baleen whales with no teeth, and these animals have had these people at least touch their mouths but realise very soon after that something wasn't right and then they usually open their mouth and eject whatever it is.
Those whales with the kayakers, those kayakers are simply basically hanging out where their dinner plate is and then the whales don't give a hoot about them. So, by no means is the whale targeting the humans.
There's never been a swallowing of a human, to my understanding.
Whales just want to eat. They don't want to hurt humans. They're not aggressive animals, are they?
Not necessarily, but nor is a shark. This is the thing. Whales just want to eat their food. That's what sharks just want to do, too. That's why there's so much anthropomorphising in these movies. But as a scientist, I welcome these movies. They're getting a whole generation of people to think about and educate them about these whales and the environment that we know so little about.
If this is showing us a fantastical version of what a whale's stomach would look like, what does a whale's digestive system look like? Do whales have the same kind of digestive acids that we do?
I've looked in many whale digestive systems and I can tell you they're slimy and they're not pretty and they stink. I don't think there'd be much air in there, although the dude is on scuba.
Yeah, he's got 60 minutes of oxygen in his tank.
They would have acids in their stomach. Sperm whales are famous for ambergris. Yeah. Whale vomit. So there probably is a whole heap of squid beaks in that stomach that are undigested because they can't digest them.
So, if hypothetically a human does make it to the stomach but things go wrong, could a whale potentially fully digest and expel a human?
OK, I've been asked lots of questions in my lifetime. But this one …
So, given the fact that this guy is inside a whale with a scuba tank, I would say the scuba tank would probably cause this whale to die. But if this dude was sucked in the whale without a scuba tank and just as a human, then there is potential for this guy to be broken down and passed out.
So, I would say the impeding factor here is the tank. But even before a tank could even get into a stomach of a whale, a whale is not dumb and would probably be like, 'What the hell is this? I'm used to eating things that are squishy, soft'.
Whalefall isn't just the name of the movie, it's a real scientific term — can you explain it to us?
See, this is again another star, in my opinion, for this movie because now I get to tell you what it is.
A whale fall is essentially when a whale dies, it will float to the surface and for a period of time sharks or other animals will break it down. Then the animal will fall to the bottom of the ocean, moving a whole heap of nutrients and carbon with it. So, even in death, whales will transfer carbon from our atmosphere down to the deepest part of the oceans and lock it away.
We've got to thank whales for so much. Whales are environmentally and economically important alive and even more so environmentally important in death.
Is there a reason we're behind in knowing about whales or is there a reason we don't know more than we should?
Yes, because so much of the world is focused on what's above and not below, and deep-sea research and research on whales is very expensive.
So, when it comes to learning about our deep blue, we know so little. In fact, we know more about space than we do about whales in terms of their environment, rather. Someone will eat me alive for saying that. So if anything, a nice silver lining is the fact that people learn about whale falls and the role of whales and their ecosystem.
What do you think people should know about whales that is largely unknown at this moment?
They're so environmentally, economically important, and their whale poo drives the movement of iron — it's called the iron pump — around the ocean. So, we have whales to thank for the functioning, healthy ecosystems that we enjoy.
But also, we can do our role for whales, and especially humpback whales, making sure that we don't remove krill from the ocean because we need to keep their food there. If you're a little kid, I always say don't release your balloons at birthday parties. If you're an adult, don't buy krill oil tablets.
Our actions for these animals can be simple, but we need to have them front of mind, not out of sight. What is it? Out of sight, out of mind? In this case, it takes a very popular movie so that we can connect and learn so much, and that's what I absolutely love about Hollywood in this case.
This interview is lightly edited for clarity and brevity. Whalefall is in Australian cinemas now.

Trump, Netanyahu and the dangerous politics of staying in power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
Trump and Netanyahu are putting the world at risk to stay in power
More often than is healthy, international news is framed in terms of the transactions of political leaders — who has come out on top on any given day — and the impact on those leaders' political fortunes at home.
This week we have seen the US president doing something different.
Donald Trump has not just been jostling with Russian president Vladamir Putin and Ukranian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He has personally gone to war with the people of Ukraine. All, it seems, to improve the political prospects of his Republican Party in the looming US midterm elections.
Trump this week reportedly turned off intelligence to the Ukrainians and ordered the speed to be slowed of Starlink services that help warn Ukrainians of incoming missiles. That he did so is chilling.
Reuters reported on Friday that "the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine for battlefield communications and drone operations came from inside the White House, according to two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter".
"The officials said leaders at the Defence Department received a message that the SpaceX Starshield service for the Ukrainian military needed to be slowed.
"The officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not specify who in the White House made the decision or who was responsible for implementing the order."
In the past six days Trump has announced a deal to buy Russian diesel (long sanctioned by the US and, indeed, the subject of threats of sanctions on others who might buy it). He has told Ukraine and European allies that the US might suspend European purchases of US weapons on behalf of Ukraine and also pressured European countries to unfreeze Russian assets.
The Trump administration is also reported to be considering easing restrictions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela.
So shutting off US intelligence and ordering a go-slow on the Starshield service might be just two more points of pressure being applied to Kyiv. But they weren't moves to apply financial pressure or shift the oil market to get oil prices down.
They weren't even simple abuse of another country's leader. ("I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," Trump told Washington reporters last Saturday).
These were explicit decisions to leave a civilian population exposed to ballistic missile attacks and to shift the balance of the war in Russia's favour
Beyond the scores killed and injured in Russian attacks on civilians in recent days, an unanswered Russian strike on energy infrastructure left at least 600,000 people in Ukraine without power on Wednesday.
Midterm predictions mount
An increasing number of analysts in the United States believe that Trump will not just lose the US House of Representatives but also the Senate. Instead of seeing that development as a harbinger of some curbs on his erratic administration, the concern is about how Trump will respond to the news.
In the American capital, there is no great confidence that Trump will respond rationally, or will feel somehow chastened and therefore constrained, to exercise power in a way which reflects the boundaries of actual laws.
That means malevolent interventions in the Russia-Ukraine conflict could continue and only spread further shock waves into a Western Europe that is desperately trying to prop Ukraine up.
There is also the question of what Trump does, or doesn't do, on Iran and whether he does, or doesn't, do something before the midterm elections in pursuit of a similar electoral boost.
The Middle East brings more tension
The conflict with Iran continues to dominate much of the coverage out of the Middle East.
But for those in the region, a much more pressing question revolves around the Israeli election, now just 10 days away.
Regional powers observe that Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done everything he could to provoke a regional confrontation — whether that be in Syria, Lebanon, within the West Bank or even with Jordan — in the run up to the election.
Like Trump, Netanyahu has played his international politics hard for domestic consumption.
Like the US president, he has often presented a spectacular failure as a sign of his strength: in Netanyahu's case, the intelligence failures of October 7, the lack of any clear victory in Gaza, or Lebanon, or Iran.
There was one contested report this week that he even pushed Washington to restart the Iran war before the Israeli vote.
The man who has emerged as Netanyahu's major opponent in the upcoming elections, Gadi Eisenkot, and two other party leaders — the right wing's Avigdor Liberman and the centre-left's Yair Golan — all warned this week that Netanyahu may start a war before the election in an attempt to stay in power.
Golan said Netanyahu will try to disrupt the democratic process before and on election day.
Recent polls have given Eisenkot a significantly larger number of seats than Netanyahu. Yet, like Trump, there is no confidence in the Middle East that he is about to lose power.
At best, the numbers are so close — when all the permutations of possible coalitions are done — that the current PM is likely to continue in the job for some time, at least as caretaker prime minister.
The biggest concern is what he might do in Syria.
The wiring of the Middle East has been rapidly rerouting since the war in Iran began on February 28: the Gulf states, Türkiye, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Lebanon, Jordan and Iraq have all been having to find new voices for themselves and new ways of getting along.
Some in the region argue that the need to keep the only recently-stabilised Syria more or less in one piece is the one thing all the locals can agree upon.
There is also an unstable Syria representing the threat of an ISIS resurgence. Conflict between the Kurds and Türkiye with spill over into Iraq and the restoration of the land bridge that Syria once represented between Iran and Hezbollah. All of these would be bad for the border security of Lebanon, Jordan and Iraq, and for a possible renewed surge of millions of refugees.
Loading
Jordan watching on
For Jordan there are particular risks, including that 40 per cent of its water supply comes from Syria.
Yet Israel has kept up destabilising actions in Syria: pushing into southern Syria and even attacking an air base close to the border with Türkiye last month.
Jordan's King Abdullah — who was visiting Australia this week in search of closer defence and intelligence ties — told the UN General Assembly last month that the Israeli government's "expansionist appetite" is now a regional threat, citing Gaza, the West Bank and southern Syria.
His tiny kingdom — which boasts one of the world's most unfortunate set of surrounding neighbours — has repeatedly expressed its alarm about Israel's actions: from the threat to its water to what King Abdullah has called an existential threat seen in Israeli talk of forcing three million Palestinians into Jordan as Israel extends its annexation of the West Bank.
Jordan has never had many cards to play in its brief history. A presumption that the US would side with Israel in any conflict would seem to make its position even weaker.
But the fact that the US has had to withdraw many of its personnel and assets from the Gulf into Jordan changes the equation of its interest in keeping Jordan stable too.
And an irony of Netanyahu's recent actions is that it is the security deals with Jordan and Egypt, and thus relative border stability, that have allowed Israel to pursue its incursions into Gaza, into Lebanon and into Syria.
That Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu is now playing with Jordan, at least rhetorically, is just one more illustration of the mess he and Donald Trump are creating around the world in their determination to stay in power.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

Hidden from view in bushland, one rehab centre is saving lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Amid national ice crisis, Aboriginal community rehabilitation centres are fighting back
Kane Wandin's withdrawn demeanour shifts when asked if he has a favourite tattoo.
The 26-year-old pulls back the sleeve of his hoodie, straightens his posture and holds his arm stiffly in front of his chest, as if providing a shield for his own body.
Etched across his forearm, in permanent black ink, is the word Wurundjeri.
"I spent basically my whole life on drugs and on the streets," he says.
"Connecting to culture was what [gave] the most strength in helping me sort myself out and get off drugs."
Hidden from view, amid the rustling gums and gentle breeze from a distant coastline, the lives of young First Nations people like Mr Wandin are quietly being changed forever.
Set in an undisclosed nook of Victoria's Mornington Peninsula, Bunjilwarra is an Aboriginal community-controlled residential rehabilitation centre and healing site for people recovering from addiction.
It is perhaps the least clinical setting imaginable.
At the heart of the grounds, a fire crackles gently throughout the day, stoked by residents on log stools.
A nearby basketball court abuts a veggie garden. The art room windows look out to a set of footy goals.
"To feel the energy here being solely run by mob, for mob … you've got Uncle over there, you've got Auntie calling out, 'Lunch is ready, come and eat,'" says Carla Lauch, a Gunditjmara Kirrae Whurrong—Bundjalung Yaegl woman and youth mentor at Bunjilwarra.
"Honestly, it feels like home."
As Australia's drug consumption reaches record levels, experts say the culturally centred model offers valuable lessons for a broader community problem.
"This place gave me stability," Mr Wandin says.
"It saved my life."
Ice 'twice the problem' of cocaine
If there is hope to be found inside the walls of Bunjilwarra, there is ringing alarm to be heard outside of them.
For those working at the intersection of drugs, crime and homelessness, the unabated rise of methamphetamine in particular — or ice — in the broader community is of profound concern.
Australia has among the world's highest per capita use of ice (also referred to by authorities as methylamphetamine), with recent national drug detection data finding record levels turning up in our wastewater.
"The methylamphetamine market is the highest risk drug market in Australia. It poses the highest threat. It also causes the most harm of the illicit drugs," says Shane Neilsen, principal drug specialist at the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission (ACIC).
"Cocaine seems to get a lot of the coverage. The point I would make is that twice as much methamphetamine is consumed in Australia as cocaine.
"It's at least twice the problem."
Mr Wandin was just 13 and living on the streets of Frankston in Melbourne's south-east when he started using ice.
"As bad as it all sounds in the news, it's worse," he says.
"Ice is everywhere at the moment."
The ACIC estimates the street value of the drug at $11 billion over the most recent 12-month reporting period.
There are growing accounts of ice turning up in the furthest corners of the country, including remote Aboriginal communities.
"If anything, per capita it's more prevalent in regional and remote areas of Australia than it is in capital cities," Mr Neilsen says.
"Serious and organised crime groups have established networks that can supply local communities.
"There's a whole series of cases in which … crime groups are cynical enough to provide methylamphetamine to users and say that they can consume a portion themselves and sell the rest to pay for it.
"That way they're outsourcing the most risky part of the supply chain — the local level distribution — to people who are also using."
Carla Lauch says Bunjilwarra, which is run by the Victorian Aboriginal Health Service, is seeing a "huge increase" in young people who have used methamphetamine.
"Meth is very scary," she says.
"Alcohol was bad enough for our mob and then you've got something as potent as methamphetamine … to see how it changes them and the effects that it has on their lives and their family and the community is devastating."
New analysis from the Penington Institute found Indigenous Australians were more than four times more likely to die from an unintentional drug overdose, with methamphetamine a significant contributing factor.
On the Central Coast of New South Wales at the Aboriginal community-controlled rehabilitation treatment centre The Glen, demand for services far outstrips capacity.
"You literally couldn't even apply for a bed at The Glen a lot of the time. I'm not saying that with pride," The Glen's executive director, Joe Coyte, says.
"We don't shut applications because beds are full. We shut because beds are full and we've already got 100 people who've been assessed and another 60 or 70 in the system being assessed.
"So there's no point us taking more applications."
'We are keeping kids out of jail'
In his time as deputy director of the National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre, Anthony Shakeshaft investigated the benefits of Indigenous-led programs in aiding rehabilitation and combating drug harm.
He believes more centres are "absolutely" needed around the country.
"If you just think about it economically, there's no reason you wouldn't do it," says Professor Shakeshaft, now head of psychology at the University of Sunshine Coast.
"A really key feature of these programs is that they improve clients' health broadly, not just in terms of substance abuse.
"Clients that go to rehab and do a period in an Indigenous drug and alcohol service are [also] much less likely to end up back in jail."
It is an argument echoed by Mel Bedford from Bunjilwarra, where six young residents at the centre are currently on bail.
"We are keeping kids out of jail here," she says.
"It's a lot cheaper for us to have a resident staying here than what it is to keep a resident in custody, and we're definitely helping their healing journey rather than being in custody."
From little things
There are only a dozen or so residents at a time at Bunjilwarra — a mere fraction of those in the wider community grappling with addiction.
That limited intake nonetheless creates fertile ground for more meaningful connection and change to occur, particularly for those experiencing intergenerational trauma.
On some days, that may take the form of a carpentry workshop or practical support around employment and nutrition.
It could also mean a walk with an elder through nearby bushland, or a conversation about culture and identity in the yarning circle around the fire.
"Some of them are so sick culturally," Ms Lauch says.
"We talk about mental health, but if they're also culturally and spiritually disconnected, that's something that needs working on as well."
The centre only became a fully Aboriginal community-controlled service in the past year, but the site is now being visited by similar organisations looking to replicate aspects of the service interstate.
"I've seen workers in this industry who have all the qualifications in the world, but they cannot sit down and hold a conversation with a young person because they can feel the clinical energy," Ms Lauch says.
"I feel like mob just understand what mob needs, and there's that immediate trust with our young people to speak to someone who's been through it."
The words "From little things, big things grow", a reference to Kev Carmody and Paul Kelly's unofficial Australian anthem, are painted on one of the yarning circle logs.
For Ms Lauch, whose mother and grandmother were part of the Stolen Generations, change is going to come, even if it is starting small.
"These young people that we have come through Bunjilwarra are our future elders," she says.
"We want them to be empowered to share culture, to right the wrongs of what our grandparents went through."

Keeping The North Sea Safe: Exercise Strike Warrior
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
19:00:00 BST
03:00:00 KST

Maritime patrol aircraft from Germany, France and the United Kingdom have joined forces in northern Scotland as part of Exercise Strike Warrior, enhancing NATO interoperability and strengthening maritime security across the North Sea.
Operating from RAF Lossiemouth, maritime patrol aircraft (MPA) worked alongside allied naval assets in waters around the UK during the Royal Navy-led exercise. The three-week programme focused on anti-submarine warfare, surface warfare and the integration of air and maritime capabilities in increasingly complex operational scenarios.
French Navy personnel from 23rd Maritime Patrol Squadron deployed to RAF Lossiemouth with their maritime patrol aircraft for the duration of the exercise.
"The maritime environment is constantly evolving, and so are the platforms and systems we operate.
Aircraft, ships and submarines are all becoming more capable, but what really matters is our ability to work together, by sharing information and combining capabilities."
Lieutenant Maxime
The German Navy also returned to RAF Lossiemouth with its P-8A Poseidon aircraft, acquired by the Bundeswehr in 2025. The deployment marks the German Poseidon force's second participation in a major exercise from the station this year, following Exercise Dynamic Mongoose.
The UK and Germany's shared operation of the Poseidon platform strengthens the wider allied fleet. It enhances collective capabilities in maritime surveillance, anti-submarine warfare, maritime security and search-and-rescue operations worldwide.
"One of the highlights of the exercise has been the opportunity to operate alongside our UK counterparts and put our crews and aircraft through realistic and demanding scenarios.
For my detachment, it has been particularly valuable to learn from one another, share experiences and understand how another Poseidon force approaches similar operational challenges."
Commander Philipp
Detachment Commander 
The close cooperation demonstrated during Strike Warrior reflects the growing defence partnership between the United Kingdom and Germany following the signing of the Trinity House Agreement in October 2024.
The agreement strengthened defence and security ties between both nations and continues to be reinforced through regular multinational training and operational activity.
Throughout the exercise, participating aircraft conducted a series of challenging maritime scenarios, operating as both defending and opposing forces alongside fighter aircraft, surface vessels and submarines. These serials tested the ability of allied forces to detect, track and respond to threats across the maritime battlespace while integrating capabilities across multiple domains.
Typhoon fighter aircraft from IX(B) Squadron, based at RAF Lossiemouth, also took part in surface warfare training, working alongside United States Navy assets to provide additional airpower and demonstrate the importance of coordinated multinational operations.
Exercise Strike Warrior continues to provide a vital opportunity for allied nations to train together, strengthen interoperability and ensure they remain ready to respond to evolving challenges in the maritime domain.

Ukraine, Hungary Open “New Page” in Relations and Unlock Two EU Negotiating Clusters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:59:46 UTC
02:59:46 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine, Hungary Open “New Page” in Relations and Unlock Two EU Negotiating Clusters
Ukraine and Hungary have opened what Kyiv called a “new page” in bilateral relations after a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry reported on October 16.
The talks unlocked two negotiating clusters in Ukraine’s EU accession process and marked a significant step toward normalizing bilateral ties.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The ministry described the meeting as a significant step toward normalizing Ukrainian-Hungarian relations. Kyiv’s next priority is to open the remaining negotiating clusters by the end of the year.
“Today we have truly opened a new page. This is a reset across all tracks: political, economic, humanitarian, and others,” Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha stated.
According to the Foreign Ministry, the talks confirmed both countries’ readiness to expand cooperation while respecting each side’s national interests.
“This is how quiet and effective diplomacy works — for the sake of the national interest, not headlines,” Sybiha added.
The two governments plan to develop economic and trade ties, border infrastructure, business contacts, and people-to-people cooperation, the ministry reported.
“Normalizing relations benefits both countries. Ukraine’s European future will be a guarantee of security for Ukraine. And Ukraine’s accession to the EU will guarantee prosperity and development for the Hungarian national minority,” Sybiha stated.
After the leaders’ meeting in Brussels, Sybiha held talks with Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orbán. The two sides reviewed progress and coordinated further steps to implement the agreements reached by Zelenskyy and Magyar.
The Foreign Ministry also pointed to renewed parliamentary contacts. On October 15, Verkhovna Rada Speaker Ruslan Stefanchuk met Hungarian parliament speaker Ágnes Forstoffer in Rome, where the two sides agreed to restart interparliamentary cooperation, including meetings of their friendship group.
The latest dialogue comes ahead of the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Ukraine and Hungary and the 70th anniversary of the 1956 Hungarian Revolution.
Sybiha linked that history to Ukraine’s current resistance to Russia, describing both as struggles against domination from Moscow.
“By normalizing Ukrainian-Hungarian relations, we are restoring justice, normal dialogue, and cooperation for the sake of a free and peaceful Europe,” he stated.
Ukraine will continue developing relations with Hungary through what the ministry described as mutual respect, constructive dialogue, and a shared commitment to a free, secure, and peaceful Europe.
The meeting comes as the EU prepares for the next stage of Ukraine’s accession process. Earlier on October 16, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated that the bloc aims to open Ukraine’s final two negotiating clusters by the end of 2026, after Kyiv completed the screening process and began opening accession chapters earlier this year.

Macron says Russia-US diesel deal 'sends a negative message'

2026-10-16

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron said on Friday that US diesel with Russia "sends a negative message" and would have no impact on global prices. 
“The volumes of diesel coming out of Russia already exist, they are being purchased by countries and are already on the global market. So it is not true that they will solve the global market problem,” Macron said after a European Council meeting. 
“I think this will have no impact for President Trump,” he added. 
Macron warned that the decision “sends a negative message and is an element of division or doubt,” describing it as “inappropriate and ineffective.” 
He said he would continue engaging with the US in good faith to explain the figures and seek effective measures to lower energy prices. 
“We all agree on one thing: diesel, gasoline and gas prices must come down, but this is not what will effectively bring them down. It is not the right answer,” he said. 
In an effort to lower prices, Trump last week lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports and said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons (2.25 million barrels) of diesel to US and global markets. 
He also announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure between Russia and Ukraine. 
Protests in France
Macron called for calm and respect amid student protests in France, while reaffirming support for the government and security forces.
“I call for calm and respect in order to preserve this right,” he said, referring to the right to demonstrate.
“There is a constitutional right to demonstrate and express oneself. It is fully respected, but I believe the right comes with a corresponding duty of respect: respect for people, respect for property, and therefore no insulting and no vandalism,” Macron said.
EU budget and competitiveness 
Macron also called for progress on new sources of revenue for the EU budget, warning against further cuts to the proposed European Competitiveness Fund. 
“Our message was to say: stop introducing new proposals that bring cuts. We must now talk about own resources,” he said. “We need new own resources for our Europe.” 
Macron said proposals to cut the competitiveness fund would reduce the new package by €30 billion (nearly $34.8 billion). 
“We have already made many cuts. In truth, the negotiating package we are approaching today has significantly reduced the Commission’s flexibility and damaged the competitiveness fund,” he said. 
He said he believed an agreement could be reached by the end of the year. 
“It is not so much about cuts today; it is much more about making progress on own resources,” Macron said. 
Support for Spain over Ceuta 
Macron also expressed France’s solidarity with Spain over the situation in Ceuta, the exclave where thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco, describing the events as “an attack undoubtedly external and multiple.” 
He said the episode highlighted the need for European solidarity, expressing surprise that some European countries had not shown support for Spain despite having benefited from solidarity in similar situations.

Trump-Putin diesel deal fractures West on Russia – ex-Austrian FM
Washington’s diesel deal with Moscow has exposed divisions within the West over its anti-Russian stance, as the US shifts toward a more pragmatic approach, former Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl has said.
US President Donald Trump announced the agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin last week, easing sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April 2027 in an effort to bring down soaring fuel prices. The move marks a departure from the Western sanctions policy imposed on Moscow since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022.
Speaking to TASS on Friday, Kneissl described the agreement as more than a “symbolic breakthrough,” pointing to the 300,000 tons of Russian diesel expected to reach the US and global markets by November.
“The EU says that this undermines the West’s united position. However, one could also say that this marks a shift by the US toward a more pragmatic approach, while the EU continues to pursue a purely ideological line,” she stated.
The agreement has drawn criticism from European leaders attending a two-day EU summit in Brussels this week. Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis accused Trump of sidelining the bloc, telling reporters that “Trump, by doing that business with Putin, stabbed us in the back. We have to do something.”
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, however, welcomed the agreement, arguing that lower fuel prices were essential to Europe’s economic competitiveness. “Any step in reducing fuel prices and to guarantee our competitiveness, we appreciate,” he said.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas described the agreement as a “gift to Putin,” while defending Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reaffirmed on Friday that the bloc would maintain its sanctions against Moscow despite Washington’s decision to ease restrictions on Russian diesel.
Brussels’ hardline stance contrasts with that of EU member Slovakia, which remains heavily dependent on Russian energy and has sought to maintain economic ties with Moscow. Prime Minister Robert Fico has repeatedly called for diplomacy rather than continued military support for Kiev.
The dispute has also strained relations between Washington and Kiev. Trump has repeatedly urged Vladimir Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming the attacks for pushing up global fuel prices.
Zelensky criticized the diesel agreement as a “weak decision” and accused Trump of “betrayal.” Ukraine continued targeting Russian energy facilities, including a refinery in Ryazan Region on Thursday, prompting Trump to condemn the attacks as a “disgrace.” At Friday’s summit, Zelensky sought additional financial and military assistance from European leaders but left empty-handed, with only renewed promises of support.
The confrontation comes as global diesel supplies remain under pressure from the US-Israeli war on Iran, which has severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The International Energy Agency agreed on Thursday to accelerate the release of emergency oil reserves, including more than 20 million barrels of diesel, in an effort to ease shortages and bring down prices.

Donald Trump’s new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, was fired on Friday, just five days after she assumed the role, according to a White House official.

Zacharia, a little-known conservative political commentator prior to her selection as the president’s chief spokesperson, came under immediate scrutiny after a widely panned inaugural briefing on Tuesday. The 14-minute exchange was soon followed by a barrage of questions over her legal credentials after she admitted she did not pass the bar exam.
In an interview on Thursday, Zacharia detailed her whirlwind sprint to the podium to replace Karoline Leavitt as the White House press secretary, stepping into the role as the president faces multiple headwinds just weeks before the midterm elections next month.
On Friday, Trump signaled that Zacharia’s tenure would be short-lived, telling reporters that he had asked his embattled press secretary to “reconsider” the job.
“I said: ‘Is this for you, Katie? Because honestly, you don’t need it,’” Trump said, speaking outside the White House. “I said to her: ‘Honestly, if I were you, I’d reconsider. You think about it, but I would reconsider.’”
During her first – and apparently only – press briefing, Zacharia stumbled through prepared remarks highlighting Trump’s accomplishments in his presidency. She made a notable gaffe when she called her husband “the president”.
Members of the White House press corps were left puzzled when she departed the podium after only taking questions from three predominantly conservative media outlets.
She spent the next hours and days trying to clarify swirling questions about her résumé, after reports emerged revealing that Zacharia, whom Trump has referred to as an “attorney”, had never passed the bar exam. She later confirmed that she took the bar once and failed.
Zacharia graduated from Pepperdine University’s law school in California, and repeatedly called herself a lawyer.
She defended using the term to describe herself professionally, claiming there was a difference between a “lawyer” and an “attorney”, a title reserved for those licensed to practice law.
She had previously shared social media posts identifying herself as an “attorney”. And when the White House officially announced her appointment, the statement described her as an “attorney”.
Over the last few days, Zacharia has spoken with members of the media in an effort to try to move past the criticism and make the case that she was ready to take on the role as the president’s chief spokesperson.
In an unexpectedly tough interview on Thursday evening, Fox host Sean Hannity grilled Zacharia about her first press briefing, asking bluntly: “What happened?”
Zacharia sought to explain that she had had little time to prep in the days between accepting the job and holding her first press briefing and argued that the conservative Daily Mail, one of only three outlets she took questions from, was “not known to be a conservative outlet”. Hannity, a Trump ally, also pressed her on her decision to identify herself as a “lawyer”.
“Why get into this long, drawn-out definition of the difference between a lawyer and an attorney? Because I don’t think most people see much of a distinction,” he asked.
In a Friday appearance on Fox & Friends, host Lawrence Jones continued, telling Zacharia: “You know, Katie, it’s been a tough week for you. It’s not an easy job to be the press secretary, and you never want to be the story.”
Jones then asked: “Do you think you still have the confidence of the president?”
“I’m standing here,” Zacharia replied, referring to the fact that she was speaking from the White House north lawn.
She said she hoped to “build the trust and confidence of everyone around me” but could not say when her next press briefing would be.

UN Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs Rosemary DiCarlo on Friday warned that the conflict in Sudan continues to deteriorate, with no breakthrough in sight, as civilians face relentless fighting, a deepening humanitarian crisis and severe economic hardship.
Addressing a Security Council meeting on Sudan, DiCarlo said little had changed since her previous briefings this year, stressing that the Sudanese people continue to endure the devastating consequences of the war, including the collapse of basic services.

Rather than moving toward dialogue, the parties appear to believe they can achieve further gains on the battlefield, she said, adding that continued external support could be encouraging them to pursue their objectives through force.
DiCarlo highlighted the diplomatic efforts of UN Secretary-General’s Personal Envoy for Sudan Pekka Haavisto, who remains in regular contact with the parties to advance confidence-building measures.
According to DiCarlo, these efforts aim to rebuild trust, encourage more constructive engagement between the sides and deliver tangible benefits to the Sudanese people.
DiCarlo called on the Security Council to make full use of the tools at its disposal to help end the conflict, stressing that Sudan’s population deserves peace and a credible path toward a better future.
“The Sudanese people have endured unimaginable suffering. They deserve peace and a credible path toward a better future.

Sudan has been engulfed in civil war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces since April 2023, leaving tens of thousands dead and displacing millions of others.

====================================================================================================

Budget, Ukraine, migration: Five takeaways from the EU leaders’ summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:38:35 UTC
02:38:35 KST

EU leaders ended their Brussels summit with no deal on the budget, a new €70bn Ukraine funding gap, open clashes over energy and migration, but fresh resolve to create new trade defence tools to battle China.
EU leaders gathered in Brussels on Thursday and Friday with a packed agenda, from the long-term budget and financial support for Ukraine to migration, energy and China.
The summit alternated between entrenched positions on the bloc’s budget, a warm welcome for Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and clashes over energy and migration policies.
Here are the five highlights.
Rallying behind Ukraine
The bitter row between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump dominated the second day of the summit.
Leaders closed ranks behind Zelenskyy and promised to keep sanctions in place for as long as Russia pursues its full-scale invasion. They also condemned the diesel deal struck by Trump with Russian President Vladimir Putin, although the Bulgarian prime minister broke ranks to support it.
The reception gave Zelenskyy a moment of diplomatic relief as Trump doubled down, claiming Zelenskyy was “more difficult” to deal with than Putin and demanding new elections in Ukraine. Trump also called Kyiv’s strikes on Russian oil refineries, its main leverage, a “disgrace”.
“I defend the interests of Ukraine and the Ukrainian people exclusively,” Zelenskyy said in a defiant tone. “We were attacked, occupied, and our people were killed. It is only logical that we have the right to defend ourselves.”
“We will keep living, fighting, and most importantly, living with dignity,” he added.
In his address, Zelenskyy asked leaders for an additional €70bn in financial and military support next year to counter Russia’s escalation.
The request upends the bloc’s plans, which assumed last year's €90bn loan would cover both 2026 and 2027. EU leaders tasked the Commission to come up with a proposal on how to address Kyiv's financial needs.
Filling the gap will be anything but easy. Soaring borrowing costs make joint debt unpalatable. The immobilised Russian assets, which Zelenskyy raised again, remain politically divisive. And bilateral contributions risk leaving the burden on a handful of wealthy countries.
EU budget
On Thursday, leaders debated the next Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) at length but, as expected, made little headway, as the “frugal” net contributors and the southern and eastern “Friends of Cohesion” dug in.
One thing is clear: the negotiating box tabled by the Irish presidency just days ago, which proposed slashing €141bn from the overall budget to appease the frugal, is now officially dead.
European Council President António Costa will take over the talks. He is due to present a new compromise in the coming weeks, which many expect to come before the special summit he has called for 26 November, just days before the Spanish elections.
Costa is expected to pursue three main lines: keep national contributions as low as possible, rework the package of EU-wide taxes, including by drawing on European Parliament proposals, and restore the flexibility instruments the Irish presidency ruthlessly cut.
That Costa would sooner or later step in was always on the cards. More worrying is that leaders on both sides now openly say they feel no pressure to close the deal by the end of the year.
Seasoned negotiators know that deadlines force concessions. Member states may be playing with fire: a no-deal in December would raise the prospect of talks slipping until after an electoral season that could reshape Europe’s political landscape.
Migration
Migration proved once again among the most contentious issues, after the last discussion, in June, descended into a shouting match between Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on one side and Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen on the other.
This time, Rome unexpectedly extended a hand to Madrid just before the dossier reached the table on Friday. Italy and Spain reached what appears to be a first step towards ending their border dispute, after a string of tit-for-tat checks introduced in the wake of the Ceuta crisis.
Italy’s temporary border controls were due to expire on Thursday evening. They were extended by a week to align with Spain’s, which expire on 22 October. The two interior ministers are due to agree on replacement measures by then.
But while Meloni opened the summit in a conciliatory tone, Sánchez’s other main European nemesis, Frederiksen, did not spare her fellow social democrat over his plan to regularise the status of 600,000 migrants.
“I have asked the European Commission to examine what happens when a country does almost the exact opposite of what the rest of us are doing,” Frederiksen said, referring to Spain in all but name.
Meloni, Frederiksen and Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten hosted an informal breakfast before the discussion with 17 other EU leaders to explore “innovative solutions” on migration. Support is growing for emergency measures allowing asylum applications to be suspended during crises.
Tensions between the migration hard-liners and Spain and France came to the fore as the Italian, Danish and Polish governments pushed to rewrite the conclusions to call for avoiding “measures that could create incentives for illegal migration.”
By contrast, the final text merely urges the Commission to coordinate with the member states "on all types of instrumentalisation."
China
On “macroeconomic imbalances”, EU jargon for avoiding naming China, leaders held their course despite the deal between the European Commission and Beijing to curb hybrid car imports.
Over lunch on Thursday, they pressed the Commission to prepare a toolbox of new trade defence instruments, including safeguards with quotas and tariffs, to shield the chemicals and machinery industries from Chinese competition.
China loomed large as the bloc faces a trade deficit of about €360bn with Beijing. Chemicals and machinery, among the sectors hardest hit by cheap Chinese imports, were singled out as the next industries needing urgent protection after the hybrid car quotas.
While the car quotas were negotiated with Beijing, leaders called on Thursday for unilateral safeguards to be introduced “without delay”, according to officials.
The Commission presented last week’s deal as the first phase of negotiations launched in June. But time is running out: the EU’s trade deficit with China keeps widening month after month, and Chinese customs data show Chinese exports to the EU up 25% over the past year.
The EU’s strategy is to keep talking as long as dialogue delivers concrete results, while strengthening its trade defences. France and Germany last week urged the Commission to develop a new instrument to respond swiftly to market disruptions caused by China, which has been accused of unfair trade practices.
“The competition must be fair. We will create instruments against leveraging capacities, against high subsidies, against undervalued currencies. And there will be a toolbox for that. The toolbox will be bigger. It will also be applied as necessary,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.
Commission President Ursula von der Leyen told leaders her institution would begin work on such a tool, though it remains unclear whether it will be ready before the end of the year.
Other instruments are in the pipeline, including a diversification tool to encourage EU companies to diversify their suppliers of strategic products such as critical raw materials, and a solidarity mechanism to help member states hit by possible Chinese countermeasures.
Energy
On Thursday, leaders were dragged into an interminable discussion on energy. The Visegrád Group (V4) and Italy asked to amend the summit conclusions to call on the Commission to propose new measures to curb short-term swings in electricity prices and to reassess the proposed Emissions Trading System (ETS).
The V4, Italy and, to a lesser extent, Greece led the push because they face some of Europe’s highest energy costs, a concern largely shared by other member states, which ultimately called for a coordinated European response to the ongoing energy crisis.
The attempt to reopen the ETS, however, triggered an ideological backlash from Finland, Denmark and Sweden. The system makes companies pay for their emissions and encourages investment in sustainability.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš, by contrast, lashed out at the carbon tax, accusing it of wrecking Europe’s competitiveness by fuelling soaring energy costs for the benefit of market speculators.
“We’ve been engaged in a drafting exercise all day at the leaders’ level about something technical,” an EU official vented at the margins of the summit. “It’s not resulting in any new measures or new policies that actually help EU member states in their problems.”
Rome and the V4 know they lack the qualified majority to reopen the EU’s carbon market rules. The aim was rather to signal to domestic audiences that they are doing what they can to contain the surge in energy prices.

Putin tightens rules for strategic Russian companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:36:22 UTC
02:36:22 KST

Putin tightens rules for strategic Russian companies
Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree tightening restrictions on the country’s strategic enterprises, requiring them to obtain government approval before taking certain actions mandated by foreign law.
Moscow established a register of strategically important companies in the early 2000s and has since gradually expanded regulations governing their activities abroad. Russian law imposes strict limits on foreign investment, takeovers, and control of such enterprises, as well as their operations overseas.
The register covers a wide range of businesses across key sectors of the Russian economy, including state-owned giants such as energy corporation Gazprom and Russian Railways (RZhD), defense manufacturers, major state-backed banks, and high-tech firms.
The latest presidential decree further restricts the freedom of such companies to operate abroad without approval from the government. The restrictions are applied “if those actions are subject to requirements imposed by foreign government authorities, international organizations, alliances of foreign states, or the bodies or institutions of such organizations and alliances, including regulatory and supervisory authorities, or by foreign legislation,” according to the Kremlin press service.
From now on, strategic enterprises, as well as their subsidiaries, will only be allowed to disclose information to foreign authorities that is disclosable under Russian laws, as well as information related to issuing and circulating securities.
Furthermore, strategic joint-stock companies will be prohibited from amending contracts with foreign counterparts on their own, as well as from disposing of equity stakes in foreign entities through sale or otherwise, getting rid of properties abroad, and ditching rights to conduct business in foreign countries.

From twenty‑five to life.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16

02:34:21 KST

Photo: Mediazona
The Southern District Military Court in Rostov-on-Don has handed down sentences to four defendants in a case involving a series of explosions in occupied Melitopol, according to a Mediazona correspondent reporting from the courtroom. The prosecutor had sought life sentences for the men and a 28-year sentence for the woman. Ihor Haranin, 38, has been sentenced to life imprisonment. Serhiy Harkusha, 54, Serhiy Yevtushenko, 58, and Olena Roi, 46, were each sentenced to 25 years in prison.
In his final statement, Ihor Haranin described himself as a Ukrainian serviceman who “was sent to Melitopol on the orders of his command to carry out reconnaissance operations” and received “lawful orders to eliminate legitimate military targets.”
Olena Roi reminded the court that her husband was an officer “who gave his life for the territorial integrity of Ukraine”, and added that she does not hold “nationalist views”, harbours no animosity towards Russian citizens and “regrets what she has done.”
Serhiy Harkusha asked to be included on the prisoner-exchange lists, while Serhiy Yevtushenko admitted that he felt betrayed. According to him, after the war began he continued to “work as usual” at a private security firm, and then found himself “drawn into” the activities of underground activists: he was asked to deliver a parcel, with the promise that “once Ukraine arrives, this will count in your favour.” “I was betrayed,” Yevtushenko said in the conclusion of his closing statement.
According to the prosecution, in 2022–2023, the four defendants, acting on instructions from the Ukrainian security services, organised several assassination attempts on collaborationist officials in occupied Melitopol. Depending on the role assigned to each of the defendants by the FSB, they were charged with membership of a terrorist organisation, the illegal trafficking of explosives, the manufacture of improvised explosive devices, a terrorist attack resulting in the death of a person, and preparation for a terrorist attack.
The first explosion, for which the Melitopol residents were charged, took place on 15 November 2022. Dmitry Trukhin, head of the department for municipal property, urban planning, property and land relations within the city’s occupying military-civilian administration, was injured on that occasion.
The second incident took place on 27 April 2023. This time, the targets were two police officers: Alexander Mishchenko, deputy head of the Melitopol District Department of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, and his colleague Yuri Akimov. Mishchenko died from his injuries.
Furthermore, according to the FSB, between February and May 2023, the group was planning an assassination attempt on Roman Pshenichny, Deputy Head for Operational Work at the Main Directorate of the Ministry of Internal Affairs for the Zaporizhzhia Region. Pshenichny declined to be registered as an injured party in the case or to participate in the proceedings.
All four defendants claimed that they had signed confessions under torture. Haranin, Harkusha and Roi deny any involvement in the plot against Pshenichny, whilst Harkusha also denies any involvement in the plot against Trukhin. All three insist that they did not know Yevtushenko prior to their arrest.
During the closing arguments, the defence insisted that the existence of a “terrorist group” in Melitopol had not been proven, and requested that the defendants be acquitted on this charge.

Promoting Italian expertise in the cybersecurity sector and deepening the dialogue on emerging challenges in cyber diplomacy were the objectives of the visit to Singapore, from October 14 to 16, by Minister Plenipotentiary Alessandro De Pedys, Director General for Cyber Affairs, Information Technology, and Technological Innovation at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, on the occasion of the Singapore International Cyber Week (SICW) 2026. The Italian pavilion at SICW—one of the leading international events dedicated to cybersecurity, promoted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Farnesina) in collaboration with the Italian Trade Agency (ICE) and the National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN)—brought together eight Italian companies interested in developing new business opportunities and partnerships in Singapore and Southeast Asia. As part of the event, De Pedys participated in the panel discussion “Italy’s Experience in Strengthening the National Cybersecurity Ecosystem,” alongside Luca Nicoletti of the ACN and Sergio Strozzi of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, which focused on Italy’s experience in strengthening the national cybersecurity ecosystem. Italy’s contribution to the international debate continued during the fair’s high-level sessions on diplomacy, with De Pedys participating in the panel “Algorithms and Alliances: Will AI Take Over Cyber Diplomacy?”, which focused on the impact of artificial intelligence on cyber diplomacy and the new challenges for international relations.
                                    
The mission included meetings with representatives of Singaporean institutions and participation in the sixth edition of the Counter Ransomware Initiative, aimed at strengthening international coordination against ransomware attacks and addressing new threats linked to technological advancements.
                                    
Rounding out the program was De Pedys’ participation in a roundtable discussion on strategic communication and combating disinformation, hosted by Italian Ambassador Dante Brandi at the embassy, as well as a visit to the “Abito” exhibition, held at the National Gallery Singapore and presented abroad for the first time, which explores the dialogue between fashion, architecture, and interior design as an expression of Italian creativity.

From Russian oil to Starlink: How the US is redrawing its Ukraine playbook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:32:49 UTC
02:32:49 KST

From Russian oil to Starlink: How the US is redrawing its Ukraine playbook
The administration of US President Donald Trump has ramped up pressure on Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries while pursuing landmark diplomacy with Moscow in a bid to bring down soaring fuel prices at home and revive stalled peace negotiations.
The overtures have left Vladimir Zelensky fuming, reigniting the bitterest public confrontation between the two since their explosive Oval Office showdown in 2025. Zelensky has fiercely criticized Trump’s Russian diesel deal and defied his demands to stop attacking Russian refineries, saying he feels “betrayed” by Washington.
In response, the US president branded the Ukrainian leader “not a good guy for us to deal with,” while suggesting that Ukraine needs a “new president,” referring to Zelensky’s long-expired presidential term.
As the dispute escalated, American officials reportedly threatened to restrict intelligence sharing and weapons supplies to Kiev, while Ukrainian commanders sounded the alarm about serious disruptions to the Starlink network, which the military heavily relies on for logistics, reconnaissance, and drone control.
Trump’s peace push has also put him on a collision course with Zelensky’s EU backers. US negotiators reportedly proposed unfreezing some Russian sovereign assets – an idea categorically rebuffed in Brussels. Zelensky then attempted to drum up support at a slightly farcical summit in Brussels where he demanded EU and NATO membership; both of which have been rejected outright in Brussels.
Moscow has welcomed Trump’s diplomatic offensive while opposing any temporary truce with Kiev, arguing that the pause will only allow Ukraine to recuperate its battered forces.
Here is how Washington is using its pressure tools and economic incentives to mediate the Ukraine conflict and meet domestic interests.
Russian diesel to the rescue
The state of US-Russia relations took a sharp turn on October 9, when Trump struck a surprise diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow additional Russian supplies onto American and global markets. The arrangement – announced just weeks before the US midterm elections – envisaged the release of more than 300,000 tons of Russian diesel, followed by larger shipments in the coming months. Trump pitched the deal as a way to rein in soaring fuel costs for American consumers, truckers and farmers.
According to a Reuters report, Trump’s envoys also told their Ukrainian counterparts that the US hoped that the deal could help soften Russia’s position on the peace talks.
How did Kiev react to the US-Russia diesel deal?
Zelensky erupted, accusing Washington of making a “weak decision” and using Kiev’s delegation as “a front” for the agreement. Trump brushed aside the criticism, telling Zelensky to “focus on making a deal, not talking about that.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described the arrangement as “mutually beneficial” and serving the interests of the global market while denouncing “the destructive position” of European countries on the matter.
Zelensky tramples over Trump’s red lines
The diesel deal came after weeks of increasingly forceful demands from Trump that Kiev halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Since September, Trump has publicly – and in an increasingly sharp tone – urged Zelensky to stop his attacks, saying on Thursday that “all he’s doing is making the world oil price higher” while denouncing the Ukrainian leader’s approach as “a disgrace.”
According to Axios, Zelensky ignored at least half a dozen American requests to stop attacking Russian refineries before Washington did the deal with Moscow, and Zelensky threw his toys out of the pram.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak confirmed on Wednesday that Ukrainian drones had targeted two Russian oil refineries: in Ryazan and Saratov Regions.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov described Zelensky’s behavior as “a direct and blatant challenge to President Trump.”
The Russian Defense Ministry issued its own warning, vowing to step up strikes on Ukraine’s military-related targets in response to Zelensky’s threats to attack oil facilities.
Starlink: Who controls the switch?
The Trump-Zelensky clash went beyond angry exchanges, with the apparent fracture having dire implications for Ukrainian troops on the ground, according to multiple media reports. The Financial Times reported that US officials had warned Ukrainian and European counterparts that continued refinery strikes could result in the suspension of intelligence sharing and the NATO-managed PURL mechanism, through which European countries purchase American weapons for Ukraine.
Zelensky subsequently confirmed that Ukrainian commanders had received warnings about a possible intelligence cutoff, although he acknowledged that cooperation had not stopped. Trump also denied suspending intelligence sharing, insisting that “we are helping them, and we are sharing intel.”
Yet on Tuesday, Zelensky complained that Kiev had received no advance warning from its partners about a Russian ballistic missile attack. He did not identify which countries had failed to provide the alerts.
At the same time, Ukrainian commanders reported serious disruptions to Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service. As a result, Ukrainian drones could not operate at speeds exceeding 160 km/h in many cases, making them more vulnerable to Russian air defenses and derailing some missions altogether.
While some Ukrainian officials already suspected that the disruptions were linked to the Trump-Zelensky feud, Reuters reported on Thursday, citing sources, that the order to restrict Starshield had originated inside the White House. A senior US official, however, denied that Trump personally ordered the restrictions. Later, Ukrainian officials reported that some Starshield connections had been restored.
Elon Musk – who has also been critical of Zelensky – confirmed that major decisions on Starshield rest with the American military or the president.
“Time for Ukraine to get a new president”
As the feud escalated, Trump turned his ire on Zelensky’s leadership, accusing him of squandering repeated opportunities to end the conflict. “I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal,” Trump told reporters on Saturday, adding that “it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
Trump’s jabs at Zelensky’s dubious legal status hark back to February 2025 when the US president branded the Ukrainian leader “a dictator without elections.”
Zelensky’s presidential term expired in May 2024, and he has refused to hold new elections, citing martial law. Russia has since declared him “illegitimate,” saying that his status is a major obstacle to signing a binding agreement.
In response to Trump’s criticism, Zelensky said that Kiev was ready to hold elections if Moscow agreed to a comprehensive 60-day ceasefire. Russia, however, offered a truce only on the day of any vote, arguing that Kiev would use a longer pause to recuperate its battered forces and receive more weapons from the West.
A thaw for Russia’s frozen billions?
Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner proposed unfreezing some of the €300 billion in sovereign Russian funds held in Euroclear in Belgium, and transferring them to a financial vehicle overseen by Washington, according to the Financial Times.
The EU has sought to seize the funds outright, but has faced strong resistance, particularly from Belgium, over fears of costly litigation, Russian retaliation, and damage to Europe’s financial reputation.
While US officials reportedly see the issue of Russian sovereign assets as part of a comprehensive peace agreement, the proposal “startled” Kiev’s intransigent European backers, who flatly rejected the initiative, and refused to relinquish control over the assets.
In addition, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing a US official, that the Trump administration was weighing sanctions relief for vessels belonging to the so-called “shadow fleet” used to transport oil from Russia, which would allow it to bring down fuel prices.
Begging in Brussels: the €27 billion hole
With his relations with Trump in tatters, Zelensky traveled to Brussels on Friday to seek financial and military backing from the EU. In a not-so-veiled swipe at the US president, he thanked unelected EU officials as “real leaders” upon his arrival.
However, Kiev’s demands for more money have already met resistance from the EU. After announcing an unexpected $27 billion defense budget hole in August, Zelensky requested the EU front load part of the €90 billion loan meant for 2027 already this year.
Brussels declined to endorse Kiev’s deficit figures while pressing it to hurry up with stalled reforms – including those tackling rampant corruption – to unlock the funds already available.
Zelensky’s bickering with Trump is forcing the EU to take an increasingly adversarial stance towards the US. According to the Financial Times, EU officials planned to urge the Ukrainian leader behind the summit scenes to tone down his public criticism of Washington.
“It might be true, but it doesn’t always need to be said out loud,” one person familiar with the discussions told the newspaper.
Bottom Line
Barely recovering from his Oval Office clash with Trump last year, Zelensky has once again gone against Ukraine’s most important backer by repeatedly ignoring American warnings over refinery strikes and challenging Washington’s diesel deal with Moscow.
As Ukraine struggles to contain Russia’s advances on the battlefield and prop up a collapsing economy while turning to the reluctant EU for help, Trump refused to cut Zelensky any slack and step back from his demands when America’s interests are at stake – and now Ukraine is facing the threat of a complete Starlink cut-off and a halt to crucial intelligence sharing.
