Production of Leopard 2A8 Tanks Begun in Norway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:32:44 UTC
02:32:44 KST

Production of Leopard 2A8 tanks for the Norwegian Army has officially begun in Levanger, Norway.
This was reported by KNDS Deutschland.
Production was launched by the German company KNDS Deutschland and the Norwegian company RITEK, which specializes in equipment maintenance and repair. The facility in Levanger plans to manufacture 37 of the 54 Leopard 2A8 tanks ordered for the Norwegian Army.
The production and testing infrastructure was established in 18 months. The facility has the capacity to produce up to 36 tanks per year.
“Today we are celebrating much more than just the start of production. We are celebrating the establishment of industrial capabilities, a long-term partnership between Germany and Norway, and an important contribution to the defense readiness of Norway and NATO,” said Markus Helm, CFO of KNDS Deutschland.
In addition to production facilities, a specialized infrastructure for testing finished armored vehicles has been established in Levanger. It includes a laser range, sections with steep slopes, and a pool for testing vehicles as they cross water obstacles.
The facility’s power supply is provided by geothermal energy.
The launch of production will allow the majority of Norway’s Leopard 2A8 order to be manufactured domestically and will establish the country’s own industrial capabilities for working with these tanks.
Previously, Militarnyi reported that in May 2026, KNDS and RITEK opened a production site in Levanger and delivered the first two Leopard 2A8NO tanks to the Norwegian Army. At that time, the launch of serial production directly in Norway was scheduled for the fall of 2026.
Now, following the completion of the production and testing infrastructure, tank assembly in Levanger has officially begun.
The launch of production in Norway comes amid the expansion of the Leopard 2A8 program, which, based on the number of customers, could become one of the most widely adopted versions of the Leopard 2.
About a dozen countries have already ordered a total of approximately 500 tanks of this variant. Due to the sharp increase in demand, KNDS is expanding its production chain and involving companies from other European countries in the manufacture of components, assembly, and maintenance of the tanks.
In addition to Norway, companies from Lithuania, the Czech Republic, Spain, and other European countries are joining the production and service partnership for the Leopard 2A8.
One of the main differences between the Leopard 2A8 and previous variants is the installation of the Israeli Trophy active protection system. Using radars, it detects anti-tank missiles and rocket-propelled grenades, after which it automatically deploys countermeasures to intercept them.
The tank also features reinforced modular armor on the hull and turret, including additional protection for the sides and upper hemisphere.
The primary armament remains the 120-mm Rh-120 L55A1 smoothbore gun, designed for use with modern armor-piercing and programmable ammunition.
The Leopard 2A8 also features an updated digital architecture, modern thermal imaging sights for the commander and gunner, and new communications and data transmission systems.

Europe may have to secure Ukraine’s victory without U.S. support, German political scientist says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Europe may have to secure Ukraine’s victory without U.S. support, German political scientist says
This was stated in an interview with Ukrinform by Stefan Meister, Head of the Center for Order and Governance in Eastern Europe, Russia and Central Asia at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP).
“We finally need a strategy for Ukraine’s victory, not merely a strategy in which it does not lose,” the expert stressed.
According to him, against the backdrop of recent decisions and statements by U.S. President Donald Trump, Europe’s role in ensuring Ukraine’s defense capabilities has become even more important. Meister did not rule out that European countries may have to pursue the strategic goal of Ukraine’s victory together with Kyiv, but without Washington’s involvement.
The political scientist believes that Ukraine should prepare for the possibility of further reductions in U.S. support, although the United States remains particularly important because of its intelligence capabilities, the Starlink system and certain types of weapons.
Meister did not rule out the possibility that Washington could restrict the provision of intelligence and targeting data to Ukraine or even completely end such cooperation.
In his view, Ukraine should maintain close contact with Washington and carefully assess the possible consequences of its actions, as the loss of U.S. intelligence support could have extremely serious consequences.
At the same time, according to the expert, France and the United Kingdom are already providing Ukraine with intelligence, including information on specific targets, but their capabilities are significantly inferior to those of the United States in terms of both scale and quality.
“We will probably have to prepare for the possibility that at some point we will be able to rely only on European and Ukrainian intelligence. However, Europe would not be able to compensate for the end of U.S. assistance 100 percent,” Meister said.
In his view, under these circumstances, Ukraine needs to develop its own weapons and defense systems more actively, while European partners need to accelerate the provision of financial and technological assistance.
“For this, it needs money and technological expertise. Europe could and should help with this much faster,” he stressed.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 14, Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, technology adviser to the Ukrainian President, said that SpaceX had introduced speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion, and that Ukraine’s Defense Forces had not been notified in advance.

Met police investigating row over founding of Your Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:29:54 UTC
02:29:54 KST

Police are carrying out a criminal investigation into a row over the founding of Your Party, which split the leftwing party as it was established last year.
A spokesperson for London’s Metropolitan police said they had launched an investigation after they received a report in September 2025 “relating to the alleged unauthorised access of a political party’s database”, the Politico website reported.
Your Party was founded in summer 2025 by the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and the former Labour MP Zarah Sultana, both of whom now sit as Your Party MPs in the House of Commons.
But relations between the different factions in the party have been strained since its creation in July last year. That September Sultana revealed a new membership portal on X, and encouraged members to become paying members for £55.
Corbyn described the site as a “false membership system” and told supporters to ignore an email requesting funds. Sultana said her only aim had been to “safeguard the grassroots involvement that is essential to building this party”, and later accused the party of being run by a “sexist boys’ club”.
Officers had now arrested a man on suspicion of an offence under the 1990 Computer Misuse Act, a police spokesperson told Politico. The man was released pending further inquiries and has not been charged.
Officers also previously interviewed a woman in her 30s under caution in connection with the same investigation. The spokesperson added: “The investigation continues.” The police spokesperson did not name any political party in their statement, and the spokesperson did not confirm which political party their investigation was related to.
Sources told the Guardian that the investigation was linked to the long-running dispute connected to the establishment of Your Party. Neither the man arrested nor the woman interviewed by police are MPs and neither have been charged with an offence. Neither Corbyn nor Sultana were accused of wrongdoing, Politico reported.
In January, it emerged that the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) advised the party that while it was taking no further action over the Your Party membership portal launch, it may have involved “serious criminal activity” and should be referred to the police.
A Your Party spokesperson said: “It would not be appropriate to comment any further about ongoing police investigations.”
They also said: “We can reassure our members and supporters that our systems are secure and that this was an isolated incident.”
Your Party has struggled to make a widespread national impact since it was founded, while the Green party of England and Wales, rebranded as an eco-socialist party, has seen its membership quadruple.
In February, Corbyn won a comprehensive victory to become the de facto leader of the leftwing startup party. He said Your Party would work with the Green party and others to push for a “coordinated left-flank offensive” against Reform and Labour. Sultana was also voted on to the party’s leadership committee under its collective leadership model.
Corbyn-backed candidates took 14 of the 24 available places on the party’s central executive committee (CEC). Sultana-backed candidates took seven of the seats and three went to independents.

Ukraine repels Russian forces as US support wavers, energy strikes escalate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:28:41 UTC
02:28:41 KST

Ukraine advances in occupied Donetsk as Trump hands Putin diesel deal
Ukraine’s ‘Operation Vivaldi’ reclaimed more occupied territory in Donetsk during a week when Trump sided with Russia.
The United States’s relationship with Ukraine came under extraordinary strain during the past week, as US President Donald Trump lifted some oil sanctions against Russia and was feared to have restricted Ukraine’s access to US intelligence and satellite services, hobbling its defences.
“It is a pity we are losing … a strong partner,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalist Piers Morgan, speaking of the US.
“It’s painful when President Trump chooses one side, not our side,” he said. “This is not [the] right side of history.”
Trump on October 9 invited Russia to sell 1.8 million tonnes of diesel to the global market by the end of the year, to help bring down transport prices.
That effectively reversed the Lindsey Graham Act, which Trump had signed into law days earlier. The law gave him the ability to punish countries buying Russian oil with secondary sanctions.
Ukraine’s partners did not share intelligence that five ballistic missiles were headed towards Kyiv on October 13, Zelenskyy said, without naming the US. Those missiles struck Kyiv’s Thermal Power Plant number 4, one of the capital’s biggest, resulting in power outages.
Russia then pounded Ukraine’s electricity infrastructure on October 14, when Ukraine reported it had restricted use of SpaceX’s satellite navigation services, which it uses to defend itself.
Over a 24-hour period, Russia launched 850 drones and 39 missiles, striking 30 energy targets across 19 regions of Ukraine, despite the fact that Trump had declared an energy ceasefire on October 11.
“This level of blatant disregard for the United States by Russia has not been seen before,” Zelenskyy said.
Starshield, the military element of the Starlink satellite network owned by SpaceX, capped Ukraine’s use of its navigation services at 160 km/h (100mph).
This meant that Ukraine lost sight of its interceptors above that speed, making it difficult or impossible to stop Russian jet-powered Geran-4 drones, which fly at speeds exceeding 500 km/h (310mph).
Six in 10 Russian drones are now jet-powered, Zelenskyy said.
“Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” wrote SpaceX owner Elon Musk.
Starshield services had begun to return to normal on October 15, sources at Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence said.
Ukraine is so heavily targeted by Russian aerial strikes that an outage in its ability to navigate interceptors for a prolonged period could be ruinous.
During September, its air force intercepted more than 4,700 drones and missiles of various kinds.
Starshield is equally important for Ukraine’s ability to hobble Russian offensive operations. Ukraine has wrought havoc with Russian supply lines for months, striking fuel trucks, bridges, ammunition warehouses and air defences.
During September alone, Ukraine’s military said it had struck 40 command posts and 50 logistics facilities.
The Unmanned Systems Forces of Ukraine’s data showed that strikes fell from a daily average of 2,300 to 1,678 on October 14 and 1,053 on October 15.
This was not the first such disruption of services under the Trump administration.
The US had also stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine in March, helping Russia reclaim its Kursk region, which Ukraine had counter-invaded.
Ukraine advances
Despite the setbacks this week, Ukraine has continued to win back territory.
Its Third Army Corps concluded a fourth phase of Operation Vivaldi in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region, reclaiming an additional 100sq km of territory (40sq miles), said Corps commander Andrii Biletskyi.
That brought the operation’s gains to 275sq km (100sq miles) and 16 settlements since August, and brought Russia’s overall gains this year close to nil.
The campaign was designed to push back against a Russian effort to seize the town of Lyman. A separate counteroffensive further south pushed back against an attempted Russian takeover of Dobropillya. Ukraine saw the two initiatives as an effort to surround the “fortress cities” of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk in a pincer movement.
Ukraine’s counteroffensives have drawn away Russian units directly facing Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, paralysing this part of the front.
“Russian forces averaged around 14 attacks per day in the Sloviansk direction in August 2026, five in September 2026, and three per day thus far in October 2026,” wrote the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank.
“Russian forces averaged around three attacks per day in the Kramatorsk direction in August 2026, one in September 2026, and only an average of 0.3 thus far in October 2026,” the ISW said.
“We are stopping all enemy attempts to advance or infiltrate,” said Zelenskyy. “Ukraine’s positions on the front remain strong, and this year they are the strongest they have been in a long time.”
Zelenskyy said Russian forces outnumber Ukraine’s by six to eight times in parts of the front, and it appeared that they have recently received reinforcements.
Robert Brovdi, the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of Ukraine, said the personnel increase “translates into a significant increase” in Russian casualties.
During the first two weeks of October, Brovdi said, Russian casualties increased by 25 percent compared with the first two weeks in September and by almost 60 percent compared with the first two weeks in August.
In Dobropyllia, the Russian casualties were higher than anywhere else on the front, he said, 43 percent above September’s rate and double the rate in August.
Ukraine’s success is due in part to its production of domestically designed drones in partnership with European allies.
Ukraine’s Defence Ministry’s orders in 2026 were higher by half than in 2025, it said, and delivery volumes were almost four times what they had been last year.
While Ukraine respected Trump’s energy ceasefire for three days, it returned to striking Russian refineries on October 15.
It also continued to strike non-energy targets throughout the week.
Ukraine struck a facility manufacturing explosives and rocket fuel in Nizhny Novgorod on October 9, and a plant making additives for missile fuels in the Tver region.
On October 15, it destroyed four Sukhoi fighters and damaged another two at the Borisoglebsk airfield in the Voronezh region.
Ukraine also targeted three data centres owned by the Russian cloud services company Yandex, destroying or crippling those in Sasovo, Kaluga and Vladimir between October 8 and 11. It also struck a data centre owned by Sberbank on October 14.
The strikes caused Russians to lose online payment and other services.

Saved from Nazi-occupied Prague, thousands of Torah scrolls find new life through a Satmar scribe

Unknown Publisher

17:26:33 UTC
02:26:33 KST

On an overcast London morning in February 1964, Satmar hassid David Eliahu Brand passed by the Westminster Reform synagogue. Looking for work as a sofer (scribe), Brand took a chance and knocked on the front door. Ruth Shaffer, a native of Warsaw, Poland, and the coordinator for the Westminster synagogue Torah restoration project, answered the door.
Speaking in his native Yiddish, Mr. Brand asked her: “Es gibt Torahs?” Do you have any Torah scrolls that have to be repaired? Ruth replied in the affirmative, but added that the synagogue possessed not just one scroll, but 1,564 Torah scrolls that had been rescued from Czechoslovakia after the war.
After that astounding revelation, Ruth introduced Brand to the synagogue’s spiritual leader, Rabbi Dr. Harold Reinhart. Thus began the most unlikely arrangement between a Satmar hassid and a Reform synagogue that would last for 27 years!
The story begins: Demise of Jewish communities of Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia: March 15, 1939
On March 15, 1939, Nazi German troops violated the Munich Agreement and marched into the capital city of Prague. This began the official annexation of Czechoslovakia. Wherever German troops entered, the Jewish communities were in danger as well.
Until 1939, the Jewish communities of Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia numbered over 120,000 Jews and boasted over 350 synagogues, including the famous Maharal synagogue in Prague.
Prague was also the home of the Old-New Synagogue, which was built in the year 1270, and the Pinkas synagogue, built in 1479.
Almost overnight, Jews were stripped of their civic rights, banned from most jobs (including the medical field), and children were expelled from all public schools.
Then, in July 1939, the Nazis established the Central Office of Jewish Emigration in Prague (directed by Adolf Eichmann), thus forcing many to abandon their communities, leaving behind their beautiful synagogues (containing hundreds of Torah scrolls) and houses of study.
The first miracle: Gathering all Torah scrolls and artifacts to the Prague Jewish Museum
The Prague Jewish Museum was built in 1906 and in 1939 was under the directorship of Dr. Karel Stein and curator Alfred Engel. Fearing that the holy and beautiful Torah scrolls in the hundreds of Czech Jewish communities would be totally lost, Stein and Engel asked permission from Nazi authorities to centralize all Jewish ritual objects in Prague in order to protect them from widespread plundering.
Over 1,800 Torah scrolls and 212,000 artifacts were transferred to the museum.
Whether the Nazi intent was merely to amass valuable silver and gold for its treasury or to build a museum to recall an extinct race (once all Jews would be murdered) is a matter of question, but nonetheless all of the Czech Torah scrolls and artifacts were brought to Prague.
There, many Jews were employed to sort, catalogue, and store all the items that arrived from over 100 synagogues in Czechoslovakia, Moravia and Bohemia. Tragically, almost all of the employees were later deported to Terezin and other death camps and perished during the Shoah.
The second miracle: Procurement of the Torah scrolls
Following the end of World War II, the Torah scrolls lay abandoned and unattended for almost 20 years in a damp, moldy warehouse in Prague.
That all changed with a tap on the shoulder in 1963. A British art dealer, Eric Estorick, was approached by a representative of the Czech State Agency to purchase some ritual objects that had been kept in storage. The Czech government, then under Communist rule, was badly in need of money and felt that this was a golden opportunity.
Estorick contacted Ralph Yablon, a British philanthropist and member of the Westminster synagogue in London. Yablon consented to provide the £30,000 necessary for the purchase and shipping of all the Torah scrolls and other religious objects that had been stored away for so long.
Yablon, aware that many of the scrolls were badly in need of repair, contacted his rabbi, Harold F. Reinhart, in order to determine which scrolls were totally unusable and which could be designated for restoration.
Finally, on February 7, 1964, two enormous trucks carrying the 1,800 stained and tightly packed scrolls arrived in London. The original idea was that these Torah scrolls would be repaired and then returned to the communities from which they came.
But soon after their arrival, it was determined that almost all of the former Czech shuls were either destroyed or the communities no longer existed.
The third miracle: Restoration of the 1,800 scrolls
By the early part of 1964, all of the Torah scrolls and hundreds of other religious objects (including 400 wimples or binders) arrived in the Westminster synagogue. That is when the divine hand of God directed David Brand to knock on the door of the synagogue.
As in the book of Shir Hashirim, which says: “the voice of my beloved knocks,” it was a most unlikely but divinely ordained moment. That is when the major work began in order to determine how many of the scrolls could actually be repaired.
Of the total of 1,800 scrolls, Brand, along with other professional scribes, slowly and meticulously determined that hundreds could simply not be repaired-the decades of storage in horrible conditions had made many unusable.
It should be noted that even if one letter of a Torah scroll is written incorrectly or if the ink dries up, the scroll cannot be used at all until repaired. Imagine what happened to the Czech scrolls when they were not used or opened for so long.
The fourth miracle: Founding of the Memorial Scrolls Trust
Of the entire collection of the 1,800 Torah scrolls, 1,564 were deemed to be usable, but then the decision had to be made as to how they would be used and to whom they would be given. In 1964, after several months of meticulous work by the scribal team, Ruth (1910-2006) took over the directorship of the Memorial Scrolls Trust (MST).
Ruth would spend almost 40 years managing, documenting, and distributing the scrolls to communities worldwide. Amazingly, the initial filing and tracking were done on index cards only, and only many years later was the entire system transferred to a digital database.
One of her early decisions was that each scroll would be given to a community or synagogue on permanent loan in order to memorialize the communities from which they came originally. In addition, since the Torah is described as a “tree of life,” the scrolls would be read and would become a living memory for all the communities that were destroyed during the Holocaust.
About six months ago, I contacted the MST to find out more information about the scrolls and where they are today. I was fortunate that Jeffrey Ohrenstein, MST trustee and chairman, wrote back, and so began a series of discussions and amazing stories.
Jeff said the oldest known scroll in the collection is one from the 13th century, and that today about 150 scrolls still remain in the museum in London. Over 1,400 Torah scrolls have been loaned out to communities around the globe, including 1,000 to the US, as well as Israel, Italy, Argentina, Chile, and the UAE (Dubai).
Over the last 62 years, these communities have become part of the ongoing memorial to the former Jewish centers, but they have also transformed the Torah scrolls into living and eternal messengers of all who perished at the hands of the Nazis.
The scrolls are not stored in the holy ark, but are read and celebrated everywhere where they have been adopted.
Like the famous and tragic death of Haninah ben Tradyon (tractate Avodah Zarah 18A), when he is asked by his students what he saw as he was being tortured by the Romans, he replied: “The parchment is burnt, but the letters are flying heavenward.” Those letters, he was saying, are eternal; they can never be destroyed by our enemies.
In the case of the Czech collection, both the scrolls and its holy letters have survived, been lovingly cared for, and preserved for eternity.

“A lad offers gold for a maiden”: a two-voice folklore gem of Bulgaria's Shopluk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:17:00 UTC
02:17:00 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
News
Highlights of Bulgarian musical culture
“A lad offers gold for a maiden”: a two-voice folklore gem of Bulgaria's Shopluk
Friday 16 October 2026 20:00
Friday, 16 October 2026, 20:00
Kremena Stancheva and Vasilka Andonova
PHOTO Archive
Font size
A young man offers gold for a maiden. He is willing to give it, but his mother refuses: “Don’t give away gold for a maiden, my son! A maiden is a great deceiver; she will lead you astray!” “She won’t deceive me, Mother,” the son replies. “She draws water from my wells, picks little posies in my gardens; her bracelet is in my pockets, and my ring adorns her little hand.”
Recorded in the small village of Vasilovtsi, in Sofia Province, this witty text brilliantly captures one of the most intricate dilemmas of traditional Bulgarian family life: the relationship between mothers-in-law and daughters-in-law.
Originating in the Shopluk, the region of west-central Bulgaria, the song is a particularly characteristic expression of the people who created it. The Shopi are known for their fiery temperament, tenacity and stubbornness, as well as their proverbial thrift, envy and pronounced conservatism. The latter trait has had a positive side, helping preserve their traditional culture in remarkable condition. The Shopi are also renowned for their keen sense of humour and self-irony. One of the most frequently lampooned figures, not only in their own folklore but in Bulgarian folk tradition as a whole, is undoubtedly the mother-in-law: a formidable lady who remains true to type in the popular song “A Young Man Offers Gold for a Maiden”.
The song exemplifies the unique, archaic tradition of two-part folk singing ("dvuglas") from Bulgaria’s Shoppe folklore region (Shopluk), distinguished by its raw, piercing and penetrating vocal sonorities.
PHOTO YouTube
Among the most remarkable exponents of the celebrated Shopski diaphony are Kremena Stancheva and Vasilka Andonova, soloists with the Bulgarian National Radio Folk Song Ensemble. Born in the same year, 1941, the two women performed as a duo for more than three decades. Their singing is distinguished by an extraordinary fusion of voices and consummate artistry.
Charismatic, radiant and captivating, with beautifully resonant voices, Kremena and Vasilka remain an undisputed benchmark for the performance of Shoppe two-voice singing. Their interpretations carry the spirit of the past while sounding vibrant and entirely contemporary. Their duets, including Veter vee, Pushka pukna, Ergen deda, and Momche dava zlato za devoyka (A Young Lad Offers Gold for a Maiden), have been cherished by generations of Bulgarians.
In an interview with the Bulgarian National Radio, renowned folk singer, researcher, producer and journalist Daniel Spasov, a former student of Kremena Stancheva and a close friend of hers, recalls the duo’s live performances:
“The whole space would fill with sound, with trills… They really were like bells, like two bells ringing out together. I don’t know how they achieved such perfection!”
Known as the “nightingales of the Shoppe song”, Kremena Stancheva and Vasilka Andonova perform this gem of Bulgarian folk music, “A Young Lad Offers Gold for a Maiden”, accompanied by the BNR Folk Music Orchestra in a masterful arrangement by the eminent folklorist, composer and conductor Anastas Naumov. A musician of exceptional distinction, Naumov made an outstanding contribution to enriching the Bulgarian National Radio’s sound archives with a vast collection of folk music recordings.
You can find more installments in Radio Bulgaria's running series "Highlights of Bulgarian Musical Culture" HERE.
English version: R. Petkova

How Ukraine’s military uses Starlink — and what would happen if the Trump administration cut off its satellite communications entirely
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:15:29 UTC
02:15:29 KST

How Ukraine’s military uses Starlink — and what would happen if the Trump administration cut off its satellite communications entirely
In its dispute with Volodymyr Zelensky, Donald Trump’s administration quickly used its strongest leverage. It did more than threaten to halt military aid to Kyiv — it immediately restricted the most important part of that aid: U.S. satellite communications. On the morning of October 14, Ukraine’s military command reported that drones equipped with Starlink terminals (more precisely, their military counterpart, Starshield) had begun losing their connections at speeds above 160 kilometers per hour (about 100 mph). This caused several operations to fail. The next day, the speed threshold at which connections cut out fell to 60–80 kilometers per hour (about 37–50 mph). This created even more serious problems for Ukraine’s armed forces, whose command and communications depend directly on satellite links. A day later, however, the speed limit rose again. It remains unclear exactly how the White House is making these decisions (sources cited by Western media say the Trump administration is behind the restrictions). All that is clear is that Washington is not seeking to cripple Ukraine’s military command system immediately. Even so, Ukrainian commanders should consider finding a replacement for this crucial system, which depends entirely on the United States.
What has happened to Ukraine’s military satellite communications in recent days?
The first speed limits on satellite terminals using Starlink, a service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, took effect in early 2026. At the time, the stated purpose was to help the Ukrainian military. The limits came in response to Russian drone units’ widespread use of the terminals to strike deep inside Ukraine. In particular, in late 2025, the Russian Defense Ministry’s Rubikon special unit set up a system for attacking moving targets on the Pokrovsk–Dnipro highway with drones guided by video feeds. The highway is the Ukrainian military’s main supply route in western Donbas. Ukrainian terminals continued to work because they had access to the protocols used by Starshield — SpaceX’s military division, created specifically to fulfill contracts with the U.S. Department of Defense (or, officially, the Department of War).
A separate SpaceX subsidiary established in late 2022 to take part in military programs. The U.S. government helps oversee the company, which has received Pentagon contracts. Musk hopes Starshield will become the main contractor for Golden Dome, the megalomaniacal missile defense system Trump is promoting.
About 180 dedicated satellites have also been launched for military use. Unlike Starlink satellites, they use cameras operating in different spectral bands to monitor Earth’s surface. In particular, the new satellites are believed to have already become part of the early-warning system for ballistic missile launches, though there is no precise information on this.
Starshield’s military satellite communications, however, still rely on the much larger civilian Starlink constellation. Software separates military communications functions — stronger encryption, protection against electronic warfare, and the ability to bypass restrictions — from civilian functions.
The speed limits were followed by a complete shutdown of all terminals in Ukraine that were not listed in a special Defense Ministry registry. According to sources cited in media reports, Ukraine’s then-defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, reached an agreement with Musk to create this system, cutting off Russian forces’ access to satellite communications through smuggled terminals. The Russian military, which had also come to rely on Starlink for both aerial and ground operations, had to scramble for alternatives. It largely solved the problem, but access to Starlink gave Ukraine’s armed forces an advantage in communications and command that they retain to this day. More on that below.
Now the Trump administration, which, unlike Joe Biden’s administration, does not consider itself obliged to support Ukraine unconditionally, has used this dependence on SpaceX’s services to pressure Kyiv.
- First, Zelensky suspects that the United States deliberately stopped supplying Ukraine with information about Russian ballistic missile launches (Starshield is part of the launch detection system). The White House is also threatening to cut off other intelligence.
- Second, on October 14, speed limits were imposed on Starlink/Starshield terminals used by the Ukrainian military.
According to Ukrainian military personnel and politicians, the speed limit changed over the following 24 hours. Some drones lost their connections for 20 seconds at speeds as low as 60 kilometers per hour (about 37 mph). Finally, former Defense Minister Fedorov said on X that, as of October 15, satellite connections were working reliably at speeds up to 160 kilometers per hour (about 100 mph). He thanked Musk personally for the fix. The SpaceX owner immediately declined to take credit, saying that all Starshield decisions are made by the U.S. Department of War and President Trump himself.
How and why does Ukraine’s military use U.S. satellite communications?
Starlink/Starshield technology has long underpinned Ukraine’s military command system and is deeply integrated into many aspects of the war. Individual infantry units use satellite communications, including units that are effectively surrounded. Many units buy terminals themselves or receive them from volunteers, then register them in the special registry mentioned above. Headquarters at various levels use satellite connections to access shared command systems and coordinate directly with other units.
Ukrainian drones equipped with Starlink terminals operate over the front line as relays, providing connections for other drones and radio-controlled ground vehicles. Another, less common way to control these ground “robots” is to install a terminal directly on each one. Without an airborne relay or a terminal of their own, these vehicles, which have become absolutely indispensable for supplying troops in recent months, cannot be controlled: They almost always operate below the radio horizon of any ground-based communications antenna.
Starlink terminals are also installed on attack drones and other weapons. Starshield communications are essential to Ukraine’s campaign of strikes on Russian forces at medium depth behind the front lines. At least some of the drones attacking Russian transport in occupied territory 50–150 kilometers (about 30–95 miles) from the front — for example, on the highway running along the Sea of Azov toward Crimea — carry Starlink terminals and act as relays for other attack drones. Ukrainian long-range drones equipped with terminals and video cameras have also long been used to strike targets in Crimea.
After the United States introduced the speed limits, Ukrainian sources reported that satellite communications were also being used on a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking on Russian jet-powered drones. In recent months, Russia has used large numbers of these drones to attack targets far behind Ukraine’s front lines. The sources did not specify how the interceptors use these connections.
Before the Trump administration began its latest pressure campaign against Kyiv, Ukraine had been trying to persuade Musk or the Pentagon to enable Starlink service over Russia — naturally, only for terminals held by Ukrainian forces. The idea was to equip long-range drones striking Russia’s rear areas with video cameras so operators could attack mobile targets as well as fixed ones with known coordinates, such as factories, warehouses, and data centers. This would allow Ukrainian forces to strike targets such as Iskander-M ballistic missile launchers and fighter-bombers at air bases.
Kyiv’s request was denied, so Ukrainian long-range drones — apart from those attacking Crimea and other occupied territories — still use inertial navigation systems combined with GPS satellite navigation rather than being controlled by operators.
What would restrictions on Starlink/Starshield use mean for Ukraine?
That depends on the speed limit.
- Cutting off connections at speeds above 160 kilometers per hour (about 100 mph) makes it extremely difficult for drones to strike mobile targets, such as trucks, at medium depth behind the front lines: Attack drones generally fly faster than that. There are ways to adapt, however, such as using slower relay drones. Satellite communications would also become completely unusable on interceptor drones capable of taking on jet-powered drones: These interceptors need to fly several times faster than the limit.
- If the limit is set at 60–80 kilometers per hour (about 37–50 mph), drone operations across the front will be disrupted, including “Baba Yaga” multicopters. Satellite communications terminals will have to be installed on all unmanned ground vehicles, substantially increasing the cost of front-line operations. Ukrainian forces will have to forgo a large share of long-distance FPV drone strikes, which are currently possible mainly thanks to relay drones.
- Finally, a complete shutdown — unlikely, but still possible if the dispute between Trump and Zelensky worsens — would deprive Ukraine’s armed forces of their established communications and command system altogether. This threat means Ukrainian commanders need to start looking for a replacement for Starlink now.
What could the Ukrainian military use instead of Starlink?
No system outside the U.S. administration’s control is available to Ukraine as a direct replacement for Starlink. Its European counterpart, Eutelsat OneWeb, has been through bankruptcy proceedings; EU and British authorities are now working to incorporate the OneWeb constellation, which has 600 satellites in orbit, into a new system called IRIS². Even if the new program goes ahead, it will have less bandwidth than Starlink. It is quite possible that the Chinese systems Guowang and Qianfan will become available to the Russian military before IRIS² becomes available to Ukraine’s military.
However, the Russian military’s experience shows that alternatives to satellite communications exist. Within a few months of the unexpected shutdown of all the smuggled Starlink terminals Russian forces had been using in Ukraine, those forces built a communications system based on mesh networks.
A technology built around computer nodes that can each act as a switch for other devices on the network.
For the military, this means a system of airborne and ground-based communications relays that can be used to control drones tens of kilometers from their operators’ positions.
The Russian military has managed to replace some of the satellite communications provided by smuggled terminals both at the front and on long-range drones. Its mesh system is, of course, inferior to Ukraine’s Starlink-based system: Mesh relays are unevenly distributed among Russian units, and much of their equipment comes from private “volunteers” rather than the Defense Ministry. The ground antennas that act as the network’s main nodes are vulnerable to detection and strikes by Ukrainian forces.
Ukraine has even threatened strikes against Belarus, where, Kyiv says, the Russian military has installed antennas used to control the mesh networks of drones attacking the Ukrainian capital. Even so, mesh networks could serve as a makeshift substitute for a Starlink-based system if satellite communications were cut off completely.

Can either side win on the battlefield? What effect are the Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia having? And will the two sides be willing to negoiate?
Joining us to explain what the Houthi are doing and why, we speak with Maysaa Shujaa al-Deen (@maysaashujaa), senior researcher at the Sanaa Centre (@SanaaCenter).
And to tell us the story of Saudi thinking and calculations we speak with Allison Minor (@AllisonMinor_) senior fellow at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (@CSISMidEast) and the former U.S. Deputy Special Envoy for Yemen.

German chancellor defends Ukraine’s strikes on Russian refineries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-16
17:13:45 UTC
02:13:45 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
16 October 2026•Update: 16 October 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday defended Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries, saying they were justified because they impair Moscow’s ability to wage war.
Speaking to reporters after an EU summit in Brussels, Merz said he sees no readiness on the Russian side, including President Vladimir Putin, to end the conflict. On the contrary, Moscow is trying to escalate the fighting further ahead of winter, he claimed.
“Above all, Ukraine’s entire energy infrastructure is being massively damaged, and its transmission networks are coming under attack. Every effort is being made to make the winter as difficult as possible for the country,” Merz said.
Against that backdrop, “it is, in my view, entirely right, reasonable and understandable for Ukraine to strike targets within Russia that hinder the war effort of the Russian government and the Russian army,” the chancellor added. “This applies to both communications and energy supplies.”
Merz argued that these are obviously the only possibilities Ukraine has to make Russia understand that it is prepared to seriously defend itself.
The chancellor reiterated that Europe and Germany will continue to stand by Ukraine. “But we are not doing it to prolong the war; we are doing it to bring Russia to the negotiating table,” he said.

Russia launched 15 "Banderols" and more than three hundred drones at Ukraine in one day — how many targets were shot down
Kyiv • UNN
Russia attacked Ukraine with 315 attack drones and 15 "Banderols." Air defense destroyed or suppressed 253 UAVs and 9 "Banderols."
Over the course of the day, the Russian army launched 315 attack drones and 15 "Banderol" missiles at Ukraine; Ukrainian forces managed to destroy more than 260 targets, UNN reports, citing the Air Force.
Details
According to the Air Force, during the day on October 16 (from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m.), the enemy attacked Ukraine with 315 attack UAVs (78 of them jet-powered), Gerbera drones and drones of other types, as well as 15 S-8000 "Banderol/Dan-T" missiles.
According to preliminary data, during the specified period, air defense shot down/suppressed 253 UAVs (49 of them jet-powered), as well as 9 S-8000 "Banderol/Dan-T" missiles
In addition
As of 7:00 p.m., about 35 attack drones were still in Ukrainian airspace, the Air Force added.
Groups of attack UAVs over the south of Kharkiv region, the north of Dnipropetrovsk region, the east of Kirovohrad region, the central part of Cherkasy region, the north of Mykolaiv and Odesa regions, as well as the southeast, center, north and west of Vinnytsia region, are moving westward

Sweden to provide Ukraine with over USD 52M ahead of winter
As reported by Ukrinform, Sweden Herald reported this.
“By striking at electricity and heating, among other things, Russia is trying to make the approaching winter unbearable for the Ukrainian people,” Minister for Development Cooperation and Foreign Trade Benjamin Dousa says in a press release.
According to the report, the funds will be used to meet the “most urgent needs” before and during this winter. This includes electricity and heating for Ukrainian households, support for energy and water supply systems, and funding for vital services such as hospitals and schools.
According to the Swedish government, the new support package brings Sweden’s total support for Ukraine since 2022 to around SEK 158 billion (about $15 billion), of which approximately SEK 29.6 billion (about $2.8 billion) is civilian support.

Kyrgyzstan and Türkiye discuss joint investment projects
During the discussions, the parties addressed current issues regarding trade and economic cooperation, as well as specific prospects for implementing joint investment projects.
Daniyar Amangeldiev emphasized that Kyrgyzstan places a high priority on deepening cooperation with Türkiye. Following the meeting, both sides reaffirmed their readiness to foster direct business contacts, support the implementation of planned initiatives, and further strengthen economic ties between Kyrgyzstan and Türkiye.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Friday that U.S. President Donald Trump's harsh remarks about the Ukrainian leadership are aimed at voters ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

"In this difficult geopolitical situation, we share a common vision: the defence of multilateralism, the promotion of peace and our unwavering solidarity with Ukraine," Rangel said.
